title: Scientific Computing
text:
Preface
These notes started as a study guide for CS 111 at UC Santa Barbara and turned into a habit. Whenever I ran into an idea I couldn’t explain from scratch, I wrote it down until I could. Feynman’s test (if you can’t explain something simply, you don’t really understand it) turns out to be a reliable way to find gaps, and research kept turning up new ones in eigenvalue algorithms, iterative solvers, spectral graph methods, and Koopman theory. What you’re reading is a working reference I wrote as a graduate student, mostly for my own use.
Computers were first built for numerical work. A ``computer’’ was originally a person, someone paid to evaluate functions by hand. During the Second World War the U.S. Army employed rooms full of them to produce artillery firing tables, and the backlog was large enough to justify building ENIAC (1945). Among the machine’s first jobs were calculations for thermonuclear weapons design, work in which John von Neumann was closely involved. His 1947 paper with Goldstine laid the foundations of numerical stability analysis. In 1950, Jule Charney’s group used ENIAC to run the first computer weather forecast, a calculation Lewis Fry Richardson had once estimated would take 64,000 people working in concert. Later, the Apollo Guidance Computer navigated to the Moon with a few kilobytes of working memory, and the Cooley–Tukey FFT (1965) cut a core signal-processing computation from \(O(n^2)\) to \(O(n \log n)\).
Most of what follows is linear algebra. Nearly every numerical method works by reducing a nonlinear problem to a sequence of linear ones, because linear problems are the ones we understand best. We know when solutions exist, how sensitive they are to perturbations, and how to compute them reliably. Newton’s method, finite element discretization, PCA, and gradient-based optimization all come down to repeated linearization. Once linear algebra feels familiar, most of the other methods in these notes are easier to follow.
For a more rigorous treatment, start with Principles of Scientific Computing by Bindel and Goodman and G. W. Stewart’s Afternotes on Numerical Analysis. For a broader tour of the literature, the CS 6241 reading list at Cornell is a great place to look. Much of the perspective here comes from CS 210A (Matrix Analysis), taught by Professor Shivkumar Chandrasekaran in the ECE department at UC Santa Barbara. If you get the chance to take it, do.
Aditya Dendukuri \ UC Santa Barbara, 2025

title: 1  Vectors, Coordinates, and Linear Maps
text:
1.1 Span, Independence, and Basis
Scientific computing begins with representation. A physical state, a polynomial, a sampled signal, and an image are different objects, yet each can be represented by a finite list of numbers. The list is useful only after we say what its entries mean. That distinction between an object and its coordinates will matter throughout these notes.
Throughout, \(\fR\), \(\fZ\), and \(\fC\) denote the real numbers, integers, and complex numbers. Most examples use real arithmetic. Complex numbers appear naturally when we study oscillations and eigenvalues.
A spanning list may contain redundant vectors. For example, \((1,1)^T\) adds no new vectors to the span of \((1,0)^T\) and \((0,1)^T\). We need a criterion for detecting this redundancy before using the list as a coordinate system.

title: 1  Vectors, Coordinates, and Linear Maps
text:
NoteDefinition: Linear Combination, Span, and Subspace



Given vectors \(\bv_1,...,\bv_k\), a linear combination is any vector of the form \[
\begin{align}
c_1\bv_1+\cdots+c_k\bv_k.
\end{align}
\] Their span is the set of all such combinations. A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\fR^n\) is a subspace if every linear combination of vectors in \(S\) remains in \(S\).








WarningExercise



Decide which of the following subsets of \(\fR^3\) are subspaces: the plane \(x_1+x_2=0\), the plane \(x_1+x_2=1\), the set of vectors with at least one zero entry, and the span of \((1,1,0)^T\) and \((0,1,1)^T\). For every negative answer, identify a subspace axiom that fails.








NoteExample



The vectors \((1,0,0)^T\) and \((0,1,0)^T\) span the coordinate plane in \(\fR^3\) on which the third coordinate is zero. A plane not passing through the origin is not a subspace: it does not contain \(\bzero\) and is not closed under scalar multiplication.









NoteDefinition: Linear Independence and Basis



Vectors \(\bv_1,...,\bv_k\) are linearly independent if \[
\begin{align}
c_1\bv_1+\cdots+c_k\bv_k=\bzero
\end{align}
\] forces every coefficient \(c_i\) to be zero. A basis of a vector space is a linearly independent spanning set.








NoteTheorem: Exchange, Extension, and Dimension



Let \(V\) be spanned by \(m\) vectors.

Every linearly independent list in \(V\) contains at most \(m\) vectors.
Any linearly independent list can be extended to a basis by adding vectors from a spanning list.
Any two bases of \(V\) contain the same number of vectors. This common number is the dimension of \(V\).









WarningExercise



Prove the referenced result. Begin with a spanning list \(\bw_1,...,\bw_m\) and a nonzero vector \(\bv_1\). Express \(\bv_1\) in the spanning list and replace one \(\bw_j\) having a nonzero coefficient by \(\bv_1\). Show that the new list still spans. Repeat with \(\bv_2,...,\bv_k\), using independence to show that a replaceable old vector always remains. Apply the result in both directions to two bases.








TipRemark



The preceding exercise supplies the replacement argument behind this theorem. This theorem justifies phrases used later such as ``extend a basis of the null space to a basis of the domain.’’








NoteTheorem: A Basis Gives Unique Coordinates



Let \(\bv_1,...,\bv_n\) be a basis of a vector space \(V\). Every \(\bx\in V\) has exactly one representation \[
\begin{align}
\bx=x_1\bv_1+\cdots+x_n\bv_n.
\end{align}
\] The scalars \(x_1,...,x_n\) are the coordinates of \(\bx\) in this basis.








TipProof





We must prove existence and uniqueness separately.

A basis is a spanning list. Consequently, the definition of span gives scalars \(x_1,...,x_n\) such that \(\bx=\sum_i x_i\bv_i\). This establishes at least one coordinate representation.
Suppose another list of scalars gives the same vector: \[
\begin{align}
\bx=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\bv_i,
  \qquad \bx=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\bv_i.
\end{align}
\] Subtract the second equality from the first. Distributivity of scalar multiplication gives \[
\begin{align}
\bzero=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-y_i)\bv_i.
\end{align}
\]
The basis vectors are linearly independent. By the definition of independence, every coefficient in a vanishing linear combination must be zero. Thus \(x_i-y_i=0\) for each \(i\), so the two coordinate lists coincide. Spanning supplied existence, whereas independence supplied uniqueness.










WarningExercise



Let \(p(t)=a+bt+ct^2\). Find its coordinates in the bases \(1,t,t^2\) and \(1,t-1,(t-1)^2\). Construct the matrix that converts the second coordinate vector into the first, and interpret each column.








TipRemark



Coordinates change when the basis changes, but the vector does not. For example, the polynomial \(p(t)=3+2t\) has coordinates \((3,2)^T\) in the basis \(1,t\) and coordinates \((5,2)^T\) in the basis \(1,t-1\). Confusing a vector with one coordinate list is a common source of conceptual errors in change-of-basis and eigenvalue arguments.

title: 1  Vectors, Coordinates, and Linear Maps
text:
1.2 Matrices and Linear Maps






NoteDefinition: Linear Map



A map \(T:V\to W\) is linear if, for all vectors \(\bx,\by\in V\) and scalars \(\alpha,\beta\), \[
\begin{align}
T(\alpha\bx+\beta\by)=\alpha T(\bx)+\beta T(\by).
\end{align}
\] Linearity says that the response to a combination of inputs is the same combination of the individual responses.








NoteDefinition: Matrix



A matrix \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\) is a rectangular array of scalars with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns. It represents a linear map from \(\fR^n\) to \(\fR^m\) once bases have been selected in the domain and range.








NoteTheorem: The Columns Determine the Map



Let \(\be_1,...,\be_n\) be the standard basis of \(\fR^n\), and let \(T:\fR^n\to\fR^m\) be linear. If the \(j\)th column of \(\bA\) is \(\ba_j=T(\be_j)\), then \[
\begin{align}
T(\bx)=\bA\bx=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\ba_j.
\end{align}
\] Thus a linear map is completely determined by what it does to a basis.








TipProof





Write an arbitrary input in the standard basis and apply linearity one operation at a time: \[
\begin{align}
\bx&=x_1\be_1+\cdots+x_n\be_n,\\
T(\bx)&=T(x_1\be_1+\cdots+x_n\be_n)\\
&=T(x_1\be_1)+\cdots+T(x_n\be_n)\\
&=x_1T(\be_1)+\cdots+x_nT(\be_n)\\
&=x_1\ba_1+\cdots+x_n\ba_n.
\end{align}
\] The second line uses preservation of addition. The third uses preservation of scalar multiplication. The final line uses the definition \(\ba_j=T(\be_j)\).
To identify this vector with the usual matrix product, take its \(i\)th entry: \[
\begin{align}
\left(\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\ba_j\right)_i
=\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j=(\bA\bx)_i.
\end{align}
\] The entries agree for every \(i\), so \(T(\bx)=\bA\bx\). In particular, two linear maps that agree on all standard basis vectors agree on every input.









TipRemark



This column view is more informative than memorizing the row-by-column rule. The set of all possible outputs \(\bA\bx\) is the span of the columns. A zero output means that one linear combination of the columns vanishes. Existence and uniqueness for linear systems will grow directly from these two observations.








NoteExample



For \[
\begin{align}
\bA=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&-1\end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \bx=\begin{pmatrix}4\\5\end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
\] the product is best read as \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bx
    =4\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}
     +5\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix}
    =\begin{pmatrix}14\\7\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
\] The same calculation can be read row by row: each output coordinate is a weighted sum of the input coordinates.

title: 1  Vectors, Coordinates, and Linear Maps
text:
1.3 Matrix Products
Composition of linear maps defines the matrix product. If \(\bB\in\fR^{n\times p}\) represents a map from \(\fR^p\) to \(\fR^n\) and \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\) represents a map from \(\fR^n\) to \(\fR^m\), then the composition sends \(\be_j\) first to the \(j\)th column \(\bb_j\) of \(\bB\) and then to \(\bA\bb_j\). By the referenced result, the matrix of the composition therefore has columns \(\bA\bb_1,...,\bA\bb_p\).






NoteDefinition: Matrix Product



For \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\) and \(\bB\in\fR^{n\times p}\), the product \(\bA\bB\in\fR^{m\times p}\) is the matrix with entries \[
\begin{align}
(\bA\bB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^n a_{ik}b_{kj}.
\end{align}
\] Equivalently, the \(j\)th column of \(\bA\bB\) is \(\bA\bb_j\). The product is defined only when the number of columns of \(\bA\) equals the number of rows of \(\bB\).








WarningExercise



For \(\bA=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\bB=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\), compute \(\bA\bB\) and \(\bB\bA\) by entries and by columns. Find a matrix other than a multiple of \(\bI\) that commutes with \(\bA\).


Because the product represents composition, it is associative and distributes over addition. It is not commutative. For \[
\begin{align}
\bA=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \bB=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
    \qquad
    \bA\bB=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\2&0\end{pmatrix}
    \neq
    \begin{pmatrix}0&2\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=\bB\bA.
\end{align}
\] Scaling the coordinates and then exchanging them is a different map from exchanging them and then scaling.
crumbs: 1  Vectors, Coordinates, and Linear Maps

title: 1  Vectors, Coordinates, and Linear Maps
text:
1.4 Transpose and Symmetry






NoteDefinition: Matrix Transpose



The transpose of \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\) is the matrix \(\bA^T\in\fR^{n\times m}\) defined by \[
\begin{align}
(\bA^T)_{ij}=a_{ji}.
\end{align}
\] It turns columns into rows and rows into columns.








NoteDefinition: Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices



A square matrix \(\bA\) is symmetric if \(\bA^T=\bA\) and skew-symmetric if \(\bA^T=-\bA\).








TipRemark



Every square matrix splits uniquely into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts: \[
\begin{align}
\bA=\frac{\bA+\bA^T}{2}+\frac{\bA-\bA^T}{2}.
\end{align}
\] Symmetric matrices will be especially important because they possess real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.








NoteTheorem: Properties of the Transpose



For conformable matrices and any scalar \(\alpha\), \[
\begin{align}
(\bA^T)^T&=\bA,&
    (\bA+\bB)^T&=\bA^T+\bB^T,\\
    (\alpha\bA)^T&=\alpha\bA^T,&
    (\bA\bB)^T&=\bB^T\bA^T.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Prove the first three transpose identities entry by entry. For the product identity, write \(((\bA\bB)^T)_{ij}\) as a sum and identify the same sum in \(\bB^T\bA^T\). Explain why the order of the factors reverses.








NoteCorollary: Reversal Law for Multiple Factors



Repeated use of the product rule gives \[
\begin{align}
(\bA_1\bA_2\cdots\bA_k)^T=\bA_k^T\cdots\bA_2^T\bA_1^T.
\end{align}
\]








NoteCorollary: Outer Product is Symmetric of Rank One



For every nonzero \(\bx\in\fR^n\), the outer product \(\bx\bx^T\) is symmetric and has rank one, meaning its column space has dimension one. Moreover, \[
\begin{align}
\bx^T\bx=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2>0.
\end{align}
\]
crumbs: 1  Vectors, Coordinates, and Linear Maps

title: 1  Vectors, Coordinates, and Linear Maps
text:
1.5 Inverses
A linear map from \(\fR^n\) to itself can be undone exactly when its matrix has an inverse. The inverse is a useful theoretical object, but, as the remark below explains, it is rarely computed.






NoteDefinition: Identity Matrix



The identity matrix \(\bI_n\) has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. It represents the map that leaves every vector unchanged: \(\bI_n\bx=\bx\). We omit the subscript when the dimension is clear. The zero matrix has every entry zero and sends every vector to the zero vector.








WarningExercise



Use the column interpretation of multiplication to prove \(\bI_m\bA=\bA=\bA\bI_n\) for \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\). Why do the two identity matrices have different dimensions when \(m\neq n\)?








NoteDefinition: Matrix Inverse



A square matrix \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) is invertible, or nonsingular, if there is a matrix \(\bA^{-1}\) with \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bA^{-1}=\bA^{-1}\bA=\bI.
\end{align}
\] The inverse is unique. If \(\bB\) and \(\bC\) both satisfy the definition, then \(\bB=\bB(\bA\bC)=(\bB\bA)\bC=\bC\).








NoteTheorem: Properties of the Inverse



Let \(\bA,\bB\in\fR^{n\times n}\) be invertible and let \(\alpha\neq0\). Then \(\bA^{-1}\), \(\bA\bB\), \(\alpha\bA\), and \(\bA^T\) are invertible, with \[
\begin{align}
(\bA^{-1})^{-1}=\bA,
    \qquad
    (\bA\bB)^{-1}=\bB^{-1}\bA^{-1},
    \qquad
    (\alpha\bA)^{-1}=\alpha^{-1}\bA^{-1},
    \qquad
    (\bA^T)^{-1}=(\bA^{-1})^T.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Prove the inverse identities by multiplying each proposed inverse on both sides. For the transpose identity, transpose \(\bA\bA^{-1}=\bI\) and use the reversal law. Which assumption is needed for the scalar identity?








TipRemark



(Factor instead of inverting) Scientific codes almost never form \(\bA^{-1}\). To solve \(\bA\bx=\bb\), they factor \(\bA\) into triangular or orthogonal factors and solve with each factor in turn, which costs less and is more accurate than forming the inverse and multiplying. The reversal law \((\bA\bB)^{-1}=\bB^{-1}\bA^{-1}\) describes this procedure. To solve \(\bA\bB\bx=\bb\), we first solve \(\bA\by=\bb\) and then \(\bB\bx=\by\).

title: 1  Vectors, Coordinates, and Linear Maps
text:
1.6 Further Exercises






WarningExercise



Prove that a list containing the zero vector is dependent. Prove that two nonzero vectors are dependent exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other. Then explain why three vectors in \(\fR^2\) cannot be independent.








WarningExercise



Suppose \(T:\fR^n\to\fR^m\) is linear and \(T(\be_j)=\bzero\) for every standard basis vector. Prove that \(T\) is the zero map. Why is checking only one vector insufficient when \(n>1\)? Would checking a redundant spanning list suffice?








WarningExercise



Write a matrix as both a collection of columns and a collection of rows. Use the two views to explain, without entrywise multiplication, what \(\bA\bx\) and \(\by^T\bA\) mean.








WarningExercise



A square matrix is involutory if \(\bA^2=\bI\). Prove that \(\bA\) is involutory exactly when \(\bA^{-1}=\bA\), and give an involutory \(2\times2\) matrix other than \(\pm\bI\). Interpret your example geometrically.








WarningExercise



Prove the referenced result. In particular, show that every column of \(\bx\bx^T\) is a multiple of \(\bx\), and identify one nonzero column.

title: 2  Inner Products, Geometry, and Norms
text:
2.1 Inner Products and Euclidean Geometry
To compare an approximation with an exact vector, we need to measure their difference. Euclidean length is one possible measurement. The largest coordinate error is another, and the two can rank approximations differently. We begin with the inner product, which defines lengths and perpendicular directions, and use it to find closest points on lines and subspaces. We then study norms that measure length without requiring an inner product.
The Euclidean formula is a familiar example of these axioms. If \(\bx=(x_1,x_2)^T\), then \(\langle\bx,\bx\rangle=x_1^2+x_2^2\) is the square of its length. An inner product allows us to use the same arguments after changing the way directions are weighted. The inequalities below follow from the axioms, so they apply to every such choice.
The square root is chosen so that scaling a vector by \(\alpha\) scales its length by \(|\alpha|\). The triangle inequality is less immediate and follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
crumbs: 2  Inner Products, Geometry, and Norms

title: 2  Inner Products, Geometry, and Norms
text:
NoteDefinition: Real Inner Product



An inner product on \(\fR^n\) is a function \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:\fR^n\times\fR^n\to\fR\) satisfying, for all vectors \(\bx,\by,\bz\) and scalars \(\alpha,\beta\),

Symmetry: \(\langle\bx,\by\rangle=\langle\by,\bx\rangle\).
Linearity: \(\langle\alpha\bx+\beta\by,\bz\rangle=\alpha\langle\bx,\bz\rangle+\beta\langle\by,\bz\rangle\).
Positive definiteness: \(\langle\bx,\bx\rangle\geq0\), with equality if and only if \(\bx=\bzero\).

The standard Euclidean inner product is \[
\begin{align}
\langle\bx,\by\rangle_2=\bx^T\by=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



For \(\bx=(1,2)^T\) and \(\by=(2,-1)^T\), compute \(\langle\bx,\by\rangle_2\). Verify the three axioms for the Euclidean inner product. Next replace it by \(\langle\bx,\by\rangle_W=4x_1y_1+x_2y_2\). Are these two vectors still orthogonal in the new inner product?









NoteDefinition: Norm Induced by an Inner Product



Every inner product defines a norm by \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|=\sqrt{\langle\bx,\bx\rangle}.
\end{align}
\] For the Euclidean inner product this gives \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_2=\sqrt{\bx^T\bx}.
\end{align}
\]









NoteTheorem: Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality



For every real inner product and all vectors \(\bx,\by\), \[
\begin{align}
|\langle\bx,\by\rangle|\leq\|\bx\|\,\|\by\|.
\end{align}
\] Equality holds if and only if \(\bx\) and \(\by\) are linearly dependent.








TipProof





If \(\by=\bzero\), both \(|\langle\bx,\by\rangle|\) and \(\|\bx\|\|\by\|\) are zero. Hence the claim holds in that case. Suppose now that \(\by\neq\bzero\), so \(\langle\by,\by\rangle>0\).

For every real scalar \(t\), positive definiteness gives \(\langle\bx-t\by,\bx-t\by\rangle\geq0\). Expand using linearity and symmetry: \[
\begin{align}
0\leq\|\bx\|^2-2t\langle\bx,\by\rangle+t^2\|\by\|^2.
\end{align}
\]
Set \(t=\langle\bx,\by\rangle/\|\by\|^2\). The denominator is positive. Substitution gives \[
\begin{align}
0\leq\|\bx\|^2-\frac{\langle\bx,\by\rangle^2}{\|\by\|^2}.
\end{align}
\] Multiply by \(\|\by\|^2\) and take nonnegative square roots. This yields \(|\langle\bx,\by\rangle|\leq\|\bx\|\|\by\|\).
Equality holds precisely when \(\|\bx-t\by\|^2=0\). Positive definiteness makes this equivalent to \(\bx=t\by\). Thus equality occurs precisely for linearly dependent vectors, including the zero-vector cases.










NoteCorollary: Triangle Inequality for an Inner-Product Norm



For all vectors \(\bx\) and \(\by\), \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx+\by\|\leq\|\bx\|+\|\by\|.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Expand \(\|\bx+\by\|^2\), bound the cross term using Cauchy–Schwarz, and take square roots. When does equality hold? Treat the case in which one vector is zero separately.








NoteDefinition: Angle and Orthogonality



For nonzero vectors \(\bx\) and \(\by\), their angle \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\) is defined by \[
\begin{align}
\cos\theta=\frac{\langle\bx,\by\rangle}{\|\bx\|\,\|\by\|}.
\end{align}
\] Cauchy–Schwarz guarantees that the right-hand side lies in \([-1,1]\). The vectors are orthogonal, written \(\bx\perp\by\), when \(\langle\bx,\by\rangle=0\).








NoteTheorem: Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse



For vectors \(\bx\) and \(\by\) in a real inner-product space, \[
\begin{align}
\bx\perp\by
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \|\bx+\by\|^2=\|\bx\|^2+\|\by\|^2.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Expand \(\langle\bx+\by,\bx+\by\rangle\) and prove both directions of the stated equivalence. Explain where the assumption of a real inner product is used.

title: 2  Inner Products, Geometry, and Norms
text:
2.3 Vector Norms
An inner product supplies both length and angle. A norm keeps only the notion of length. This weaker structure is enough for error bounds and convergence, even when no meaningful angle is available.






NoteDefinition: Vector Norm



A function \(\|\cdot\|:\fR^n\to\fR\) is a vector norm if, for all vectors \(\bx,\by\) and scalars \(\alpha\),

\(\|\bx\|\geq0\), with equality if and only if \(\bx=\bzero\).
\(\|\alpha\bx\|=|\alpha|\|\bx\|\).
\(\|\bx+\by\|\leq\|\bx\|+\|\by\|\).









NoteDefinition: The Standard \(1\)-, \(2\)-, and Infinity Norms



For \(\bx\in\fR^n\), \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_1&=\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|,
  &
  \|\bx\|_2&=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right)^{1/2},
  &
  \|\bx\|_\infty&=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i|.
\end{align}
\] More generally, for \(1\leq p<\infty\), \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_p=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^p\right)^{1/p}.
\end{align}
\]


For an exact vector \(\bx\) and an approximation \(\hat{\bx}\), the absolute error in a chosen norm is \(\|\hat{\bx}-\bx\|\). If \(\bx\neq\bzero\), its relative error is \(\|\hat{\bx}-\bx\|/\|\bx\|\). The norm and scale must be stated together. An error of one unit may be small in one application and unacceptable in another.
Each norm answers a different question. The \(1\)-norm measures total magnitude across coordinates. The \(2\)-norm measures Euclidean energy. The infinity norm measures the largest coordinate error. A tolerance stated without a norm is therefore incomplete.






NoteExample



Let \(\bx=(1,1,1,1)^T\) and \(\by=(4,0,0,0)^T\). Both vectors satisfy \(\|\bx\|_1=\|\by\|_1=4\), but \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_2=2,
  \qquad
  \|\by\|_2=4,
  \qquad
  \|\bx\|_\infty=1,
  \qquad
  \|\by\|_\infty=4.
\end{align}
\] The vectors have the same total magnitude, but one distributes it evenly and the other concentrates it in one coordinate. No single norm measures every interpretation of size.








NoteTheorem: Sharp Comparisons of the Standard Norms



For every \(\bx\in\fR^n\), \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_\infty
  \leq\|\bx\|_2
  \leq\|\bx\|_1
  \leq\sqrt{n}\,\|\bx\|_2
  \leq n\|\bx\|_\infty.
\end{align}
\] The factors \(\sqrt n\) and \(n\) cannot be replaced by smaller constants that work for every vector.








TipProof





We prove all four comparisons and show that their constants are attained.

Choose \(k\) with \(|x_k|=\|\bx\|_\infty\). Then \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_\infty^2=x_k^2\leq\sum_i x_i^2=\|\bx\|_2^2.
\end{align}
\] Taking square roots gives \(\|\bx\|_\infty\leq\|\bx\|_2\). Also \(|x_i|\leq\|\bx\|_\infty\) for every \(i\), so \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_2^2=\sum_i|x_i|^2\leq n\|\bx\|_\infty^2.
\end{align}
\]
To compare the \(1\)- and \(2\)-norms, expand \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_1^2
  =\sum_i|x_i|^2+2\sum_{i<j}|x_i||x_j|
  \geq\sum_i|x_i|^2=\|\bx\|_2^2.
\end{align}
\] For the reverse estimate, apply Cauchy–Schwarz to \((|x_1|,...,|x_n|)^T\) and the all-ones vector: \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_1=\sum_i|x_i|\leq\sqrt{\sum_i|x_i|^2}\sqrt{\sum_i1^2}
  =\sqrt n\|\bx\|_2.
\end{align}
\]
For a coordinate vector, all three norms equal one, so neither lower comparison can have a larger constant. For the all-ones vector, the three norms are \(1\), \(\sqrt n\), and \(n\). Thus neither factor \(\sqrt n\) in the upper comparisons can be reduced.










WarningExercise



Prove the remaining comparisons in the referenced result. For \(\|\bx\|_2\leq\|\bx\|_1\), expand the square of the right side. For \(\|\bx\|_\infty\leq\|\bx\|_2\), select an entry of largest magnitude. Use a coordinate vector and the all-ones vector to show that the constants cannot be improved. Find all equality cases in \(\|\bx\|_1\leq\sqrt n\|\bx\|_2\).








NoteTheorem: Equivalence of Norms in Fixed Finite Dimension



For any two norms \(\|\cdot\|_\alpha\) and \(\|\cdot\|_\beta\) on \(\fR^n\), there are constants \(c,C>0\) such that \[
\begin{align}
c\|\bx\|_\beta\leq\|\bx\|_\alpha\leq C\|\bx\|_\beta
  \qquad\text{for every }\bx\in\fR^n.
\end{align}
\] Consequently, the two norms define the same convergent sequences on a fixed \(\fR^n\).








TipProof





We first compare one arbitrary norm with the Euclidean norm. Let \(\be_1,...,\be_n\) be the coordinate vectors and define the finite constant \[
\begin{align}
C_\alpha=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\|\be_i\|_\alpha^2\right)^{1/2}.
\end{align}
\] Writing \(\bx=\sum_i x_i\be_i\), and applying the triangle inequality followed by scalar Cauchy–Schwarz, gives \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx\|_\alpha
&\leq\sum_i\|x_i\be_i\|_\alpha
=\sum_i|x_i|\|\be_i\|_\alpha\\
&\leq\left(\sum_i|x_i|^2\right)^{1/2}
       \left(\sum_i\|\be_i\|_\alpha^2\right)^{1/2}
=C_\alpha\|\bx\|_2.
\end{align}
\] This provides an upper bound without assuming continuity of the arbitrary norm.
The triangle inequality also gives \(\|\bx\|_\alpha\leq\|\by\|_\alpha+\|\bx-\by\|_\alpha\). Interchange \(\bx\) and \(\by\) and combine the two inequalities: \[
\begin{align}
|\|\bx\|_\alpha-\|\by\|_\alpha|
\leq\|\bx-\by\|_\alpha\leq C_\alpha\|\bx-\by\|_2.
\end{align}
\] Thus Euclidean-close vectors have close \(\alpha\)-norms. This establishes continuity in the Euclidean coordinates.
The Euclidean unit sphere is closed and bounded, hence compact in finite dimensions. A continuous real function on a compact set attains its minimum and maximum. Let those values of \(\|\cdot\|_\alpha\) be \(m_\alpha\) and \(M_\alpha\). The attained minimum cannot be zero: a vector attaining it is on the unit sphere and is nonzero, while positive definiteness makes its \(\alpha\)-norm positive. Hence \(m_\alpha>0\).
For \(\bx\neq\bzero\), the vector \(\bx/\|\bx\|_2\) lies on that sphere. Homogeneity gives \[
\begin{align}
m_\alpha\leq\frac{\|\bx\|_\alpha}{\|\bx\|_2}\leq M_\alpha.
\end{align}
\] Apply the same reasoning to the \(\beta\)-norm. The inequalities \(\|\bx\|_\beta\leq M_\beta\|\bx\|_2\) and \(m_\beta\|\bx\|_2\leq\|\bx\|_\beta\) then give \[
\begin{align}
\frac{m_\alpha}{M_\beta}\|\bx\|_\beta
\leq\|\bx\|_\alpha
\leq\frac{M_\alpha}{m_\beta}\|\bx\|_\beta.
\end{align}
\] Both constants are positive and independent of \(\bx\). The zero vector satisfies the same inequalities because every term is zero.









TipRemark



(Equivalent does not mean interchangeable) Norm equivalence says that convergence in one norm implies convergence in another when the dimension is fixed. It does not say that the numerical values or bounds are equally useful. The comparison constants may grow with \(n\). A bound containing \(\sqrt n\) may be harmless for ten unknowns and useless for ten million.


The \(2\)-norm is induced by an inner product. The \(1\)- and infinity norms are not. The difference is visible in the geometry of their unit balls and in a simple algebraic identity.






NoteTheorem: Parallelogram Identity



Every norm induced by an inner product satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\|\bx+\by\|^2+\|\bx-\by\|^2
  =2\|\bx\|^2+2\|\by\|^2.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



A norm without angles. Use the parallelogram identity to prove that neither \(\|\cdot\|_1\) nor \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) on \(\fR^2\) can be induced by an inner product. Explain which step of the projection argument fails when only a general norm is available.








WarningExercise



Expand the two squared norms and add. Which cross terms cancel? Use the identity to recover \(\langle\bx,\by\rangle\) from the three lengths \(\|\bx+\by\|\), \(\|\bx\|\), and \(\|\by\|\).








NoteExample



Take \(\bx=(1,0)^T\) and \(\by=(0,1)^T\). For the \(1\)-norm, the left side of the parallelogram identity equals \(2^2+2^2=8\), while the right side equals \(2+2=4\). Thus the \(1\)-norm cannot come from any inner product. The same test shows that the infinity norm is not induced by an inner product.








NoteDefinition: Weighted Inner Product



Let \(\bW\in\fR^{n\times n}\) be symmetric and satisfy \(\bx^T\bW\bx>0\) for every nonzero \(\bx\). Then \[
\begin{align}
\langle\bx,\by\rangle_{\bW}=\bx^T\bW\by,
  \qquad
  \|\bx\|_{\bW}=\sqrt{\bx^T\bW\bx}
\end{align}
\] define an inner product and its induced norm.








WarningExercise



Weighted geometry. Let \[
\begin{align}
\bW=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
\] Verify the inner-product axioms for \(\langle\bx,\by\rangle_{\bW}\). Sketch the unit ball \(\|\bx\|_{\bW}=1\), find the \(\bW\)-orthogonal complement of \((1,1)^T\), and compute the \(\bW\)-orthogonal projection of \((1,0)^T\) onto the line spanned by \((1,1)^T\).


A weighted inner product changes the geometry in which lengths and angles are measured. Directions with large quadratic weight are expensive, and directions with small weight are cheap. In a finite-element method the weight may represent physical energy. In statistics it may account for unequal uncertainty. In optimization it may encode local curvature. The chapter on positive definite matrices develops this geometry further.

title: 3  Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers
text:
3.1 Induced Matrix Norms
A matrix changes the size of a vector. To bound the effect of an error in the input, we need the largest possible ratio between output length and input length. This ratio defines the induced matrix norm. We distinguish it from the Frobenius norm, which measures the entries of a matrix as data.
An invertible matrix may stretch one direction and compress another. Solving a system reverses that action. The condition number compares the largest stretch with the smallest and will explain why a small residual can accompany a large solution error.
The quotient is unchanged when \(\bx\) is rescaled, so only directions matter. Restricting to the unit sphere removes the irrelevant magnitude. In finite dimensions the unit sphere is compact and the objective is continuous, so the maximum is attained.
The second expression follows by squaring the output norm. It already shows why \(\bA^T\bA\) appears in questions about Euclidean amplification. Once the singular value decomposition is available, the referenced result proves the computable formula \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_2=\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\bA^T\bA)}=\sigma_{\max}(\bA).
\end{align}
\]
crumbs: 3  Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers

title: 3  Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers
text:
NoteDefinition: Induced Operator Norm



Let \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{in}}\) be a norm on \(\fR^n\) and let \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{out}}\) be a norm on \(\fR^m\). For \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\), the induced operator norm is \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|
  =\sup_{\bx\neq\bzero}
  \frac{\|\bA\bx\|_{\mathrm{out}}}{\|\bx\|_{\mathrm{in}}}
  =\max_{\|\bx\|_{\mathrm{in}}=1}\|\bA\bx\|_{\mathrm{out}}.
\end{align}
\] When the same \(p\)-norm is used in the domain and range, we write \(\|\bA\|_p\).








WarningExercise



For \(\bA=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), compare \(\|\bA\bx\|_2/\|\bx\|_2\) for \(\bx=(1,1)^T\) and \(\bx=(1,-1)^T\). Find the largest ratio by expanding \(\|\bA\bx\|_2^2\). Explain why neither one test vector nor the largest matrix entry determines the induced norm.









NoteTheorem: Fundamental Properties of Induced Norms



For compatible matrices and vectors,

Consistency: \(\|\bA\bx\|\leq\|\bA\|\,\|\bx\|\).
Submultiplicativity: \(\|\bA\bB\|\leq\|\bA\|\,\|\bB\|\).
Identity: \(\|\bI\|=1\).
Norm axioms: the induced norm is positive definite, absolutely homogeneous, and satisfies the triangle inequality.









TipProof





We verify each assertion from the definition. All norms on intermediate vector spaces must be compatible, so the output norm for \(\bB\) is the input norm for \(\bA\).

If \(\bx=\bzero\), the inequality reads \(0\leq0\). Otherwise the quotient \(\|\bA\bx\|/\|\bx\|\) is one of the values bounded by the supremum defining \(\|\bA\|\). Multiplication by \(\|\bx\|>0\) gives the result.
For any unit vector \(\bx\), apply consistency twice: \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bB\bx\|\leq\|\bA\|\|\bB\bx\|
  \leq\|\bA\|\|\bB\|\|\bx\|=\|\bA\|\|\bB\|.
\end{align}
\] The right side does not depend on \(\bx\). Taking the maximum over unit inputs proves submultiplicativity.
When the same norm is used on input and output, \(\|\bI\bx\|/\|\bx\|=1\) for every nonzero input. Its supremum is therefore one.
Every quotient is nonnegative. If \(\bA=\bzero\), all quotients vanish. Conversely, if \(\|\bA\|=0\), consistency gives \(\bA\be_j=\bzero\) for each coordinate vector. These are exactly the columns of \(\bA\), so \(\bA=\bzero\).
For \(\|\bx\|=1\), \(\|\alpha\bA\bx\|=|\alpha|\|\bA\bx\|\). Taking maxima yields \(\|\alpha\bA\|=|\alpha|\|\bA\|\).
For every unit input, \[
\begin{align}
\|(\bA+\bB)\bx\|\leq\|\bA\bx\|+\|\bB\bx\|
  \leq\|\bA\|+\|\bB\|.
\end{align}
\] Taking the maximum gives \(\|\bA+\bB\|\leq\|\bA\|+\|\bB\|\).










WarningExercise



Submultiplicativity from amplification. Prove \(\|\bA_1\cdots\bA_k\|\leq\prod_{j=1}^k\|\bA_j\|\). Explain why this bound may be conservative when the direction of greatest stretch for one factor is not mapped into the direction of greatest stretch for the next.








NoteExample



For the diagonal matrix \[
\begin{align}
\bD=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
\] the Euclidean unit circle is sent to an ellipse with semiaxis lengths \(4\) and \(1/2\). Hence \(\|\bD\|_2=4\). The norm records the greatest stretch, not the average stretch and not the largest entry by convention. In this example those quantities happen to agree because the coordinate axes are the stretching directions.








NoteTheorem: The Induced \(1\)- and Infinity Norms



For \(\bA=(a_{ij})\in\fR^{m\times n}\), \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_1
  &=\max_{1\leq j\leq n}\sum_{i=1}^m|a_{ij}|,
  &
  \|\bA\|_\infty
  &=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\sum_{j=1}^n|a_{ij}|.
\end{align}
\] Thus the induced \(1\)-norm is the largest absolute column sum, while the induced infinity norm is the largest absolute row sum.








TipProof





For each formula we need an upper bound for every input and an input that attains it.
Let \(C=\max_j\sum_i|a_{ij}|\), the largest absolute column sum. Expanding each output entry and using the triangle inequality gives \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bx\|_1
&=\sum_{i=1}^m\left|\sum_{j=1}^na_{ij}x_j\right|\\
&\leq\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n|a_{ij}||x_j|\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^n|x_j|\left(\sum_{i=1}^m|a_{ij}|\right)
\leq C\sum_{j=1}^n|x_j|=C\|\bx\|_1.
\end{align}
\] The interchange of sums is legitimate because both are finite. For unit inputs this proves \(\|\bA\|_1\leq C\).
Choose a column \(j_*\) attaining \(C\). The input \(\be_{j_*}\) has \(1\)-norm one, and multiplying by it selects that column. Therefore \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\be_{j_*}\|_1=\sum_i|a_{ij_*}|=C.
\end{align}
\] The maximum is at least \(C\), so the upper bound is exact.
For the infinity norm, put \(R=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|\). For any input, \[
\begin{align}
|(\bA\bx)_i|
&\leq\sum_j|a_{ij}||x_j|
\leq\left(\sum_j|a_{ij}|\right)\|\bx\|_\infty
\leq R\|\bx\|_\infty.
\end{align}
\] This holds for every row, so taking their maximum gives \(\|\bA\|_\infty\leq R\).
Choose a maximizing row \(i_*\). Set \(x_j=1\) when \(a_{i_*j}\geq0\) and \(x_j=-1\) when \(a_{i_*j}<0\). In particular choose \(1\) for a zero entry, so the input has infinity norm one even for the zero matrix. Each product in that row is \(a_{i_*j}x_j=|a_{i_*j}|\). Thus \((\bA\bx)_{i_*}=R\), proving attainment and the second formula.









WarningExercise



Three induced norms. For \[
\begin{align}
\bA=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\3&4\end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
\] compute \(\|\bA\|_1\) and \(\|\bA\|_\infty\). Estimate \(\|\bA\|_2\) from below by testing at least four unit vectors and from above using \(\|\bA\|_F\).








NoteDefinition: The Induced Euclidean Norm



The induced Euclidean norm is \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_2
  =\max_{\|\bx\|_2=1}\|\bA\bx\|_2.
\end{align}
\] Equivalently, \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_2^2
  =\max_{\|\bx\|_2=1}\bx^T\bA^T\bA\bx.
\end{align}
\]









NoteTheorem: Orthogonal Transformations Have Unit Euclidean Norm



If \(\bQ^T\bQ=\bI\), then \[
\begin{align}
\|\bQ\bx\|_2=\|\bx\|_2
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \|\bQ\|_2=1.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Compute \(\|\bQ\bx\|_2^2\) using \(\bQ^T\bQ=\bI\). Then take the maximum over unit vectors. Does the argument require \(\bQ\) to be square?

title: 3  Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers
text:
3.2 Dual Norms
An inner product turns a vector \(\by\) into the linear measurement \(\bx\mapsto\by^T\bx\). The dual norm measures the largest value of this measurement on the unit ball.






NoteDefinition: Dual Norm



For a norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on \(\fR^n\), its dual norm is \[
\begin{align}
\|\by\|_*
  =\max_{\|\bx\|=1}|\by^T\bx|.
\end{align}
\] Consequently, \[
\begin{align}
|\by^T\bx|\leq\|\by\|_*\|\bx\|.
\end{align}
\]








NoteTheorem: Duals of the Standard Norms



The Euclidean norm is self-dual. The \(1\)- and infinity norms are dual to one another: \[
\begin{align}
\|\by\|_{2,*}=\|\by\|_2,
  \qquad
  \|\by\|_{1,*}=\|\by\|_\infty,
  \qquad
  \|\by\|_{\infty,*}=\|\by\|_1.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





For a dual norm, an upper estimate alone is insufficient. We must also find a unit vector attaining that estimate. If \(\by=\bzero\), every claimed norm is zero. Assume below that \(\by\neq\bzero\).

For \(\|\bx\|_2=1\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(|\by^T\bx|\leq\|\by\|_2\). Choose \(\bx=\by/\|\by\|_2\). It is a unit vector, and \(\by^T\bx=\|\by\|_2\). Hence the maximum is exactly \(\|\by\|_2\).
For \(\|\bx\|_1=1\), \[
\begin{align}
|\by^T\bx|\leq\sum_i|y_i||x_i|
  \leq(\max_i|y_i|)\sum_i|x_i|=\|\by\|_\infty.
\end{align}
\] Choose an index \(j\) of largest \(|y_j|\) and set \(\bx=\operatorname{sign}(y_j)\be_j\). Its \(1\)-norm is one and \(\by^T\bx=|y_j|=\|\by\|_\infty\).
For \(\|\bx\|_\infty=1\), \[
\begin{align}
|\by^T\bx|\leq\sum_i|y_i||x_i|\leq\sum_i|y_i|=\|\by\|_1.
\end{align}
\] Set \(x_i=1\) if \(y_i\geq0\) and \(x_i=-1\) if \(y_i<0\). Then \(\|\bx\|_\infty=1\) and every product \(y_ix_i\) equals \(|y_i|\). Thus equality is attained.




Dual norms explain why the norm used for a residual determines the norm that appears in the corresponding linear functional. They also explain the row-sum and column-sum formulas above. The transpose interchanges inputs with linear measurements, giving the useful identity \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_1=\|\bA^T\|_\infty.
\end{align}
\]
crumbs: 3  Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers

title: 3  Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers
text:
3.3 The Frobenius Norm
Matrices themselves form a vector space. When a matrix is being treated as data rather than as an operator, the natural Euclidean measurement is entrywise.






NoteDefinition: Frobenius Inner Product and Norm



For matrices \(\bA,\bB\in\fR^{m\times n}\), the Frobenius inner product is \[
\begin{align}
\langle\bA,\bB\rangle_F
  =\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}b_{ij}
  =\operatorname{trace}(\bA^T\bB).
\end{align}
\] Its induced norm is \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_F
  =\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}^2\right)^{1/2}.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Frobenius geometry. Verify the inner-product axioms for \(\langle\bA,\bB\rangle_F\). Prove the matrix Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(|\langle\bA,\bB\rangle_F|\leq\|\bA\|_F\|\bB\|_F\) by treating the entries as vectors.








TipRemark



(Two different questions) The Frobenius norm measures the collective size of the entries. The induced \(2\)-norm measures the largest amplification of a vector. Both are useful, but they answer different questions. Calling both a ``matrix norm’’ does not make them interchangeable.








NoteTheorem: Bounds Relating Frobenius and Operator Norms



For \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\), \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_2\leq\|\bA\|_F\leq\sqrt n\,\|\bA\|_2.
\end{align}
\] For compatible matrices \(\bA\) and \(\bB\), \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bB\|_F\leq\|\bA\|_2\|\bB\|_F.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Let \(\ba_i^T\) denote row \(i\) of \(\bA\). For \(\|\bx\|_2=1\), each output entry is \(\ba_i^T\bx\). Cauchy–Schwarz applies separately in each row: \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bx\|_2^2
=\sum_{i=1}^m|\ba_i^T\bx|^2
\leq\sum_{i=1}^m\|\ba_i\|_2^2\|\bx\|_2^2
=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2=\|\bA\|_F^2.
\end{align}
\] Taking the maximum over unit \(\bx\) and then square roots gives \(\|\bA\|_2\leq\|\bA\|_F\).
For the opposite comparison, use columns instead of rows. Column \(j\) is \(\bA\be_j\), and \(\|\be_j\|_2=1\). Consistency gives \(\|\bA\be_j\|_2\leq\|\bA\|_2\). Summing the squared estimates over all \(n\) columns yields \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_F^2=\sum_{j=1}^n\|\bA\be_j\|_2^2
\leq\sum_{j=1}^n\|\bA\|_2^2=n\|\bA\|_2^2.
\end{align}
\] The nonnegative square root gives the factor \(\sqrt n\).
Finally let \(\bB\in\fR^{n\times k}\) have columns \(\bb_1,...,\bb_k\). Column \(j\) of the product is \(\bA\bb_j\). Apply consistency to each such column before summing: \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bB\|_F^2
&=\sum_{j=1}^k\|\bA\bb_j\|_2^2\\
&\leq\sum_{j=1}^k\|\bA\|_2^2\|\bb_j\|_2^2\\
&=\|\bA\|_2^2\|\bB\|_F^2.
\end{align}
\] Taking square roots proves the product estimate. The dimensions \(n\) and \(k\) enter only through the corresponding sums over columns.

title: 4  Floating Point Arithmetic
text:
4.1 Floating Point Representation
Digital computers store only finitely many real numbers. Even when a formula is exact on paper, its implementation rounds intermediate results to this finite set. We need to determine the size of one rounding error before studying how an algorithm propagates many of them.
Floating-point arithmetic is usually accurate locally, since one elementary operation is rounded to a nearby representable number. Instability appears when an algorithm repeatedly amplifies these tiny local errors, or when it subtracts nearly equal quantities and exposes digits that were already contaminated by rounding.
In binary floating-point arithmetic, a normalized number is stored in the form \(x=(-1)^s(1.f)_2\,2^e\). The subscript \(2\) means that the digits after the point represent powers \(2^{-1},2^{-2},...\). IEEE 754 specifies common formats and rounding rules. The fields have the following roles.
The exponent controls scale and the significand controls precision. This means floating-point numbers have roughly fixed relative spacing, not fixed absolute spacing. There are many representable numbers near zero and far fewer, in absolute terms, near \(10^{100}\). The gap between adjacent numbers near \(x\) is proportional to \(|x|\).

title: 4  Floating Point Arithmetic
text:
s: Sign bit, determining whether the number is positive or negative.
f: Fractional significand (mantissa). The leading 1 is implicit to maximize precision.
e: Unbiased exponent. The stored exponent field adds a fixed bias to \(e\); reserved fields encode zeros, subnormals, infinities, and NaNs.








TipRemark



(IEEE 754 Standards)

Single (32-bit): 1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 fraction bits.
Double (64-bit): 1 sign, 11 exponent, 52 fraction bits.









NoteExample



A binary16 number has one sign bit, five exponent bits, and ten fraction bits. The exponent bias is \(15\). To store \(-3.25\), we compute the fields as follows.

\(s=1\).
\(3.25_{10} = 11.01_2 = 1.101_2 \times 2^1\).
\(e = 1+15 = 16 = 10000_2\).
\(f = 1010000000_2\).

Result: 1 10000 1010000000.








WarningExercise




Encode \(+5.5\) in 16-bit format.
How many distinct normalized numbers for 5 exp bits, 10 frac bits?









NoteDefinition: Machine Epsilon (\(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}\))



Machine epsilon is the distance from \(1\) to the next larger floating-point number. It is a spacing, rather than the threshold at which an increment first changes a rounded sum. It characterizes the spacing of representable numbers near \(1\) and is given by \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} = 2^{1-p}\), where \(p\) is the number of bits in the significand.

For double precision (64-bit), \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} \approx 2.22 \times 10^{-16}\).









TipRemark



(Spacing rule) Near a normalized number \(x\), the distance to the next representable number is approximately \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}|x|\). Near \(10^{16}\), the gap is on the order of \(1\), whereas near \(1\), the gap is on the order of \(10^{-16}\). This explains why adding a small number to a sufficiently large number has no effect.








NoteTheorem: Absorption Criterion



Let \(x\) be a representable number with two finite neighbors. In round-to-nearest arithmetic, if \(|y|\) is less than half the smaller of the two distances from \(x\) to its neighbors, then \[
\begin{align}
\operatorname{fl}(x+y)=x.
\end{align}
\] Equivalently, small increments disappear when they are below the local resolution of the floating-point grid.








WarningExercise




Use the referenced result to predict whether 1.0 + 1e-16 and 1.0 + 2e-16 differ from 1.0. Then test the prediction in Python.
Find \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}\) empirically via loop.
Use the referenced result to predict the smallest power of \(10\) for which 1e16 + 10**k changes 1e16.
Explain why the answer changes if 1e16 is replaced by 1.0.









NoteDefinition: Unit Roundoff (\(u\))



Unit roundoff bounds the relative error caused by rounding a nonzero real number within the normalized range to the nearest floating-point number: \[
\begin{align}
\frac{|\text{fl}(x) - x|}{|x|} \leq u.
\end{align}
\] For round-to-nearest arithmetic, \(u = \varepsilon_{\text{mach}}/2 = 2^{-p}\).








TipRemark



(Machine epsilon vs. unit roundoff) \(\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}\) is a spacing near \(1\). The unit roundoff \(u\) is an error bound for rounding to nearest. Many texts use ``machine epsilon’’ for both quantities, so always check the convention. In these notes, elementary rounding errors are bounded by \(u\).








NoteTheorem: Fundamental Axiom



Suppose the exact result \(a\circ b\) is finite, nonzero, and lies in the normalized floating-point range. In round-to-nearest arithmetic, \[
\begin{align}
\operatorname{fl}(a\circ b)=(a\circ b)(1+\delta),
    \qquad |\delta|\leq u,
\end{align}
\] for \(\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}\). Overflow and gradual underflow require separate absolute-error models.








TipProof





Assume rounding to nearest, and exclude overflow and the subnormal range as in the theorem. It suffices to consider \(|x|\), because the representable numbers and rounding rule are symmetric about zero.

Choose the integer \(e\) such that \(2^e\leq|x|<2^{e+1}\). In this interval, changing the last stored significand bit changes the value by \(s=2^{e+1-p}\). Thus consecutive representable normalized values are separated by \(s\).
Rounding to nearest selects one of the two representable values surrounding \(|x|\). Its distance is at most half their separation. Therefore \[
\begin{align}
|\operatorname{fl}(x)-x|\leq\frac{s}{2}=2^{e-p}.
\end{align}
\] At an exactly representable value the error is zero, which also satisfies this bound.
Since \(|x|\geq2^e>0\), \[
\begin{align}
\frac{|\operatorname{fl}(x)-x|}{|x|}
  \leq\frac{2^{e-p}}{2^e}=2^{-p}=u.
\end{align}
\] Define \(\delta=(\operatorname{fl}(x)-x)/x\). Then \(\operatorname{fl}(x)=x(1+\delta)\) and \(|\delta|\leq u\). For \(x=0\), take \(\delta=0\).










TipRemark



(Accumulation of rounding errors) A sequence of \(n\) benign operations often produces an error proportional to \(nu\) when \(nu\ll1\). The rule is a heuristic. Cancellation and ill-conditioning can amplify the perturbations well beyond \(nu\). Operation order matters because every intermediate result is rounded.








WarningExercise



Let \(x=1\) and \(y=1-10^{-12}\) be exact real data, and let \(\hat x\) and \(\hat y\) be their rounded values. Distinguish the error made when subtracting \(\hat x-\hat y\) from the error caused by rounding \(x\) and \(y\) before subtraction. Which error does the fundamental rounding model bound? Estimate the amplification of the operand errors relative to \(x-y\).

title: 4  Floating Point Arithmetic
text:
4.2 IEEE 754 Special Values

Signed Zero: \(+0, -0\). \(1/(+0) = \infty\), \(1/(-0) = -\infty\).
Subnormals: Fill the gap between 0 and the smallest normalized number. Reduced precision, allows gradual underflow.
Infinities: \(\pm\infty\). Result of overflow or \(x/0\).
NaN: Not a Number (\(0/0\), \(\infty-\infty\)). Unequal to everything, including itself.







TipRemark



(NaN propagation) A NaN usually contaminates all later arithmetic. This behavior helps with debugging, because the NaN marks an invalid operation that happened earlier even if the failure is observed much later.








WarningExercise




Using NumPy scalars, compare np.float64(1.0)/np.float64(0.0) with division by np.float64(-0.0). Explain the warnings and the signs of the results. (Python’s built-in float division raises ZeroDivisionError instead.)
Evaluate float('inf') - float('inf') and float('nan') == float('nan').

title: 4  Floating Point Arithmetic
text:
4.3 Arithmetic Pitfalls
Because floating-point numbers are discrete, the standard laws of algebra do not always hold. In particular, operations are neither associative nor distributive in general.

Non-Associativity: The order of operations can change the result, i.e., \((a+b)+c \neq a+(b+c)\).
Non-Distributivity: \(a(b+c) \neq ab + ac\).
Absorption: If \(|a|\) is much larger than \(|b|\), then \(a+b\) may equal \(a\) exactly because \(b\) is smaller than the gap between representable numbers near \(a\).







NoteExample



(Absorption) In double precision, 1e16 + 1.0 == 1e16 is true. The number \(1\) is smaller than the spacing between adjacent representable numbers near \(10^{16}\), so it is rounded away. Consequently (1e16 + 1.0) - 1e16 returns 0.0, not 1.0.








NoteExample



(Non-associativity) Let \(a=10^{16}\), \(b=-10^{16}\), and \(c=1\). Then \[
\begin{align}
(a+b)+c = 1, \qquad a+(b+c) = 0
\end{align}
\] in double precision. The second expression first rounds \(b+c\) back to \(-10^{16}\), so the \(1\) is lost before the final addition.








TipRemark



(Summation rule) Add numbers of similar magnitude when possible. Summing from smallest to largest, pairwise summation, or compensated summation reduces the loss of small terms. Consequently, library reductions may give different answers than a hand-written loop and still be more accurate.








WarningExercise




Before running Python, use the referenced result to predict (1e16 + 1.0) - 1e16.
a=1e16, b=1. Find (a+b)-a in Python. Explain result.
Find \(a, b, c\) where a*(b+c) != a*b + a*c.
Before running Python, predict the results of summing \([10^{16}, 1, -10^{16}]\) in the listed order and in the order \([10^{16}, -10^{16}, 1]\).
Compare naive summation, pairwise summation, and Kahan summation on a list containing one large number and many small numbers. Which method best preserves the small terms?

title: 4  Floating Point Arithmetic
text:
5.1 Absolute and Relative Errors

Absolute Error: \(|\hat{x} - x|\).
Relative Error: \(\varepsilon = \frac{|\hat{x} - x|}{|x|}\). This is the standard measure for precision in numerical computing.

Absolute error measures the size of the mistake in the original units. Relative error measures the size of the mistake compared to the quantity being computed. In numerical computing, relative error is usually more informative. An error of \(10^{-6}\) is excellent for a number of size \(10^3\) and terrible for a number of size \(10^{-9}\).






TipRemark



(Comparing floating-point numbers) Avoid testing computed real numbers with exact equality. Use a tolerance such as \[
\begin{align}
|\hat{x}-x| \leq \text{atol} + \text{rtol}|x|.
\end{align}
\] This principle underlies np.isclose. The absolute tolerance bounds errors near zero, whereas the relative tolerance scales with magnitude.








WarningExercise




Compute the absolute and relative errors of using \(1.414\) for \(\sqrt2\).
Let \(\hat x=x(1+\delta_x)\) and \(\hat y=y(1+\delta_y)\) with \(xy\neq0\). Derive the exact relative perturbation of \(\hat x\hat y\) before rounding the product. Bound it when \(|\delta_x|,|\delta_y|\leq u\), and identify the first-order term.









NoteDefinition: Catastrophic Cancellation



Catastrophic cancellation occurs when two nearly equal approximations are subtracted. The leading digits cancel, so errors already present in the operands become large relative to the small difference.

For \(x\neq y\) and operand errors \(|\hat x-x|\leq u|x|\), \(|\hat y-y|\leq u|y|\), exact subtraction of the perturbed operands has relative error at most \(u(|x|+|y|)/|x-y|\). Rounding that subtraction contributes a further local error.
As \(x \to y\), the amplification factor \((|x|+|y|)/|x-y|\) can become arbitrarily large.









TipProof





We distinguish errors in the operands from any additional rounding of the subtraction itself. Assume \(x-y\neq0\), since relative error with respect to a zero answer is undefined. Write the perturbed operands as \[
\begin{align}
\hat x=x(1+\varepsilon_x),\qquad
\hat y=y(1+\varepsilon_y),\qquad
|\varepsilon_x|,|\varepsilon_y|\leq u.
\end{align}
\] First regard \(\hat x-\hat y\) as an exact real subtraction of these perturbed data. Expand and cancel the unperturbed terms: \[
\begin{align}
(\hat x-\hat y)-(x-y)
&=x+x\varepsilon_x-y-y\varepsilon_y-x+y\\
&=x\varepsilon_x-y\varepsilon_y.
\end{align}
\] The triangle inequality and the operand bounds give \[
\begin{align}
|(\hat x-\hat y)-(x-y)|
&\leq |x||\varepsilon_x|+|y||\varepsilon_y|\\
&\leq u(|x|+|y|).
\end{align}
\] Dividing by \(|x-y|>0\) yields the stated amplification factor.
This factor can be large when the operands have comparable nonzero magnitude but their difference is small. It measures sensitivity to the operand errors. If the subtraction is also rounded, the floating-point model adds a further error bounded by \(u|\hat x-\hat y|\) in absolute value. That additional operation error is separate from the potentially amplified operand errors. The bound does not assert that every subtraction exhibits its worst possible error.









TipRemark



(Numerical stability principle) Rounding error is an inevitable consequence of finite precision. However, catastrophic cancellation is an algorithmic flaw that can often be avoided by mathematically rearranging the problem.








NoteExample



(Stabilizing Cancellation) \(f(x) = \sqrt{x+1} - \sqrt{x}\) for \(x = 10^{16}\).

Direct: In double precision, both square roots round to \(10^8\), so the computed difference is zero.
Stable: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+1} + \sqrt{x}} \approx 5 \times 10^{-9}\).









NoteExample



(Quadratic formula) The roots of \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) are \[
\begin{align}
x_{\pm} = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}.
\end{align}
\] If \(b^2 \gg 4ac\), one numerator subtracts nearly equal numbers. A stable strategy computes the root with no cancellation first, then uses \(x_1x_2=c/a\) to recover the other root.








TipRemark



(Use stable library functions) Functions such as log1p(x), expm1(x), and hypot(x, y) implement stable rearrangements for common cancellation and overflow patterns. Prefer them over hand-expanded formulas when the inputs may be small, large, or nearly cancelling.








WarningExercise



Stabilize:

Use the referenced result to explain why \((1-\cos x)/x^2\) is unstable for small \(x\), then derive a stable form.
Use the referenced result to identify which root of \(x^2 - 10^8 x + 1 = 0\) is unstable in the quadratic formula, then compute it using \(x_1x_2=c/a\).
Use the Taylor series of \(e^x\) to explain why \(e^x - 1\) loses relative accuracy for small \(x\). Compare with np.expm1.

title: 4  Floating Point Arithmetic
text:
5.2 Error Analysis
A computed result can be judged in two ways. Forward error analysis bounds the distance between the computed output and the exact output. Backward error analysis instead seeks the smallest perturbation of the input for which the computed output is exact. An algorithm is backward stable if this perturbation is a modest multiple of the unit roundoff \(u\) for every input.
Backward error is often easier to bound than forward error, and it is directly comparable with the uncertainty in the data. If the input is known only to a relative accuracy larger than the backward error, the algorithm has introduced no error beyond what the data already contain. The condition number then converts a backward error into a forward error.






NoteDefinition: Condition Number (\(\kappa\))



The condition number measures the local sensitivity of a problem’s output to perturbations in its input. For sufficiently small relative perturbations, the first-order relation has the form \[
\begin{align}
\text{relative forward error}
    \lesssim \kappa\,\text{relative backward error},
\end{align}
\] with the precise definition of \(\kappa\) determined by the problem and the chosen norms. For the linear system \(\bA\bx=\bb\), the referenced section shows that this role is played by the matrix condition number of the referenced result.








TipRemark



(Stability vs. conditioning) Conditioning is a property of the mathematical problem. Stability is a property of the algorithm. A stable algorithm can still return a poor answer on an ill-conditioned problem, because the problem itself amplifies small perturbations.








WarningExercise



A problem has condition number \(\kappa=10^8\), and an algorithm computes a solution with relative backward error \(10^{-15}\). Use the referenced result to estimate the largest relative forward error, and state how many correct significant digits the result can be expected to have.

title: 5  Cost Models and Sparse Storage
text:
5.1 Asymptotic Notation and Operation Counts
To choose between algorithms, we compare both arithmetic and storage. A matrix may be small enough to store but too expensive to factor. A sparse matrix has sufficiently few nonzero entries that storing only those entries changes the cost of its basic operations.
We count additions and multiplications for dense products, then describe storage by coordinates and by rows. These formats also show how to assemble a sparse matrix from local contributions without first allocating a dense array.
The order of evaluation matters even when the result does not change. For \(\bA,\bB\in\fR^{n\times n}\) and \(\bx\in\fR^n\), forming \((\bA\bB)\bx\) costs about \(2n^3\) flops, whereas \(\bA(\bB\bx)\) costs about \(4n^2\) flops. The factorizations of later sections have costs of the same kind. Dense LU factorization requires about \(\tfrac23n^3\) flops (the referenced result), Cholesky about \(\tfrac13n^3\), and Householder QR of an \(m\times n\) matrix about \(2mn^2-\tfrac23n^3\).
crumbs: 5  Cost Models and Sparse Storage

title: 5  Cost Models and Sparse Storage
text:
NoteDefinition: Asymptotic Notation



Let \(f\) and \(g\) be positive functions of an integer \(n\). We write \(f(n)=O(g(n))\) if there are constants \(C>0\) and \(n_0\) such that \(f(n)\leq Cg(n)\) for every \(n\geq n_0\). We write \(f(n)=\Theta(g(n))\) if both \(f(n)=O(g(n))\) and \(g(n)=O(f(n))\) hold.








WarningExercise



Show that \(3n^2+100n+5=\Theta(n^2)\), and arrange \(5n^3+n\), \(100n^2\), \(n^2\log n\), and \(2^{10}n^2\) in order of growth.








NoteDefinition: Flop



A flop is one floating-point addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, or square root.








NoteTheorem: Costs of the Basic Dense Kernels



Let \(\bx,\by\in\fR^n\), \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\), \(\bB\in\fR^{n\times p}\), and let \(\bL\in\fR^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular and lower triangular. The standard algorithms require

\(2n-1\) flops for the inner product \(\bx^T\by\),
\(m(2n-1)\) flops for the product \(\bA\bx\),
\(mp(2n-1)\) flops for the product \(\bA\bB\),
\(n^2\) flops for the solution of \(\bL\bz=\by\) by forward substitution.









TipProof





We count scalar arithmetic operations and exclude assignments and index calculations.

To form \(\sum_{j=1}^nx_jy_j\), first compute its \(n\) products. Adding \(n\) numbers requires \(n-1\) additions. The total is \(n+(n-1)=2n-1\) operations.
Each output entry is an inner product between one row of length \(n\) and the input vector. There are \(m\) output entries. The count is therefore \(m(2n-1)\), whose leading term is \(2mn\).
If \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\) and \(\bB\in\fR^{n\times p}\), there are \(mp\) output entries. Each entry uses an inner product of length \(n\). Hence the count is \(mp(2n-1)\), with leading term \(2mnp\).
In forward substitution, row \(i\) forms \(i-1\) products, subtracts those \(i-1\) terms from the right-hand side, and divides by the diagonal entry. The diagonal is nonzero by triangular nonsingularity. The count per row is \(2(i-1)+1\). Therefore \[
\begin{align}
\sum_{i=1}^n[2(i-1)+1]
  =2\frac{n(n-1)}2+n=n^2.
\end{align}
\]

For square matrices, put \(m=n=p\) to obtain the familiar leading count \(2n^3\). These counts describe the straightforward algorithms under the stated convention.










NoteExample



(The dense barrier) At a sustained rate of \(10^{10}\) flops per second, a dense LU factorization with \(n=10^4\) requires about \(\tfrac23\cdot10^{12}\) flops, or roughly one minute. With \(n=10^5\) it requires about \(\tfrac23\cdot10^{15}\) flops, or roughly nineteen hours, and storing the matrix in double precision requires \(8\cdot10^{10}\) bytes. A finite-difference discretization on a \(300\times300\times300\) grid already has \(n\approx2.7\times10^7\) unknowns. Dense methods are therefore out of reach for such problems, and the matrix must be stored and used in a form that exploits its zero entries.








TipRemark



(Memory traffic) Flop counts ignore the cost of moving data between memory and the processor. A dense matrix–matrix product reuses each loaded entry \(O(n)\) times, and blocked implementations run close to the peak arithmetic rate. A sparse matrix–vector product performs two flops for each stored nonzero but reads at least one value and one index for it. Its running time is therefore set by memory bandwidth rather than by the flop count, and reducing the number of stored entries reduces the running time directly.
crumbs: 5  Cost Models and Sparse Storage

title: 5  Cost Models and Sparse Storage
text:
5.2 Sparse Matrix Storage
A matrix is sparse when the number of its nonzero entries, written \(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)\), is much smaller than \(n^2\). The finite-difference Poisson matrix on an \(N\times N\) grid has \(n=N^2\) unknowns and fewer than \(5n\) nonzero entries. Stored densely, it would occupy \(n^2\) words, and a matrix–vector product would cost \(2n^2\) flops. A sparse format stores only the nonzero entries and their positions.






NoteDefinition: Coordinate and Compressed Sparse Row Formats



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) have \(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)\) nonzero entries.

The coordinate (COO) format stores three arrays of length \(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)\) that list each nonzero entry as a triplet \((i,j,a_{ij})\). The triplets may appear in any order, and repeated positions are understood to be summed.
The compressed sparse row (CSR) format stores the nonzero values row by row in an array \(`val`\), their column indices in an array \(`col`\) of the same length, and an array \(`ptr`\) of length \(n+1\). The entries of row \(i\) occupy positions \(`ptr`_i,...,`ptr`_{i+1}-1\) of \(`val`\) and \(`col`\).



The arrays below use mathematical indexing, beginning at one. In a Python implementation, column indices and positions begin at zero, and the first row pointer is zero. The difference \(`ptr`_{i+1}-`ptr`_i\) counts stored entries in row \(i\) under either convention. An empty row has equal consecutive pointers.






WarningExercise



Write the COO triplets and the CSR arrays of the \(5\times5\) matrix \(\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1)\). Then compute \(\bA\bx\) for \(\bx=(1,2,3,4,5)^T\) directly from the CSR arrays.








NoteExample



The matrix \[
\begin{align}
\bA=\begin{pmatrix}4&0&-1&0\\0&3&0&0\\-1&0&5&2\\0&0&2&6\end{pmatrix}
\end{align}
\] has eight nonzero entries. Its CSR arrays are \[
\begin{align}
`val`&=(4,-1,\;3,\;-1,5,2,\;2,6), &
    `col`&=(1,3,\;2,\;1,3,4,\;3,4), &
    `ptr`&=(1,3,4,7,9).
\end{align}
\] Row \(3\) occupies positions \(`ptr`_3=4\) through \(`ptr`_4-1=6\).








NoteTheorem: Cost of a CSR Matrix–Vector Product



For \(\bA\) stored in CSR format, the product \(\by=\bA\bx\) computed by \[
\begin{align}
y_i=\sum_{k=`ptr`_i}^{`ptr`_{i+1}-1}`val`_k\,x_{`col`_k},
    \qquad i=1,...,n,
\end{align}
\] requires at most \(2\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)\) flops. The format stores \(2\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)+n+1\) numbers.








TipProof





Consider the computation row by row. For each stored entry \(a_{ij}\), compute the product \(a_{ij}x_j\) and add it to the accumulator for output entry \(i\). This uses one multiplication and at most one addition per stored entry. Thus at most \(2\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)\) arithmetic operations are needed for the contributions.
There are also \(n\) row accumulators to initialize or write. Traversing the row pointers takes \(O(n)\) work. Consequently the complete count is \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)+n)\). In the common case of at least one stored entry in every row, \(n\leq\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)\) and the count simplifies to \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA))\).
Storage consists of one value and one column index per stored entry, together with \(n+1\) row pointers. Its size is also \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)+n)\). Empty rows explain why the row-pointer term cannot be discarded without an assumption.



The CSR format is efficient for computing \(\bA\bx\) but inconvenient for constructing a matrix, because the position of an entry in \(`val`\) depends on how many entries precede it. Matrices are therefore usually assembled in COO format, where a new entry is simply appended, and converted to CSR once assembly is complete.






NoteTheorem: Conversion from COO to CSR



A matrix given by \(t\) triplets can be converted to CSR format in \(O(t+n)\) operations.








TipProof





We describe an explicit algorithm. The matrix has \(n\) rows and columns, and \(t\) is the number of input triplets, including duplicates.

Initialize \(n\) counters to zero. For each triplet \((i,j,a)\), increment the counter for row \(i\). Initialization costs \(O(n)\) and the pass costs \(O(t)\).
Starting with \(`ptr`_1=1\), add the row counts successively. This prefix sum costs \(O(n)\) and gives the start and end positions of every row in an intermediate array of length \(t\).
Keep a next-free-position counter for each row. Pass over the input again and place the column and value of each triplet in its row’s next free slot. Each placement and increment takes constant time. This pass costs \(O(t+n)\) including counter initialization.
Use arrays of length \(n\) called \(`stamp`\) and \(`pos`\). When processing row \(i\), a column \(j\) has already appeared in that row exactly when \(`stamp`_j=i\). If it has appeared, add the value to output slot \(`pos`_j\). Otherwise append a new output entry and set \(`stamp`_j=i\) and \(`pos`_j\) to its slot. The row stamp avoids clearing a length-\(n\) array for each row. Each intermediate entry is examined once.
There are a fixed number of passes of length \(t\), and a fixed number of arrays initialized or scanned in \(O(n)\) time. The total is \(O(t+n)\). The resulting CSR columns need not be sorted within a row. Requiring sorted column indices is an additional operation and is not included in this bound.










NoteExample



(Assembling the Poisson matrix) For the one-dimensional Poisson matrix, we append for each \(i=1,...,n\) the triplet \((i,i,2h^{-2})\), together with \((i,i-1,-h^{-2})\) when \(i>1\) and \((i,i+1,-h^{-2})\) when \(i<n\). The result has \(3n-2\) triplets and converts to CSR in \(O(n)\) operations. Finite-element matrices are assembled in the same way by looping over elements, and each element contributes a small block of triplets that overlaps the contributions of its neighbors. The overlapping triplets are summed during the conversion.








TipRemark



(Column storage and transposes) The compressed sparse column (CSC) format stores \(\bA\) column by column and is the CSR format of \(\bA^T\). Column-oriented algorithms, such as sparse Cholesky factorization and column-oriented triangular solves, use CSC. A product \(\bA^T\bx\) with a CSR matrix is computed by scattering \(x_i\,`val`_k\) into position \(`col`_k\) of the result. The scatter has the same flop count as the CSR product, but parallel threads that process different rows may then write to the same output entry.

title: 6  Linearity and Fundamental Subspaces
text:
6.1 Linear Systems and Geometric Interpretations
A linear system asks for coefficients that combine the columns of a matrix to produce a prescribed vector. The answer depends on two different questions. Is the prescribed vector in the span of the columns? If it is, can two different coefficient vectors produce it? The range and null space express these questions directly.
A matrix equation \(\bA\bx = \bb\) expresses the requirement that a data vector \(\bb\) be produced by a linear combination of the columns of \(\bA\), weighted by the unknown coordinates \(\bx\).

title: 6  Linearity and Fundamental Subspaces
text:
NoteDefinition: Linear System



A linear system of \(m\) equations in \(n\) unknowns is written in matrix-vector form as \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bx = \bb,
\end{align}
\] where \(\bA \in \fR^{m \times n}\) is the coefficient matrix, \(\bx \in \fR^n\) is the unknown solution vector, and \(\bb \in \fR^m\) is the right-hand side vector.








WarningExercise



Consider \[
\begin{align}
\bA=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
\] Find every solution for \(\bb=(1,2)^T\), then show that no solution exists for \(\bb=(1,3)^T\). Interpret the two systems as pairs of lines. Which multiples of the columns can the matrix produce, and which nonzero vectors does it send to zero?








TipRemark



(Row versus column perspectives) There are two complementary geometric interpretations of \(\bA\bx = \bb\):

Row view: Each nonzero row \(\ba_i^T\bx=b_i\) defines an affine hyperplane in \(\fR^n\). A zero row gives either no restriction or an inconsistent equation, depending on \(b_i\). Solving the system means locating the mutual intersection of these \(m\) hyperplanes.
Column view: Partitioning \(\bA = [\ba_1, ..., \ba_n]\) into its columns, the product evaluates to \(\bA\bx = \sum_{j=1}^n x_j \ba_j\). Solving the system means expressing the vector \(\bb\) as a linear combination of the column vectors of \(\bA\).









NoteTheorem: Superposition Principle



Let \(\bA \in \fR^{m \times n}\) define a linear operator. If \(\bA\bx_1 = \bb_1\) and \(\bA\bx_2 = \bb_2\), then for any scalars \(\alpha, \beta \in \fR\), \[
\begin{align}
\bA(\alpha\bx_1 + \beta\bx_2) = \alpha\bb_1 + \beta\bb_2.
\end{align}
\] Consequently, the solution to a linear system with a composite source term decomposes into a linear combination of individual response vectors.








WarningExercise



Prove superposition by distributing \(\bA\) over the linear combination. If \(\bA\) is singular and the two systems are consistent, explain why the conclusion still holds even though their solutions may not be unique.
