title: 13  Eigenvalues, Invariant Subspaces, and Their Sensitivity
text:
NoteDefinition: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors



Let \(\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}\). A nonzero vector \(\bv \in \fC^n\) is an eigenvector of \(\bA\) associated with eigenvalue \(\lambda \in \fC\) if \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bv = \lambda\bv.
\end{align}
\] The set of eigenvalues is the spectrum \(\sigma(\bA)\). When eigenvalues are listed as \(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_n\), repetitions are included according to algebraic multiplicity.








WarningExercise



For \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)\), compute \(\bA^k\bx\) for \(\bx=(x_1,x_2)^T\) and identify its invariant coordinate lines. Next solve the eigenvalue equation for \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). Why are complex scalars needed for the rotation even though all matrix entries are real?








NoteDefinition: Invariant Subspace



A subspace \(S\subseteq\fC^n\) is invariant under \(\bA\) if \(\bA\bx\in S\) whenever \(\bx\in S\). An eigenvector spans a one-dimensional invariant subspace. Higher-dimensional invariant subspaces remain meaningful even when no basis of eigenvectors exists.








NoteExample



Three two-dimensional examples show what the definition can and cannot promise.

A diagonal matrix scales the coordinate axes, leaving both axes invariant.
The shear \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has only one independent eigenvector. Repeated application keeps sliding vectors in the same direction, so a repeated eigenvalue need not supply a full eigenbasis.
A planar rotation through an angle that is not an integer multiple of \(\pi\) has no real invariant line, but it has complex eigenvectors. The complex eigenvalues encode the rotation as multiplication by a complex phase.









NoteDefinition: Similarity and a Change of Basis



Matrices \(\bA\) and \(\bB\) are similar if \[
\begin{align}
\bB=\bS^{-1}\bA\bS
\end{align}
\] for some nonsingular \(\bS\). They represent the same linear map in different bases: the columns of \(\bS\) are the new basis vectors written in the old coordinates.








NoteTheorem: Similarity Preserves Eigenvalues



If \(\bB=\bS^{-1}\bA\bS\), then \(\bA\) and \(\bB\) have the same eigenvalues. More precisely, \(\bA\bv=\lambda\bv\) if and only if \[
\begin{align}
\bB(\bS^{-1}\bv)=\lambda(\bS^{-1}\bv).
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Multiply \(\bA\bv=\lambda\bv\) by \(\bS^{-1}\) and insert \(\bS\bS^{-1}\) to prove the forward implication. Prove the reverse implication and explain why the transformed eigenvector is nonzero. Use determinants to show that algebraic multiplicities are preserved as well.








NoteTheorem: Diagonalization Means an Eigenvector Basis



A matrix \(\bA\in\fC^{n\times n}\) is similar to a diagonal matrix if and only if it has a basis of eigenvectors. If \(\bS=(\bv_1\ \cdots\ \bv_n)\) contains such a basis, then \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bS=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda},
    \qquad
    \bA=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bS^{-1}.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Compare the \(j\)th columns of \(\bA\bS\) and \(\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) to prove both implications. Explain why linear independence of the eigenvectors is essential.

title: 14  Vector Iterations and the QR Algorithm
text:
14.2 The Practical QR Algorithm






NoteDefinition: Basic QR Iteration



Given \(\bA_0 = \bA\), the unshifted QR iteration generates orthogonally similar matrices via \[
\begin{align}
\bA_k = \bQ_k \bR_k, \qquad \bA_{k+1} = \bR_k \bQ_k = \bQ_k^T \bA_k \bQ_k.
\end{align}
\] All iterates share the same eigenvalues. Under suitable separation conditions the subdiagonal entries tend to zero and the iterates reveal a Schur form. Shifts and deflation are essential for a reliable practical method.








NoteLemma: Invariance of Hessenberg Structure under QR Iteration



Let \(\bH \in \fR^{n \times n}\) be an upper Hessenberg matrix (\(H_{ij} = 0\) for all \(i > j + 1\)). If \(\bH=\bQ\bR\) is computed by successive adjacent-row Givens rotations, then the reversed product \(\bH_+ = \bR\bQ\) is also upper Hessenberg.








TipProof





Use the QR factorization obtained by eliminating successive subdiagonal entries with rotations of adjacent rows. This is the structure-preserving QR factorization used by the practical algorithm.
At column \(j\), the current matrix has no entries below row \(j+1\) in that column. A rotation of rows \(j,j+1\) eliminates that one entry. Previously treated columns already have zeros in both of those rows, so this rotation does not spoil their zeros. Continuing gives an upper triangular matrix \[
\begin{align}
\bR=\bG_{n-1}\cdots\bG_1\bH,
\qquad \bQ=\bG_1^T\cdots\bG_{n-1}^T.
\end{align}
\] A zero entry requires no rotation, so this construction also covers singular matrices.
We check that \(\bQ\) is upper Hessenberg. For column \(j<n\), the rightmost factors \(\bG_{n-1}^T,...,\bG_{j+1}^T\) leave \(\be_j\) unchanged. The next factor \(\bG_j^T\) can introduce only coordinate \(j+1\). Subsequent factors have smaller row indices and cannot introduce any coordinate beyond \(j+1\). Thus \(Q_{ij}=0\) for \(i>j+1\).
For an entry \((i,j)\) of \(\bR\bQ\) below that subdiagonal, \(i>j+1\), write \[
\begin{align}
(\bR\bQ)_{ij}=\sum_{l=1}^nR_{il}Q_{lj}.
\end{align}
\] If \(l<i\), triangularity makes \(R_{il}=0\). If \(l\geq i\), then \(l>j+1\), and the Hessenberg property makes \(Q_{lj}=0\). Every summand is therefore zero. This proves that the reversed product is upper Hessenberg without assuming an inverse of \(\bR\).









NoteTheorem: Practical Shifted QR Framework



A standard dense nonsymmetric eigenvalue computation has two phases:

Hessenberg reduction: Compute \(\bH_0=\bU_0^T\bA\bU_0\) with Householder reflectors. This one-time reduction costs \(O(n^3)\) operations and preserves the eigenvalues.
Implicit shifted QR steps: Apply shifts while preserving Hessenberg form. A schematic single-shift step is \[
\begin{align}
\bH_k - \mu_k \bI = \bQ_k \bR_k, \qquad \bH_{k+1} = \bR_k \bQ_k + \mu_k \bI.
\end{align}
\] the referenced result explains why each step costs \(O(n^2)\) rather than \(O(n^3)\). Real nonsymmetric codes use implicit single or double shifts so that complex conjugate pairs can remain in real arithmetic. A small subdiagonal entry permits deflation and splits the problem into smaller blocks.

For a real symmetric matrix, Hessenberg form reduces to tridiagonal form. Wilkinson shifts from the trailing two by two block and implicit bulge chasing then give a particularly efficient symmetric algorithm.

title: 14  Vector Iterations and the QR Algorithm
text:
14.4 Shifted Hessenberg Systems
Several calculations require the solution of \((s\bI-\bA)\bx=\bb\) for many complex shifts \(s\) with the same \(\bA\) and \(\bb\). The vector \((s\bI-\bA)^{-1}\bb\) is the resolvent of \(\bA\) applied to \(\bb\). Resolvents appear in Laplace transforms of solutions of linear differential equations, in frequency responses, and in contour-integral formulas for matrix functions. Factoring \(s\bI-\bA\) separately for each of \(N\) shifts costs about \(\tfrac23n^3\) flops per shift. The Hessenberg reduction of the referenced result removes this repetition, because adding a multiple of the identity does not change Hessenberg structure.






NoteTheorem: Shifted Solves with a Hessenberg Matrix



Let \(\bA=\bQ\bH\bQ^T\) with \(\bQ\) orthogonal and \(\bH\) upper Hessenberg, and let \(s\) not be an eigenvalue of \(\bA\). Then \(\bx=(s\bI-\bA)^{-1}\bb\) is given by \[
\begin{align}
(s\bI-\bH)\by=\bQ^T\bb,
    \qquad
    \bx=\bQ\by.
\end{align}
\] Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting solves the Hessenberg system in \(O(n^2)\) operations. At each step, the only possible row interchange is between the pivot row and the row directly below it.








TipProof





Since \(\bQ\bQ^T=\bI\), we have \(s\bI-\bA=\bQ(s\bI-\bH)\bQ^T\), so \(\bx=\bQ(s\bI-\bH)^{-1}\bQ^T\bb\). This reduction can also be obtained without forming an inverse. Set \(\bx=\bQ\by\) in \((s\bI-\bA)\bx=\bb\), then multiply by \(\bQ^T\). Orthogonality gives exactly \((s\bI-\bH)\by=\bQ^T\bb\). Nonsingularity follows because \(s\) is not an eigenvalue.
The matrix \(s\bI-\bH\) differs from \(-\bH\) only on the diagonal, so it is upper Hessenberg. Suppose that after \(k-1\) elimination steps the active submatrix is upper Hessenberg. Its first column then has a single nonzero entry below the diagonal, in row \(k+1\). Partial pivoting compares only rows \(k\) and \(k+1\), computes one multiplier, and updates one row of length at most \(n-k+1\). Rows \(k+2,...,n\) are untouched, so the next active submatrix is again upper Hessenberg. Summing the work over \(k=1,...,n-1\) gives \(O(n^2)\) operations, and the triangular solve that follows costs another \(O(n^2)\).
The total row-update length is bounded by a constant times \(\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k+1)\). This sum is \((n-1)(n+2)/2=O(n^2)\). Pivot comparisons and swaps cost at most the same order. An upper triangular solve also has a quadratic count, so adding it leaves the overall order unchanged.



Reducing \(\bA\) to Hessenberg form with Householder reflectors costs about \(\tfrac{10}{3}n^3\) flops when \(\bQ\) is kept as a product of reflectors, and this reduction is done once (Golub and Van Loan 2013). Applying \(\bQ^T\) and \(\bQ\) to a vector costs \(O(n^2)\) flops. For \(N\) shifts, the total cost is therefore about \(\tfrac{10}{3}n^3+O(Nn^2)\) flops, compared with about \(\tfrac23Nn^3\) for separate factorizations. The reduction pays for itself after five shifts, and with one hundred shifts it reduces the cost by a factor of about twenty.






TipRemark



(Contour integrals for the matrix exponential) The Cauchy integral formula for matrix functions gives \[
\begin{align}
e^{t\bA}\bb=\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}\int_\Gamma e^{ts}(s\bI-\bA)^{-1}\bb\,ds,
\end{align}
\] where \(\Gamma\) is a contour that encloses the spectrum of \(\bA\) (Higham 2008). When the spectrum lies in the left half-plane, as for Markov generators and discretized diffusion operators, \(\Gamma\) can be chosen to wrap around the negative real axis so that \(e^{ts}\) decays along it. After a parametrization of \(\Gamma\), the trapezoid rule with \(N\) nodes approximates the integral by a sum of \(N\) resolvent applications, each computed by the referenced result. For suitable Talbot-type contours the error decreases geometrically in \(N\), and a few tens of nodes commonly reach double-precision accuracy (Weideman and Trefethen 2007). The geometric convergence is the same mechanism as the spectral accuracy of the trapezoid rule for periodic analytic integrands in the referenced section. For large sparse matrices, the Krylov approximations of the referenced section are usually preferable, because they avoid the dense Hessenberg reduction.

title: 15  The Singular Value Decomposition
text:
15.1 The SVD Theorem and Subspace Characterization
An eigenvector compares input and output in the same space. A rectangular matrix may have different input and output dimensions, so we instead seek orthonormal input directions whose images are mutually orthogonal. In those coordinates, the map merely scales each direction and may send some directions to zero.
The singular value decomposition makes this construction precise. It will evaluate the matrix norm, expose directions that are poorly determined by a least-squares problem, and identify which components can be discarded in an approximation of smaller rank.
Suppose unit input vectors \(\bv_i\) have images \(\bA\bv_i=\sigma_i\bu_i\) with orthonormal \(\bu_i\) and nonnegative \(\sigma_i\). Applying \(\bA\) then consists of expanding an input in the \(\bv_i\) basis, multiplying its coefficients by \(\sigma_i\), and expressing the output in the \(\bu_i\) basis. To find such input vectors, observe that \[
\begin{align}
(\bA\bv_i)^T(\bA\bv_j)=\bv_i^T(\bA^T\bA)\bv_j.
\end{align}
\] An orthonormal eigenbasis of the symmetric matrix \(\bA^T\bA\) therefore makes the images orthogonal. This observation supplies the proof.
If \(m<n\), apply the theorem to \(\bA^T\) and transpose the factorization. The left and right factors exchange roles, and the rectangular diagonal factor is transposed. Thus the decomposition exists for every rectangular matrix. When \(r=0\), the outer-product sum is empty and \(\bA=\bzero\).

title: 15  The Singular Value Decomposition
text:
NoteTheorem: The Singular Value Decomposition Theorem



Let \(\bA \in \fR^{m \times n}\) with \(m \geq n\). There exist orthogonal matrices \(\bU \in \fR^{m \times m}\) and \(\bV \in \fR^{n \times n}\), and a rectangular diagonal matrix \(\bsigma \in \fR^{m \times n}\), such that \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \bU \bsigma \bV^T,
\end{align}
\] where the diagonal entries of \(\bsigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1, \sigma_2, ..., \sigma_n)\) are real, non-negative, and sorted in non-increasing order: \[
\begin{align}
\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n\geq0,\qquad
    \sigma_i>0\ (1\leq i\leq r),\qquad
    \sigma_i=0\ (r<i\leq n).
\end{align}
\] The number of strictly positive singular values \(r = \operatorname{rank}(\bA)\) equals the rank of \(\bA\). In dyadic outer-product form, \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i \bu_i \bv_i^T.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Consider the Gram matrix \(\bA^T\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}\). Because \((\bA^T\bA)^T = \bA^T\bA\), it is symmetric, and for every \(\bx \in \fR^n\), \(\bx^T(\bA^T\bA)\bx = \|\bA\bx\|_2^2 \geq 0\), so \(\bA^T\bA\) is positive semidefinite.
By the Spectral Theorem (the referenced result), \(\bA^T\bA\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors \(\bv_1, ..., \bv_n \in \fR^{n}\) with corresponding real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq ... \geq \lambda_n \geq 0\). Define the singular values \(\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i} \geq 0\) for \(i = 1, ..., n\), and let \(r\) denote the number of strictly positive singular values, with positivity for \(1\leq i\leq r\) and zeros for \(r<i\leq n\). Either index range may be empty.
For each index \(i \in \{1, ..., r\}\), define the normalized vectors in \(\fR^m\): \[
\begin{align}
\bu_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_i} \bA \bv_i.
\end{align}
\] We verify that \(\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_r\}\) form an orthonormal set in \(\fR^m\): \[
\begin{align}
\bu_i^T \bu_j
    =
    \frac{1}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} (\bA\bv_i)^T (\bA\bv_j)
    =
    \frac{1}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} \bv_i^T (\bA^T\bA\bv_j)
    =
    \frac{\lambda_j}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} \bv_i^T \bv_j
    =
    \frac{\sigma_j^2}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} \delta_{ij}
    =
    \delta_{ij}.
\end{align}
\] When \(i=j\), the displayed inner product is \(\sigma_i^2/\sigma_i^2=1\). When \(i\neq j\), it is zero because \(\bv_i^T\bv_j=0\). All divisions used only positive singular values, so no zero singular value was divided by.
Using Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization, extend \(\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_r\}\) to a complete orthonormal basis \(\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_m\}\) for \(\fR^m\). Assemble the orthogonal matrices \(\bU = [\bu_1, ..., \bu_m] \in \fR^{m \times m}\) and \(\bV = [\bv_1, ..., \bv_n] \in \fR^{n \times n}\).
Evaluating the \((i, j)\) entry of \(\bU^T\bA\bV\): \[
\begin{align}
(\bU^T\bA\bV)_{ij} = \bu_i^T \bA \bv_j.
\end{align}
\] For \(j \leq r\), \(\bA\bv_j = \sigma_j \bu_j\), so \(\bu_i^T \bA\bv_j = \sigma_j \bu_i^T\bu_j = \sigma_j \delta_{ij}\). For \(j > r\), \(\lambda_j = 0\), so \(\|\bA\bv_j\|_2^2 = \bv_j^T\bA^T\bA\bv_j = 0\), which implies \(\bA\bv_j = \bzero\) and \(\bu_i^T\bA\bv_j = 0\). Thus \(\bU^T\bA\bV = \bsigma\), which gives \(\bA = \bU\bsigma\bV^T\).
The images of the first \(r\) right singular vectors are nonzero multiples of the independent vectors \(\bu_1,...,\bu_r\). The remaining right singular vectors map to zero. Since these vectors form a basis of the domain, the range has dimension exactly \(r\). This proves the rank assertion in addition to the factorization.










WarningExercise



Construct an SVD of \(\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\). Describe the image of the unit circle, then identify the range and the null space of the transpose. Repeat after replacing the entry \(1\) by zero. Which input direction has become invisible?








NoteTheorem: Thin SVD and the Four Fundamental Subspaces



Let \(\bA \in \fR^{m \times n}\) have rank \(r \leq n \leq m\). The thin SVD is \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \bU_1 \bsigma_1 \bV_1^T,
\end{align}
\] where \(\bU_1 \in \fR^{m \times r}\) and \(\bV_1 \in \fR^{n \times r}\) have orthonormal columns, and \(\bsigma_1 = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1, ..., \sigma_r) \in \fR^{r \times r}\) has strictly positive entries. The complete singular vectors partition the domain and codomain into the four fundamental subspaces:

Column space (range): \(\mathcal{R}(\bA) = \operatorname{span}\{\bu_1, ..., \bu_r\} \subset \fR^m\).
Left null space: \(\mathcal{N}(\bA^T) = \operatorname{span}\{\bu_{r+1}, ..., \bu_m\} \subset \fR^m\).
Row space: \(\mathcal{R}(\bA^T) = \operatorname{span}\{\bv_1, ..., \bv_r\} \subset \fR^n\).
Null space (kernel): \(\mathcal{N}(\bA) = \operatorname{span}\{\bv_{r+1}, ..., \bv_n\} \subset \fR^n\).









TipProof





Expand \(\bx\) in the complete orthonormal right singular basis: \(\bx=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i\bv_i\), where \(c_i=\bv_i^T\bx\). The SVD gives \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bx=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i c_i\bu_i.
\end{align}
\] Thus every output lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{\bu_1,...,\bu_r\}\). Conversely, for \(i\leq r\), \(\bu_i=\bA(\bv_i/\sigma_i)\) is an output. Hence that span is exactly the range, not merely a space containing it.
For the null space, take the squared Euclidean norm of the output. Orthonormality of the left singular vectors gives \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bx\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i^2c_i^2.
\end{align}
\] Every \(\sigma_i\) in this sum is positive. The sum vanishes if and only if \(c_i=0\) for every \(i\leq r\). The remaining coefficients are arbitrary, so the null space is exactly \(\operatorname{span}\{\bv_{r+1},...,\bv_n\}\).
For the transpose, expand \(\by=\sum_{i=1}^m d_i\bu_i\). Transposing the SVD gives \[
\begin{align}
\bA^T\by=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i d_i\bv_i.
\end{align}
\] Every output is in the first \(r\) right singular directions, and each \(\bv_i=\bA^T(\bu_i/\sigma_i)\) is an output. This proves the row-space claim. Likewise \(\|\bA^T\by\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i^2d_i^2\), which vanishes precisely when the first \(r\) coefficients are zero. The left null space is therefore the span of the remaining \(\bu_i\).

title: 15  The Singular Value Decomposition
text:
15.2 Norms and Condition Numbers
The induced Euclidean norm of the referenced result is the largest amplification of a unit vector, and the condition number of the referenced result compares the largest and the smallest amplification. Both were defined as optimization problems over the unit sphere. Because orthogonal matrices preserve Euclidean length, the SVD reduces these problems to a diagonal matrix, where they can be solved by inspection.






NoteTheorem: Norms and Condition Numbers from the SVD



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\) with \(m\geq n\) have singular values \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n\geq0\). Then \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\|_2=\sigma_1,
    \qquad
    \min_{\|\bx\|_2=1}\|\bA\bx\|_2=\sigma_n,
    \qquad
    \|\bA\|_F=\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i^2\Big)^{1/2}.
\end{align}
\] If \(\bA\) has full column rank, we define \(\kappa_2(\bA)=\sigma_1/\sigma_n\). The condition number satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\kappa_2(\bA^T\bA)=\kappa_2(\bA)^2.
\end{align}
\] If \(\bA\) is square and nonsingular, then \(\|\bA^{-1}\|_2=1/\sigma_n\), so \(\kappa_2(\bA)=\|\bA\|_2\|\bA^{-1}\|_2\) agrees with the referenced result.








TipProof





Let \(\bx\) be a unit vector and let \(\by=\bV^T\bx\), which is also a unit vector. Since \(\bU\) preserves Euclidean length, \[
\begin{align}
\|\bA\bx\|_2^2=\|\bU\bsigma\bV^T\bx\|_2^2=\|\bsigma\by\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i^2y_i^2.
\end{align}
\] The sum is a weighted average of the \(\sigma_i^2\), so it lies between \(\sigma_n^2\) and \(\sigma_1^2\). The upper value is attained at \(\by=\be_1\), that is, at \(\bx=\bv_1\), and the lower value is attained at \(\bx=\bv_n\). These two cases prove the first two identities.
For any unit vector, \(\sum_i y_i^2=1\). Therefore \(\sum_i\sigma_i^2y_i^2\leq\sigma_1^2\sum_i y_i^2=\sigma_1^2\), and the analogous lower inequality uses \(\sigma_n^2\). These inequalities become equalities for the indicated coordinate vectors. Thus they give extrema, not just bounds.
For the Frobenius norm, \(\|\bA\|_F^2=\operatorname{trace}(\bA^T\bA)\) and \(\bA^T\bA=\bV\bsigma^T\bsigma\bV^T\). The identity \(\operatorname{tr}(\bB\bC)=\operatorname{tr}(\bC\bB)\) follows by interchanging the two finite sums over entries. Applying it to this product gives \[
\begin{align}
\operatorname{tr}(\bV\bsigma^T\bsigma\bV^T)
=\operatorname{tr}(\bsigma^T\bsigma\bV^T\bV)
=\operatorname{tr}(\bsigma^T\bsigma).
\end{align}
\] Thus the trace is invariant under the similarity by \(\bV\), so \(\|\bA\|_F^2=\operatorname{trace}(\bsigma^T\bsigma)=\sum_i\sigma_i^2\).
The factorization \(\bA^T\bA=\bV(\bsigma^T\bsigma)\bV^T\) is itself an SVD of \(\bA^T\bA\) with singular values \(\sigma_1^2\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n^2\). When \(\bA\) has full column rank these are positive, and \(\kappa_2(\bA^T\bA)=\sigma_1^2/\sigma_n^2=\kappa_2(\bA)^2\). Finally, if \(\bA\) is square and nonsingular, then \(\bA^{-1}=\bV\bsigma^{-1}\bU^T\) is an SVD whose largest singular value is \(1/\sigma_n\).









NoteCorollary: Symmetric Positive Definite Matrices



If \(\bA\) is symmetric positive definite, its singular values are its eigenvalues, and \(\kappa_2(\bA)=\lambda_{\max}(\bA)/\lambda_{\min}(\bA)\). If \(\bA=\bL\bL^T\) is the Cholesky factorization of the referenced result, then \(\kappa_2(\bL)=\sqrt{\kappa_2(\bA)}\).








TipProof





For an SPD matrix, the spectral theorem gives \(\bA=\bQ\boldsymbol\Lambda\bQ^T\) with positive eigenvalues. Order them in decreasing order. Both outer factors are orthogonal, and the middle factor is diagonal with nonnegative decreasing entries. It therefore satisfies every condition of an SVD. Its singular values are the positive eigenvalues themselves.
Now suppose \(\bA=\bL\bL^T\) is the Cholesky factorization. To find singular values of \(\bL^T\), form its Gram matrix: \[
\begin{align}
(\bL^T)^T\bL^T=\bL\bL^T=\bA.
\end{align}
\] The SVD construction shows that squared singular values of a matrix are the eigenvalues of its Gram matrix. Thus \(\sigma_i(\bL^T)=\sqrt{\lambda_i(\bA)}\). Transposing an SVD exchanges its two orthogonal factors and transposes its diagonal factor, preserving the singular values. Hence the same formula holds for \(\bL\).
The smallest eigenvalue is positive, so both extreme singular values are nonzero. Consequently \[
\begin{align}
\kappa_2(\bL)
=\frac{\sigma_{\max}(\bL)}{\sigma_{\min}(\bL)}
=\frac{\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\bA)}}{\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\bA)}}
=\sqrt{\kappa_2(\bA)}.
\end{align}
\]



The identity \(\kappa_2(\bA^T\bA)=\kappa_2(\bA)^2\) explains the preference for QR in the referenced section. When the normal equations are formed and solved by a backward stable method, the forward error can be as large as a modest multiple of \(\kappa_2(\bA)^2u\), where \(u\) is the unit roundoff. Householder QR works with \(\bA\) directly, and when the least-squares residual is small its forward error is a modest multiple of \(\kappa_2(\bA)u\) (Higham 2002). For \(\kappa_2(\bA)=10^6\) in double precision, these two estimates are of order \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-10}\).

title: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process
text:
16.1 Krylov Subspaces
The QR algorithm of the referenced result computes every eigenvalue of a dense matrix in \(O(n^3)\) operations. Many applications instead require a few eigenvalues of a large sparse matrix, and the matrix is often available only through the product \(\bv\mapsto\bA\bv\). Power iteration (the referenced result) uses only such products, but at step \(k\) it retains only the last vector \(\bA^{k-1}\bv\) and discards the earlier ones.
The Arnoldi process retains the span of \(\bv,\bA\bv,...,\bA^{k-1}\bv\) through an orthonormal basis. We first define the subspace spanned by this sequence and explain why its natural basis is unusable in floating-point arithmetic. We then construct an orthonormal basis one vector at a time and derive the Arnoldi relation. The same relation underlies the Lanczos algorithm in the next section, the GMRES method for linear systems, and the Krylov approximation of the matrix exponential.
The \(k\)th power iterate is a multiple of \(\bA^{k-1}\bv\), so it lies in \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\). Power iteration therefore selects one particular vector from the Krylov subspace, namely the one produced by the polynomial \(p(t)=t^{k-1}\). Any method that searches the whole subspace can do at least as well with the same number of matrix–vector products. the referenced section makes this comparison precise for symmetric matrices.

title: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process
text:
NoteDefinition: Krylov Subspace



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) and let \(\bv\in\fR^n\) be nonzero. The \(k\)th Krylov subspace generated by \(\bA\) and \(\bv\) is \[
\begin{align}
\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)=\operatorname{span}\{\bv,\bA\bv,...,\bA^{k-1}\bv\}.
\end{align}
\] Equivalently, \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)=\{p(\bA)\bv : p\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}\}\), where \(\mathcal{P}_{k-1}\) denotes the polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\).








WarningExercise



For \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,3)\) and \(\bv=(1,1,0)^T\), find the dimensions of \(\mathcal K_1\), \(\mathcal K_2\), and \(\mathcal K_3\). Find a polynomial of degree two for which \(p(\bA)\bv=\bzero\). Explain why no number of matrix products can recover the third coordinate direction from this starting vector.








WarningExercise



(Shift invariance) Show that \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA-\sigma\bI,\bv)=\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\) for every scalar \(\sigma\). Conclude that the Arnoldi iteration applied to \(\bA-\sigma\bI\) produces the same basis \(\bV_k\) and the Hessenberg matrix \(\bH_k-\sigma\bI\).









NoteLemma: Krylov Subspaces Stop Growing at an Invariant Subspace



If \(\mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\bA,\bv)=\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\), then \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\) is invariant under \(\bA\) in the sense of the referenced result, and \(\mathcal{K}_j(\bA,\bv)=\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\) for every \(j\geq k\).








TipProof





Write \(\mathcal K_j=\mathcal K_j(\bA,\bv)\).

Every \(\bx\in\mathcal K_k\) can be written as \(\bx=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}c_i\bA^i\bv\). Multiplying gives \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bx=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}c_i\bA^{i+1}\bv\in\mathcal K_{k+1}.
\end{align}
\] If \(\mathcal K_{k+1}=\mathcal K_k\), this image belongs to \(\mathcal K_k\). This is exactly the definition of invariance.
The equality of the two spaces implies \(\bA^k\bv\in\mathcal K_k\). By invariance, applying \(\bA\) again gives \(\bA^{k+1}\bv\in\mathcal K_k\). Repeating this reasoning gives \(\bA^j\bv\in\mathcal K_k\) for every \(j\geq k\).
For \(j\geq k\), all generators of \(\mathcal K_j\) now lie in \(\mathcal K_k\), so \(\mathcal K_j\subseteq\mathcal K_k\). The reverse inclusion follows because the generators of \(\mathcal K_k\) are among those of \(\mathcal K_j\). Therefore the spaces are equal.










TipRemark



(Ill-conditioned monomial basis) The vectors \(\bv,\bA\bv,...,\bA^{k-1}\bv\) form a basis of \(\mathcal{K}_k\) whenever the subspace has dimension \(k\), but this basis can be severely ill-conditioned. When a unique dominant eigendirection is present in the starting vector, the power-iteration argument shows that the normalized vectors \(\bA^j\bv/\|\bA^j\bv\|_2\) converge to the dominant eigenvector, so the later columns of the basis matrix become nearly parallel. The resulting near dependence makes the basis sensitive to rounding errors, which can destroy the information carried by the smaller components.

title: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process
text:
16.2 The Arnoldi Process
The remedy is to orthonormalize the Krylov sequence as it is generated. If \(\bv_1,...,\bv_j\) is an orthonormal basis of \(\mathcal{K}_j\), we obtain a new direction by multiplying the latest basis vector by \(\bA\) instead of forming \(\bA^j\bv\). We then remove its components along the existing basis by Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization (the referenced result).






NoteDefinition: The Arnoldi Iteration



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) and let \(\bv\in\fR^n\) be nonzero. Set \(\bv_1=\bv/\|\bv\|_2\). For \(j=1,2,...,k\):

Compute \(\bw=\bA\bv_j\).
For \(i=1,...,j\), compute \(h_{ij}=\bv_i^T\bw\) and update \(\bw\leftarrow\bw-h_{ij}\bv_i\).
Compute \(h_{j+1,j}=\|\bw\|_2\).
If \(h_{j+1,j}=0\), stop. Otherwise, set \(\bv_{j+1}=\bw/h_{j+1,j}\).

Step 2 is modified Gram–Schmidt. The coefficients \(h_{ij}\) are collected in the \(k\times k\) upper Hessenberg matrix \(\bH_k\) and in the \((k+1)\times k\) matrix \(\bar{\bH}_k\), which is \(\bH_k\) with the additional row \(h_{k+1,k}\be_k^T\).








NoteTheorem: The Arnoldi Relation



Suppose the Arnoldi iteration completes \(k\) steps with \(h_{j+1,j}\neq0\) for \(j=1,...,k\), and let \(\bV_k=(\bv_1\ \cdots\ \bv_k)\). Then:

The columns of \(\bV_k\) are orthonormal and span \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\).
The matrices satisfy $$ \[\begin{align}
\bA\bV_k=\bV_k\bH_k+h_{k+1,k}\bv_{k+1}\be_k^T=\bV_{k+1}\bar{\bH}_k.

\end{align}\] $$
The Hessenberg matrix is the projection of \(\bA\) onto the Krylov subspace, \(\bH_k=\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k\).









TipProof





All assertions concern exact arithmetic. We verify orthogonality, the matrix identity, the span, and the projected matrix in that order.

Assume \(\bv_1,...,\bv_j\) are orthonormal. At inner-loop position \(i\), replace the current \(\bw\) by \(\bw-h_{ij}\bv_i\), where \(h_{ij}=\bv_i^T\bw\). Its inner product with \(\bv_i\) becomes \(h_{ij}-h_{ij}\bv_i^T\bv_i=0\). For an earlier vector \(\bv_l\), \(l<i\), the inner product remains zero because \(\bv_l^T\bv_i=0\). Thus the final \(\bw\) is perpendicular to every previous basis vector. Dividing by its nonzero norm gives a new unit vector. The starting vector is unit by construction, so induction establishes orthonormality at every step.
The inner loop subtracts \(\sum_{i=1}^jh_{ij}\bv_i\) from the original vector \(\bA\bv_j\). Its remaining vector is \(h_{j+1,j}\bv_{j+1}\). Consequently \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bv_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j+1}h_{ij}\bv_i.
\end{align}
\] Putting the first \(k\) such equations side by side gives \(\bA\bV_k=\bV_{k+1}\bar{\bH}_k\). The coefficients in column \(j\) have no indices beyond \(j+1\), which is why the matrix is upper Hessenberg. Separating its final row gives the other form of the Arnoldi relation.
The first vector spans \(\mathcal K_1\). Suppose the first \(j\) vectors span \(\mathcal K_j\). The column identity expresses \(\bv_{j+1}\) as a combination of \(\bA\bv_j\) and previous basis vectors. Each belongs to \(\mathcal K_{j+1}\), so \(\bv_{j+1}\) does too. There are \(j+1\) independent orthonormal vectors in this space, whose definition supplies at most \(j+1\) generators. Its dimension is therefore exactly \(j+1\), and these vectors span it.
Multiply the Arnoldi relation by \(\bV_k^T\) on the left: \[
\begin{align}
\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k
  &=\bV_k^T\bV_k\bH_k
    +h_{k+1,k}\bV_k^T\bv_{k+1}\be_k^T\\
  &=\bI_k\bH_k+\bzero=\bH_k.
\end{align}
\] The two simplifications follow from orthonormality proved in the first step.

For the standard Arnoldi construction and its use in Krylov methods, see Saad (2003).









TipRemark



(Arnoldi cost) Step \(j\) requires one product with \(\bA\) and \(j\) inner products and vector updates of length \(n\). After \(k\) steps the iteration has used \(k\) matrix–vector products and \(O(k^2n)\) additional operations, and it stores \(k+1\) vectors of length \(n\). The orthogonalization cost and storage both grow with \(k\). For a symmetric matrix, the referenced section shows that most of the coefficients \(h_{ij}\) vanish and that the growth disappears.

title: 16  Krylov Subspaces and the Arnoldi Process
text:
16.3 Ritz Pairs and Breakdown
The matrix \(\bH_k\) is small, so its eigenvalues can be computed by the dense QR algorithm. Its eigenpairs, lifted back to \(\fR^n\) through \(\bV_k\), serve as approximate eigenpairs of \(\bA\). The Arnoldi relation measures their quality without any further products with \(\bA\).






NoteDefinition: Ritz Pairs



Let \(\bH_k\bs=\theta\bs\) with \(\|\bs\|_2=1\). The scalar \(\theta\) is a Ritz value and the unit vector \(\tilde{\bu}=\bV_k\bs\in\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\) is the corresponding Ritz vector of \(\bA\) with respect to \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\).








NoteTheorem: Residual of a Ritz Pair



Let \((\theta,\tilde{\bu})\) be a Ritz pair with \(\tilde{\bu}=\bV_k\bs\), and let \(s_k\) denote the last entry of \(\bs\). Then \[
\begin{align}
\bA\tilde{\bu}-\theta\tilde{\bu}=h_{k+1,k}s_k\,\bv_{k+1},
    \qquad
    \|\bA\tilde{\bu}-\theta\tilde{\bu}\|_2=h_{k+1,k}|s_k|.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Multiply the Arnoldi relation by \(\bs\) and use \(\bH_k\bs=\theta\bs\). Identify the single remaining term, and take its norm. Explain why this residual evaluation needs no new product with \(\bA\).


The residual norm depends only on \(h_{k+1,k}\) and the last entry of a \(k\)-dimensional eigenvector. We can therefore monitor convergence of every Ritz pair at each step and form \(\tilde{\bu}=\bV_k\bs\) only for the pairs that have converged. A small residual shows that \((\theta,\tilde{\bu})\) is an exact eigenpair of a nearby matrix. For a symmetric matrix, the referenced result then places an eigenvalue within the residual norm of \(\theta\). For a nonnormal diagonalizable matrix, the referenced result multiplies this distance by the condition number of the eigenvector basis, which can be large.






NoteCorollary: Breakdown Gives Exact Eigenvalues



If the Arnoldi iteration stops at step \(k\) because \(h_{k+1,k}=0\), then \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)\) is invariant under \(\bA\), and every Ritz pair is an exact eigenpair of \(\bA\).








TipProof





At breakdown, the unnormalized vector remaining after orthogonalization is zero. A vector \(\bv_{k+1}\) is therefore not defined, but it is also unnecessary: the column equations give the shortened identity \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bV_k=\bV_k\bH_k.
\end{align}
\]

An arbitrary vector in the Krylov space has the form \(\bx=\bV_k\by\). Applying \(\bA\) gives \(\bA\bx=\bV_k\bH_k\by\), which is another linear combination of the columns of \(\bV_k\). Thus the space is invariant.
Let \(\bH_k\bs=\theta\bs\) with \(\bs\neq\bzero\). Multiply by \(\bV_k\) and use the shortened identity: \[
\begin{align}
\bA(\bV_k\bs)=\bV_k\bH_k\bs=\theta(\bV_k\bs).
\end{align}
\] The lifted vector is nonzero because \(\|\bV_k\bs\|_2=\|\bs\|_2>0\). It is therefore an eigenvector, not merely a zero vector satisfying the equation. Every Ritz pair is consequently exact.










WarningExercise



(Exact termination) Suppose \(\bv\) is a combination of exactly \(m\) eigenvectors of a diagonalizable matrix \(\bA\), with nonzero coefficients and distinct eigenvalues. Prove that \(\dim\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv)=\min(k,m)\), and use the referenced result and the referenced result to conclude that the Arnoldi iteration stops at step \(m\) with those \(m\) eigenvalues as its Ritz values.

title: 17  The Lanczos Algorithm
text:
17.1 The Three-Term Recurrence
When \(\bA\) is real symmetric, the Arnoldi process of the referenced section simplifies in two ways. First, the projected matrix \(\bH_k=\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k\) is symmetric as well as Hessenberg, so it is tridiagonal. Each new basis vector then needs to be orthogonalized only against the two preceding ones, and the cost per step no longer grows with \(k\). Second, the Rayleigh quotient characterization of the referenced result applies to the projected matrix. The characterization shows that the extreme Ritz values are the best estimates of the extreme eigenvalues available from the Krylov subspace.
We first derive the three-term recurrence that defines the Lanczos algorithm (Lanczos 1950). We then show that the extreme Ritz values move monotonically toward the extreme eigenvalues and that they are never worse than the power-iteration estimate obtained with the same number of products. A numerical example compares the two methods. The section ends with the loss of orthogonality that occurs in floating-point arithmetic.
In the Arnoldi iteration, the coefficient \(h_{ij}\) is the component of \(\bA\bv_j\) along \(\bv_i\). the referenced result shows that these components vanish for \(i<j-1\) in exact arithmetic, so the inner loop of Step 2 reduces to two subtractions. The coefficient for \(i=j-1\) is already known from the previous step. Substituting these facts into the referenced result gives the Lanczos iteration.

title: 17  The Lanczos Algorithm
text:
NoteTheorem: Tridiagonal Projection



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and suppose the Arnoldi iteration (the referenced result) completes \(k\) steps. Then \(\bH_k\) is symmetric tridiagonal. Writing \(\alpha_j=h_{jj}\) and \(\beta_j=h_{j+1,j}\), we have \[
\begin{align}
\bH_k=\bT_k=\begin{pmatrix}
        \alpha_1 & \beta_1 & & \\
        \beta_1 & \alpha_2 & \ddots & \\
        & \ddots & \ddots & \beta_{k-1} \\
        & & \beta_{k-1} & \alpha_k
    \end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
\] and the Arnoldi coefficients satisfy \(h_{ij}=0\) for \(i<j-1\) and \(h_{j-1,j}=\beta_{j-1}\).








TipProof





The Arnoldi matrix has two structural properties.

Since \(\bH_k=\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k\) and \(\bA^T=\bA\), \[
\begin{align}
\bH_k^T=(\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k)^T
  =\bV_k^T\bA^T\bV_k=\bH_k.
\end{align}
\] Thus \(h_{ij}=h_{ji}\) for every pair of indices.
Arnoldi constructs an upper Hessenberg matrix, so \(h_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i>j+1\).
If \(i<j-1\), then \(j>i+1\). The Hessenberg property applied to entry \((j,i)\) gives \(h_{ji}=0\). Symmetry gives \(h_{ij}=h_{ji}=0\). Hence only the main diagonal and its two immediate neighbors can be nonzero.
The diagonal is \(\alpha_j=h_{jj}\). Arnoldi defines \(h_{j+1,j}=\beta_j\). Symmetry makes \(h_{j,j+1}=\beta_j\) as well. These are exactly the displayed tridiagonal entries, and \(h_{j-1,j}=\beta_{j-1}\).










WarningExercise



Use symmetry directly to explain why \(\bv_i^T\bA\bv_j=0\) for \(i<j-1\): move \(\bA\) to \(\bv_i\) and locate \(\bA\bv_i\) in the earlier Krylov subspace. This gives a second explanation of why the recurrence needs only two previous directions in exact arithmetic.









NoteDefinition: The Lanczos Iteration



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) be symmetric and let \(\bv_1\) be a unit vector. Set \(\bv_0=\bzero\) and \(\beta_0=0\). For \(j=1,2,...,k\):

Compute \(\bw=\bA\bv_j-\beta_{j-1}\bv_{j-1}\).
Compute \(\alpha_j=\bv_j^T\bw\) and update \(\bw\leftarrow\bw-\alpha_j\bv_j\).
Compute \(\beta_j=\|\bw\|_2\).
If \(\beta_j=0\), stop. Otherwise, set \(\bv_{j+1}=\bw/\beta_j\).









NoteCorollary: The Lanczos Relation



After \(k\) steps of the Lanczos iteration without breakdown, the matrix \(\bV_k=(\bv_1\ \cdots\ \bv_k)\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bv_1)\), and \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bV_k=\bV_k\bT_k+\beta_k\bv_{k+1}\be_k^T,
    \qquad
    \bT_k=\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Compare one Lanczos step with the corresponding Arnoldi column equation. For a symmetric matrix, the preceding theorem makes that equation \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bv_j=\beta_{j-1}\bv_{j-1}+\alpha_j\bv_j+\beta_j\bv_{j+1}.
\end{align}
\] Every earlier coefficient is zero in exact arithmetic. Subtracting the first two terms from \(\bA\bv_j\), then normalizing the remainder, is exactly the Lanczos recurrence. Thus, from the same starting vector and positive normalization by a norm, the two processes generate the same basis vectors until termination.
The Arnoldi theorem consequently supplies orthonormality and the Krylov span. To see the matrix identity directly, place the first \(k\) three-term equations side by side. The first \(k\) components form \(\bV_k\bT_k\). The only term outside these columns comes from the last equation, giving \[
\begin{align}
\bA\bV_k=\bV_k\bT_k+\beta_k\bv_{k+1}\be_k^T.
\end{align}
\] Multiplication by \(\bV_k^T\) makes the last term vanish and gives \(\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k=\bT_k\). The use of exact arithmetic matters: omitted coefficients may become nonzero under rounding.









WarningExercise



Carry out two steps of the Lanczos iteration by hand for \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(4,2,1)\) and \(\bv_1=(1,1,1)^T/\sqrt{3}\). Write down \(\alpha_1\), \(\beta_1\), \(\alpha_2\), and \(\bT_2\), and compute \(\beta_2\).








TipRemark



(Lanczos cost) In exact arithmetic, each step requires one product with \(\bA\) and \(O(n)\) further operations, independent of \(k\). Reorthogonalization in floating-point arithmetic adds work and may require storing the earlier vectors. If only eigenvalues are wanted, the iteration needs to keep just \(\bv_{j-1}\), \(\bv_j\), and the scalars \(\alpha_j,\beta_j\). If Ritz vectors are also wanted, we either store \(\bV_k\) or run the recurrence a second time to form \(\bV_k\bs\).

title: 17  The Lanczos Algorithm
text:
17.2 Rayleigh–Ritz Approximation
The Ritz pairs of the referenced result are now the eigenpairs of the symmetric tridiagonal matrix \(\bT_k\), so the Ritz values are real. the referenced result gives their residuals as \(\beta_k|s_k|\). Symmetry also lets us say how good the Ritz values are. Throughout, let \(\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\) be the eigenvalues of \(\bA\) and let \(\theta_1^{(k)}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_k^{(k)}\) be the eigenvalues of \(\bT_k\).






NoteTheorem: Rayleigh–Ritz Optimality



Let \(R(\bx)=\bx^T\bA\bx/\bx^T\bx\). The extreme Ritz values are the extreme values of the Rayleigh quotient over the Krylov subspace, \[
\begin{align}
\theta_k^{(k)}=\max_{\bx\in\mathcal{K}_k,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R(\bx),
    \qquad
    \theta_1^{(k)}=\min_{\bx\in\mathcal{K}_k,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R(\bx).
\end{align}
\] Consequently, \(\lambda_1\leq\theta_1^{(k)}\) and \(\theta_k^{(k)}\leq\lambda_n\).








TipProof





We compare two Rayleigh quotients by writing the same vector in two coordinate systems.

Since the columns of \(\bV_k\) are an orthonormal basis of \(\mathcal K_k\), each \(\bx\in\mathcal K_k\) has a unique representation \(\bx=\bV_k\by\). It is nonzero precisely when \(\by\neq\bzero\), because \(\|\bV_k\by\|_2=\|\by\|_2\).
Direct substitution gives \[
\begin{align}
\bx^T\bx&=\by^T\bV_k^T\bV_k\by=\by^T\by,\\
  \bx^T\bA\bx&=\by^T(\bV_k^T\bA\bV_k)\by=\by^T\bT_k\by.
\end{align}
\] Hence \(R(\bx)=\by^T\bT_k\by/(\by^T\by)\).
Expand \(\by\) in an orthonormal eigenbasis of the symmetric matrix \(\bT_k\). Its quotient is a weighted average of the Ritz values. Its minimum is \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) and maximum is \(\theta_k^{(k)}\), attained at the corresponding eigenvectors. The parametrization in the first step ranges over the whole Krylov space, so these are exactly the extrema claimed there.
The Rayleigh quotient of \(\bA\) is between \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_n\) on every nonzero vector. Restricting the vectors to a subspace cannot move the minimum below \(\lambda_1\) or the maximum above \(\lambda_n\). Thus \(\lambda_1\leq\theta_1^{(k)}\) and \(\theta_k^{(k)}\leq\lambda_n\).










NoteCorollary: Monotone Convergence of the Extreme Ritz Values



The Ritz values at consecutive steps interlace, \[
\begin{align}
\theta_i^{(k+1)}\leq\theta_i^{(k)}\leq\theta_{i+1}^{(k+1)},
    \qquad i=1,...,k.
\end{align}
\] In particular, \(\theta_k^{(k)}\) is nondecreasing and bounded above by \(\lambda_n\), and \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) is nonincreasing and bounded below by \(\lambda_1\). They reach the extreme eigenvalues represented in the starting vector when the corresponding invariant Krylov subspace is exhausted. Reaching \(\lambda_n\) or \(\lambda_1\) requires a nonzero starting component in its eigenspace.








WarningExercise



Apply Cauchy interlacing to \(\bT_k\) as a principal submatrix of \(\bT_{k+1}\). Deduce monotonicity of the two extreme Ritz values. Does monotonicity alone show that their limits are the extreme eigenvalues of \(\bA\)? Examine a starting vector orthogonal to an extreme eigenspace.








WarningExercise



For \(\bT_2\) from the previous exercise, compute both Ritz values and their residuals using the referenced result. Verify the interlacing inequalities of the referenced result between the Ritz value \(\theta_1^{(1)}=\alpha_1\), the two eigenvalues of \(\bT_2\), and the eigenvalues of \(\bA\).








NoteCorollary: Lanczos Improves on Power Iteration



Let \(\bA\) be symmetric positive definite, and let \(\lambda^{(k-1)}\) be the Rayleigh quotient estimate of the referenced result after \(k-1\) power steps from \(\bv^{(0)}=\bv_1\). Both \(\lambda^{(k-1)}\) and \(\theta_k^{(k)}\) require \(k\) products with \(\bA\), and \[
\begin{align}
\lambda^{(k-1)}\leq\theta_k^{(k)}\leq\lambda_n.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





After \(k-1\) normalized power steps, the vector \(\bv^{(k-1)}\) is a nonzero scalar multiple of \(\bA^{k-1}\bv_1\). This follows by induction, since normalizing after each multiplication changes only a scalar factor. Therefore it belongs to \(\mathcal K_k\).
The Rayleigh–Ritz theorem maximizes the Rayleigh quotient over every nonzero vector in this space. The power iterate is one candidate, so \[
\begin{align}
\lambda^{(k-1)}=R(\bv^{(k-1)})
\leq\max_{\bx\in\mathcal K_k\setminus\{\bzero\}}R(\bx)
=\theta_k^{(k)}\leq\lambda_n.
\end{align}
\] Each comparison concerns the same initial vector and the same matrix.
For the product count, \(k-1\) multiplications form the power iterate. Computing its Rayleigh quotient requires one more product with \(\bA\). Thus the quoted power estimate uses \(k\) products. Lanczos uses one product in each of \(k\) steps and obtains \(\bT_k\) from those products. Its largest eigenvalue needs no further product with \(\bA\).
Positive definiteness ensures all eigenvalues are positive. Hence the eigenvalue of largest magnitude targeted by power iteration is the largest algebraic eigenvalue \(\lambda_n\), the same endpoint being estimated by the largest Ritz value.



The polynomial form of the referenced result explains the size of the improvement. Every vector in \(\mathcal{K}_k\) is \(p(\bA)\bv_1\) for some \(p\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}\). Expanding \(\bv_1=\sum_i c_i\bq_i\) in the eigenvectors of \(\bA\) gives \[
\begin{align}
\theta_k^{(k)}=\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}}R(p(\bA)\bv_1)
    =\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\,p(\lambda_i)^2c_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n p(\lambda_i)^2c_i^2}.
\end{align}
\] The quotient is close to \(\lambda_n\) when \(p\) is large at \(\lambda_n\) and small on the rest of the spectrum. Power iteration is restricted to \(p(t)=t^{k-1}\), which separates \(\lambda_n\) from \(\lambda_{n-1}\) only by the factor \((\lambda_{n-1}/\lambda_n)^{k-1}\). Lanczos implicitly selects the best polynomial. A shifted Chebyshev polynomial, which is bounded by one on \([\lambda_1,\lambda_{n-1}]\) and grows rapidly outside it, gives the following bound.






TipRemark



(Kaniel–Paige bound) Assume \(\lambda_n>\lambda_{n-1}>\lambda_1\) and \(\bv_1^T\bq_n\neq0\). Let \(\phi\in[0,\pi/2)\) be the acute angle between \(\bv_1\) and the eigenvector \(\bq_n\), let \(\gamma=(\lambda_n-\lambda_{n-1})/(\lambda_{n-1}-\lambda_1)\), and let \(T_m(x)=\cosh(m\operatorname{arccosh}x)\) for \(x\geq1\). Then \[
\begin{align}
0\leq\lambda_n-\theta_k^{(k)}\leq(\lambda_n-\lambda_1)\left(\frac{\tan\phi}{T_{k-1}(1+2\gamma)}\right)^2.
\end{align}
\] A proof is given by Golub and Van Loan (Golub and Van Loan 2013). Since \(T_m(1+2\gamma)\) grows roughly like \((1+2\sqrt{\gamma})^m\) when \(\gamma\) is small, the error decreases geometrically at a rate set by the square root of the relative gap. A square root of the same kind appears in the conjugate gradient bound of the referenced result. The analogous bound for \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) follows by applying the result to \(-\bA\). Interior eigenvalues admit weaker bounds and converge more slowly, because no low-degree polynomial can be large at an interior point and small on both sides of it.








NoteExample



(Lanczos and power iteration on a model spectrum) Let \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,...,100)\) and \(\bv_1=(1,...,1)^T/10\). We run Lanczos with full reorthogonalization, so that the computed Ritz values agree with exact arithmetic to rounding level, and compare the error in the largest Ritz value with the error in the power-iteration estimate after the same number of products.
The relative gap is \(\gamma=1/98\), and the power-iteration ratio is \(\lambda_{99}/\lambda_{100}=0.99\). After 40 products the power-iteration estimate still has an absolute error of about \(0.82\), whereas the largest Ritz value is correct to about eight significant digits. The bound is valid but conservative at every step. By the symmetry of this spectrum about \(50.5\) and of the starting vector, the error in \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) is the same as the error in \(\theta_k^{(k)}\).
At \(k=40\) the residual of the referenced result for the largest Ritz pair is \(3.7\times10^{-3}\), about four orders of magnitude larger than the eigenvalue error. the referenced result explains the difference. The corollary bounds the distance from the Ritz value to the nearest eigenvalue by the squared residual divided by the distance \(\delta\) from the Ritz value to the other eigenvalues. Here \(\delta\) is about one, and the bound \(1.4\times10^{-5}\) is consistent with the observed error.








TipRemark



(Lanczos and conjugate gradients) The conjugate gradient method of the referenced section builds the same Krylov subspace \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\br^{(0)})\) for a symmetric positive definite system. Its residuals are multiples of the Lanczos vectors started from \(\bv_1=\br^{(0)}/\|\br^{(0)}\|_2\), and its coefficients determine the entries of \(\bT_k\). the referenced section derives this correspondence and uses it to estimate the extreme eigenvalues during a CG solve.

title: 17  The Lanczos Algorithm
section: 17.3 Loss of Orthogonality and Ghost Eigenvalues
text:
17.3 Loss of Orthogonality and Ghost Eigenvalues
the referenced result relies on the exact orthogonality of \(\bv_{j+1}\) to \(\bv_1,...,\bv_{j-2}\). The Lanczos iteration never enforces this orthogonality explicitly, so rounding errors are free to destroy it.






TipRemark



(Paige’s analysis) In floating-point arithmetic, the computed Lanczos vectors gradually lose mutual orthogonality. Paige showed that the loss is not random (Paige 1976). Let \((\theta_i,\tilde{\bu}_i)\) be a Ritz pair computed from \(\bT_k\), and let \(u\) denote the unit roundoff. Paige’s analysis gives \[
\begin{align}
\beta_k|s_{k,i}|\,|\tilde{\bu}_i^T\bv_{k+1}|\ \text{has a rounding-error scale of order }u\|\bA\|_2.
\end{align}
\] The denominator is the residual of the referenced result. This relation describes a rounding-level scale rather than an equality or a universal estimate for each run. The new Lanczos vector can therefore acquire a component along \(\tilde{\bu}_i\) precisely as that Ritz pair converges, and orthogonality is lost in the directions of converged Ritz vectors. Once orthogonality to a converged Ritz vector is lost, the iteration begins to approximate the same eigenvalue again and produces repeated copies of it, known as ghost eigenvalues. The number of such copies and the steps at which they appear depend on rounding and implementation. The experiment below asks you to observe their appearance rather than predict a fixed count.








TipRemark



(Remedies for ghost eigenvalues) Practical implementations use one of three strategies.

Full reorthogonalization. We orthogonalize each new vector against all previous Lanczos vectors. This restores the behavior of exact arithmetic at the Arnoldi cost of \(O(k^2n)\) operations and \(O(kn)\) storage.
Selective reorthogonalization. We orthogonalize only against converged Ritz vectors, and only when Paige’s analysis indicates that orthogonality to them has been lost. The cost is proportional to the number of converged Ritz vectors.
Cullum–Willoughby identification. We run the iteration without reorthogonalization and discard spurious Ritz values afterward by comparing the eigenvalues of \(\bT_k\) with those of the matrix obtained by deleting its first row and column.

text:
17.4 Further Exercises






WarningExercise



Using the referenced result, show that \(\theta_{k-1}^{(k)}=\max_{S}\min_{\bx\in S,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R(\bx)\), where \(S\) ranges over two-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathcal{K}_k\). Conclude that \(\theta_{k-1}^{(k)}\leq\lambda_{n-1}\).








WarningExercise



Let \(\bA\) be symmetric positive definite. Show that the power-iteration estimate satisfies \(\lambda_n-\lambda^{(k-1)}\leq(\lambda_n-\lambda_1)\tan^2\phi\,(\lambda_{n-1}/\lambda_n)^{2(k-1)}\), where \(\phi\) is the angle between \(\bv_1\) and \(\bq_n\). Compare the rate with the Kaniel–Paige bound when \(\gamma\) is small.








WarningExercise



Implement the referenced result with an option for full reorthogonalization. Reproduce the table in the example above, and plot all Ritz values against \(k\) for \(k\leq200\) with and without reorthogonalization. Identify the steps at which ghost copies of \(\lambda_{100}\) appear, and relate them to the step at which the largest Ritz value converged.








WarningExercise



Repeat the previous computation with \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,...,99,110)\). Explain, using the polynomial characterization, why the largest Ritz value now converges much faster while the convergence of \(\theta_1^{(k)}\) is essentially unchanged.

Horn and Johnson are a reference for the matrix structure behind the spectral results (Horn and Johnson 2012). The computational treatment in Golub and Van Loan includes symmetric eigensolvers and the SVD (Golub and Van Loan 2013). The original Lanczos and Golub–Kahan papers show how two algorithms in these chapters first appeared (Lanczos 1950; Golub and Kahan 1965).

title: 18  Polynomial and Spline Interpolation
text:
18.1 Existence, Uniqueness, and the Vandermonde Matrix
Suppose a function is known only through measured or computed values at a few points. To estimate a value between those points, we can construct a simpler function that agrees with the available values. Interpolation imposes exact agreement at the data points. It differs from least squares, which permits a nonzero residual there.
Two distinct points determine a line. We ask whether \(n+1\) distinct points similarly determine a polynomial of degree at most \(n\), how to evaluate it, and how far it can lie from the function that supplied the data. When a single polynomial is unsuitable, we use a different cubic polynomial on each subinterval and join the pieces smoothly.

title: 18  Polynomial and Spline Interpolation
text:
NoteTheorem: Existence and Uniqueness of the Interpolating Polynomial



Let \(x_0, x_1, ..., x_n\) be \(n+1\) pairwise distinct real numbers, and let \(y_0, y_1, ..., y_n\) be arbitrary real numbers. There exists a unique polynomial \(P_n \in \mathcal{P}_n\) of degree at most \(n\) such that \(P_n(x_i) = y_i\) for all \(i = 0, 1, ..., n\).








TipProof





We first prove that two candidate interpolants cannot differ. Suppose \(P_n(x_i)=Q_n(x_i)=y_i\) for every node. Their difference \(R=P_n-Q_n\) has degree at most \(n\) and vanishes at all \(n+1\) distinct nodes. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(n\) has at most \(n\) distinct roots. Hence \(R\) must be the zero polynomial, so \(P_n=Q_n\).
This proves at most one interpolant exists. To prove that one actually exists for arbitrary data, write \[
\begin{align}
P_n(x)=c_0+c_1x+\cdots+c_nx^n.
\end{align}
\] The interpolation condition at node \(x_i\) is \(\sum_{j=0}^nc_jx_i^j=y_i\). These \(n+1\) equations form a square system \(\bV\bc=\by\), where row \(i\) of \(\bV\) is \((1,x_i,...,x_i^n)\).
Suppose \(\bV\bc=\bzero\). Then the polynomial with coefficients \(\bc\) vanishes at every node. By the same root-count argument it is the zero polynomial, meaning every \(c_j\) is zero. Thus \(\bV\) has a trivial null space. Rank–nullity makes its rank \(n+1\), so its range is all of \(\fR^{n+1}\). It therefore has a solution for every data vector \(\by\).
The coefficients of that solution define an interpolating polynomial, proving existence. The uniqueness argument applies to every pair of such polynomials and completes the theorem. Distinctness of the nodes was essential to the root count.









TipRemark



Although the Vandermonde matrix provides a constructive proof of existence, solving \(\bV\bc=\by\) in the monomial basis is often a poor numerical representation. Its condition number depends on the nodes and their scaling and can grow rapidly with degree. A large coefficient error does not imply that the interpolation problem itself is ill-posed. It may instead reflect an ill-conditioned choice of basis. The Lagrange and barycentric forms avoid solving for monomial coefficients.

title: 18  Polynomial and Spline Interpolation
18  Polynomial and Spline Interpolation
18  Polynomial and Spline Interpolation
18  Polynomial and Spline Interpolation
text:
18.5 Runge’s Phenomenon and Chebyshev Nodes
The error bound contains two decoupled components: \[
\begin{align}
\|f - P_n\|_\infty \leq \frac{\|f^{(n+1)}\|_\infty}{(n+1)!} \|\omega_{n+1}\|_\infty.
\end{align}
\] The derivative term \(\|f^{(n+1)}\|_\infty\) depends entirely on the analytical smoothness of \(f\), while \(\|\omega_{n+1}\|_\infty = \max_{x \in [a, b]} |\prod_{j=0}^n (x - x_j)|\) depends exclusively on the geometric placement of the interpolation nodes.






TipRemark



(Runge phenomenon) Analyticity alone does not make equally spaced interpolation converge. For Runge’s function \(f(x)=1/(1+25x^2)\), the interpolants on equally spaced nodes develop increasing endpoint oscillations and satisfy \[
\begin{align}
\lim_{n \to \infty} \|f - P_n\|_\infty = \infty,
\end{align}
\] even though \(f\) is analytic on the real interval. The growing Lebesgue constant amplifies the approximation error, while the nearby complex poles at \(\pm i/5\) limit the rate of polynomial approximation. The derivative remainder bound above warns that convergence is not automatic, but a divergent upper bound by itself would not prove divergence.


The nodal factor can be made small by placing the nodes well. On \([-1,1]\), the best choice is the set of Chebyshev points \(x_k=\cos\big((2k+1)\pi/(2n+2)\big)\), \(k=0,...,n\), the roots of the Chebyshev polynomial \(T_{n+1}\). For these nodes \(\|\omega_{n+1}\|_\infty=2^{-n}\), the smallest value attained by any monic polynomial of degree \(n+1\). the referenced section proves this minimax property and shows that interpolation at Chebyshev points converges geometrically for functions that are analytic in a neighborhood of \([-1,1]\).






TipRemark



The Lebesgue constant \(\Lambda_n = \max_{x \in [a, b]} \sum_{i=0}^n |L_i(x)|\) bounds the stability of polynomial interpolation: \(\|f - P_n\|_\infty \leq (1 + \Lambda_n) \min_{Q \in \mathcal{P}_n} \|f - Q\|_\infty\).

For equally spaced nodes, \(\Lambda_n = \Theta\left(\frac{2^n}{n \log n}\right)\) grows exponentially.
For Chebyshev nodes, \(\Lambda_n = \frac{2}{\pi} \log(n+1) + O(1)\) grows only logarithmically, remaining near-optimal.

title: 19  Chebyshev Polynomials and Minimax Approximation
text:
19.1 Interpolation Error and Conditioning
The interpolation error contains a product of distances to the nodes. We can reduce its largest value by changing the nodes. Chebyshev polynomials solve this particular optimization problem. Their roots give nodes that cluster near the endpoints, where equally spaced interpolation can oscillate badly.
The construction begins with equally spaced angles and the substitution \(x=\cos\theta\). We derive the polynomial recurrence from a cosine identity, then use alternating extreme values to prove the minimax property. The final convergence result requires complex analysis and can be read after the polynomial arguments.
Approximating a continuous function \(f \in C([-1, 1])\) by polynomial interpolation encounters two distinct failure modes. The first is algebraic. Vandermonde systems in the monomial basis are often ill-conditioned, so a coefficient calculation may lose accuracy even when the interpolating polynomial is well defined. The second is analytical. For functions such as Runge’s example, interpolation at equally spaced nodes diverges near the endpoints even in exact arithmetic. These are different failures and require different remedies.
To study the effect of the nodes, begin with the referenced result. With \(n\) nodes \(x_1,...,x_n\) and the monic nodal polynomial \(\omega_n(x)=\prod_{j=1}^n(x-x_j)\), the theorem bounds the interpolation error by \[
\begin{align}
\|f-p_{n-1}\|_\infty\leq\frac{\|f^{(n)}\|_\infty}{n!}\,\|\omega_n\|_\infty.
\end{align}
\] The first factor depends only on \(f\), and the second only on the nodes. Choosing the nodes to minimize \(\|\omega_n\|_\infty\) is therefore a minimax problem over monic polynomials of degree \(n\), which this section solves.

title: 19  Chebyshev Polynomials and Minimax Approximation
text:
19.4 The Minimax Property and Equioscillation






NoteTheorem: Chebyshev Minimax Theorem



Let \(\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_n\) denote the set of all monic polynomials of degree \(n\) with real coefficients. Then \(2^{1-n}T_n\) is the unique solution to the minimax problem on \([-1, 1]\): \[
\begin{align}
\min_{q \in \widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_n} \|q\|_\infty = \|2^{1-n}T_n\|_\infty = 2^{1-n}.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Let \(m(x) = 2^{1-n}T_n(x) \in \widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_n\). By the referenced result, \(\|m\|_\infty = 2^{1-n}\). At the \(n+1\) extreme points \(y_j = \cos(j\pi/n)\) for \(j = 0, ..., n\), \[
\begin{align}
m(y_j) = 2^{1-n}(-1)^j.
\end{align}
\] Suppose there exists a monic polynomial \(q \in \widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_n\) such that \(\|q\|_\infty < 2^{1-n}\). Consider the difference polynomial \[
\begin{align}
r(x) = m(x) - q(x).
\end{align}
\] Because both \(m\) and \(q\) are monic polynomials of degree \(n\), the leading terms \(x^n\) cancel. Thus \(r \in \mathcal{P}_{n-1}\) has degree at most \(n-1\).
Evaluating \(r(x)\) at each extreme point \(y_j\): \[
\begin{align}
r(y_j) = m(y_j) - q(y_j) = 2^{1-n}(-1)^j - q(y_j).
\end{align}
\] Because \(|q(y_j)| \leq \|q\|_\infty < 2^{1-n}\), the sign of \(r(y_j)\) is dictated entirely by \(m(y_j)\):

When \(j\) is even, \(m(y_j) = 2^{1-n}\), so \(r(y_j) = 2^{1-n} - q(y_j) > 0\).
When \(j\) is odd, \(m(y_j) = -2^{1-n}\), so \(r(y_j) = -2^{1-n} - q(y_j) < 0\).

Thus \(r(x)\) alternates sign across the \(n+1\) ordered points \(1 = y_0 > y_1 > ... > y_n = -1\). By the Intermediate Value Theorem, \(r(x)\) must vanish at least once in each of the \(n\) disjoint open intervals \((y_{j+1}, y_j)\) for \(j = 0, ..., n-1\).
Consequently, \(r(x)\) has at least \(n\) distinct real zeros in \((-1, 1)\). However, a nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(n-1\) cannot have \(n\) roots. Therefore, \(r(x)\) must be identically zero, which contradicts the strict inequality \(\|q\|_\infty < 2^{1-n}\). This proves that \(\|q\|_\infty \geq 2^{1-n}\) for all monic \(q \in \widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_n\).
The strict sign-change argument proves minimality, but it does not by itself prove uniqueness: with a competing norm equal to the minimum, some signs may be zero. We now handle these weak inequalities separately.
To establish uniqueness, suppose \(\|q\|_\infty=2^{1-n}\) and retain \(r=m-q\in\mathcal{P}_{n-1}\). The weak inequalities \[
\begin{align}
(-1)^j r(y_j)\geq0,
    \qquad j=0,...,n,
\end{align}
\] follow from \(m(y_j)=2^{1-n}(-1)^j\) and \(|q(y_j)|\leq2^{1-n}\). The difference has degree at most \(n-1\) because the leading coefficients of the two monic degree-\(n\) polynomials cancel.
Interpolate \(r\) at \(y_0,...,y_n\) using the Lagrange formula. Its coefficient of \(x^n\) is zero because \(\deg r\leq n-1\). Comparing that coefficient gives \[
\begin{align}
0
    =\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{r(y_j)}{\prod_{k\neq j}(y_j-y_k)}.
\end{align}
\] Because the nodes are ordered \(1 = y_0 > y_1 > ... > y_n = -1\), the product in the denominator has exactly \(j\) negative factors: \[
\begin{align}
\operatorname{sign}\left(\prod_{k\neq j}(y_j-y_k)\right)
    = \operatorname{sign}\left(\prod_{k<j}(y_j-y_k) \prod_{k>j}(y_j-y_k)\right)
    = (-1)^j.
\end{align}
\] Therefore \[
\begin{align}
\frac{r(y_j)}{\prod_{k\neq j}(y_j-y_k)}
    = \frac{(-1)^j r(y_j)}{\left|\prod_{k\neq j}(y_j-y_k)\right|} \geq 0.
\end{align}
\] A sum of non-negative terms can vanish only if each numerator \((-1)^j r(y_j)\) is zero. Thus \(r(y_j) = 0\) for all \(j = 0, ..., n\). Since \(r \in \mathcal{P}_{n-1}\) has \(n+1\) distinct roots, \(r \equiv 0\), proving \(q \equiv m\).
All terms in the zero sum have been shown nonnegative individually. If one were positive, the entire sum would be positive. Hence each must be zero. Since every denominator is nonzero, this forces \(r(y_j)=0\) at all nodes, completing the uniqueness argument without assuming strict sign changes.









WarningExercise



(Equioscillation on a concrete polynomial) Let \(m(x)=2^{1-4}T_4(x)\).

Expand \(m\) in the monomial basis and verify that it is monic.
Evaluate \(m\) at \(y_j=\cos(j\pi/4)\) for \(j=0,...,4\) and verify the alternating values \(\pm1/8\).
Choose any monic quartic \(q\neq m\), evaluate it on a fine grid, and confirm numerically that \(\|q\|_\infty>1/8\), as predicted by the referenced result.









TipRemark



(Lebesgue constant growth) For any grid of \(n\) interpolation nodes \(X_n\), the interpolation projection \(I_n: C([-1, 1]) \to \mathcal{P}_{n-1}\) satisfies the Lebesgue inequality \(\|f - I_n f\|_\infty \leq (1 + \Lambda_n) \min_{p \in \mathcal{P}_{n-1}} \|f - p\|_\infty\), where \(\Lambda_n\) is the Lebesgue constant. For equally spaced nodes, \(\Lambda_n \sim \frac{2^n}{e n \log n}\), which diverges exponentially and induces Runge’s phenomenon. For Chebyshev nodes, \(\Lambda_n \leq \frac{2}{\pi}\log n + 1\), guaranteeing that Chebyshev interpolation converges at a rate within a logarithmic factor of the optimal polynomial approximation.

title: 20  Numerical Quadrature
text:
20.1 Degree of Exactness and Interpolatory Quadrature
Numerical quadrature approximates the definite integral of a continuous function \(f : [a, b] \to \fR\) by a finite linear combination of sampled function values: \[
\begin{align}
I(f) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \approx Q_n(f) = \sum_{i=0}^n w_i f(x_i).
\end{align}
\] The points \(x_i \in [a, b]\) are the quadrature nodes, and the scalar coefficients \(w_i \in \fR\) are the quadrature weights. The design of quadrature rules balances algebraic precision, computational cost, and numerical stability.
The standard criterion for evaluating a quadrature rule is its algebraic precision, defined by the highest degree of polynomials it integrates without error.

title: 20  Numerical Quadrature
text:
NoteExample



On \([0,1]\), suppose we use just the two endpoint values and seek \(Q(f)=w_0f(0)+w_1f(1)\). Exact integration of \(1\) requires \(w_0+w_1=1\). Exact integration of \(x\) requires \(w_1=1/2\). Thus both weights are \(1/2\), giving the trapezoidal rule.








WarningExercise



Test this rule on \(x^2\). Is the quadrature value above or below the integral? Derive the endpoint weights on \([a,b]\) in the same way. Relate the result to the area under the line joining the two endpoint values.








NoteDefinition: Degree of Exactness (Algebraic Precision)



A quadrature rule \(Q_n\) has degree of exactness \(m\) if \[
\begin{align}
Q_n(p) = \int_a^b p(x)\,dx \qquad \text{for all } p \in \mathcal{P}_m,
\end{align}
\] and there exists at least one polynomial \(q \in \mathcal{P}_{m+1}\) for which \(Q_n(q) \neq \int_a^b q(x)\,dx\).








NoteTheorem: Interpolatory Quadrature Rules



Let \(x_0, x_1, ..., x_n\) be \(n+1\) distinct nodes in \([a, b]\). The interpolatory quadrature rule approximates \(I(f)\) by integrating the polynomial interpolant \(P_n(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n f(x_i) L_i(x)\) in Lagrange form: \[
\begin{align}
Q_n(f) = \int_a^b P_n(x)\,dx = \sum_{i=0}^n w_i f(x_i), \qquad w_i = \int_a^b L_i(x)\,dx.
\end{align}
\] Every interpolatory quadrature rule with \(n+1\) distinct nodes has degree of exactness at least \(n\).








TipProof





The Lagrange polynomials satisfy \(L_i(x_j)=\delta_{ij}\). Therefore for any data values \(f(x_i)\), the polynomial \[
\begin{align}
P_n(x)=\sum_{i=0}^n f(x_i)L_i(x)
\end{align}
\] interpolates those values. Its integral is a finite sum, so linearity of integration gives \[
\begin{align}
\int_a^bP_n(x)\,dx
=\sum_{i=0}^nf(x_i)\int_a^bL_i(x)\,dx
=\sum_{i=0}^nw_i f(x_i).
\end{align}
\] This is the proposed quadrature rule.
To establish exactness, take a polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(n\). It already satisfies the interpolation conditions for its own data. Uniqueness of interpolation implies that the constructed \(P_n\) equals \(p\) everywhere, not only at the nodes. Consequently \[
\begin{align}
Q_n(p)=\int_a^bP_n(x)\,dx=\int_a^bp(x)\,dx.
\end{align}
\] The argument applies to every polynomial in \(\mathcal P_n\). Thus the rule has degree of exactness at least \(n\). It may be exact for higher degrees because additional cancellation can occur, so this argument establishes a lower bound for the degree rather than its exact value.









WarningExercise



Integrate \(p(x)=\sum_i p(x_i)L_i(x)\) term by term to prove the theorem. Deduce \(\sum_iw_i=b-a\) by choosing \(p=1\). For the nodes \(-1,0,1\), integrate the three Lagrange basis polynomials to obtain Simpson’s weights. Use symmetry to explain why the rule is exact for cubics as well as quadratics.

title: 20  Numerical Quadrature
20  Numerical Quadrature
text:
20.3 Peano Kernel Error Representation
A quadrature error \(E(f)\) is linear in \(f\). If the rule integrates every polynomial of degree at most \(m\) exactly, those polynomial terms contribute no error. Taylor’s formula then lets us express the whole error using \(f^{(m+1)}\). The function multiplying this derivative under the integral is called the Peano kernel. Once we know that function, we can estimate the error for many different integrands without repeating the derivation.






NoteTheorem: Peano Kernel Theorem



Let \(Q\) be a quadrature rule on \([a, b]\) with error functional \(E(f) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx - Q(f)\). If \(E(p) = 0\) for all \(p \in \mathcal{P}_m\), then for every \(f \in C^{m+1}[a, b]\), \[
\begin{align}
E(f) = \int_a^b f^{(m+1)}(t) K(t)\,dt,
\end{align}
\] where the Peano kernel \(K(t)\) is defined by applying the error functional to the truncated power function: \[
\begin{align}
K(t) = \frac{1}{m!} E_x \left( (x - t)_+^m \right), \qquad (x - t)_+ = \max(0, x - t).
\end{align}
\] For \(m=0\), interpret \((x-t)_+^0\) as \(1\) when \(x>t\) and \(0\) when \(x\leq t\).
If \(K(t)\) does not change sign on \([a, b]\), then there exists \(\xi \in (a, b)\) such that \[
\begin{align}
E(f) = \frac{f^{(m+1)}(\xi)}{(m+1)!} E(x^{m+1}).
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





By Taylor’s theorem with integral remainder expanded about \(a\): \[
\begin{align}
f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^m \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!} (x - a)^k + \frac{1}{m!} \int_a^x f^{(m+1)}(t) (x - t)^m\,dt.
\end{align}
\] Extending the upper integration limit using the truncated power notation \((x - t)_+^m\) allows writing the remainder as \(\frac{1}{m!} \int_a^b f^{(m+1)}(t) (x - t)_+^m\,dt\). The truncated power makes the integrand zero for \(t>x\), so extending the upper limit adds only zeros. It is useful because both the quadrature sum and the integral can then act on functions of \(x\) over a fixed interval.
Applying the linear functional \(E\) to both sides, the polynomial terms vanish because \(E(p) = 0\) for all \(p \in \mathcal{P}_m\). Exchanging the order of integration and the functional gives \[
\begin{align}
E(f)&=E_x\left(\frac1{m!}\int_a^b
         f^{(m+1)}(t)(x-t)_+^m\,dt\right)\\
    &=\int_a^b f^{(m+1)}(t)
       \left[\frac1{m!}E_x((x-t)_+^m)\right]dt\\
    &=\int_a^b f^{(m+1)}(t)K(t)\,dt.
\end{align}
\] Interchanging a finite quadrature sum with integration follows from linearity. Interchanging the two ordinary integrals follows from continuity and integrability on the compact triangle. Thus no convergence of an infinite sum is needed in this step.
If \(K\) has constant sign, the weighted mean-value theorem gives \[
\begin{align}
E(f)=f^{(m+1)}(\xi)\int_a^b K(t)\,dt.
\end{align}
\] Testing the identity with \(f(x) = x^{m+1}\), we have \(f^{(m+1)}(x) = (m+1)!\), which yields \(E(x^{m+1}) = (m+1)! \int_a^b K(t)\,dt\). Substituting this integral proves the claim.
If \(K\) is identically zero, the error is zero and the final identity is immediate. Otherwise use \(|K|\) as a nonnegative weight: the integral average of the continuous derivative lies between its minimum and maximum, so the intermediate value theorem supplies a point attaining that average. This is the weighted mean-value step used above.









WarningExercise



Peano kernel of the trapezoidal rule. Consider the single-panel trapezoidal rule on \([0, h]\) with error functional \(E(f) = \int_0^h f(x)\,dx - \frac{h}{2}[f(0) + f(h)]\).

Show that \(E(1) = 0\) and \(E(x) = 0\), so \(m = 1\).
Evaluate the Peano kernel \(K(t) = E_x((x - t)_+) = \int_0^h (x - t)_+\,dx - \frac{h}{2}[(0 - t)_+ + (h - t)_+]\).
Show that \(K(t) = \frac{1}{2}t(t - h) \leq 0\) for all \(t \in [0, h]\).
Apply the referenced result to compute \(\int_0^h K(t)\,dt = -\frac{h^3}{12}\) and recover the exact error term \(-\frac{h^3}{12} f''(\xi)\).

title: 21  Fourier Analysis
text:
21.1 The Discrete Fourier Transform
A periodic vector can be described by the amplitude of each oscillation it contains. The discrete Fourier transform is a change from its sampled values to these amplitudes. We construct the oscillating basis vectors, prove their orthogonality, and use the basis to simplify shifts and circular convolution.
The fast Fourier transform computes the same change of basis by dividing one transform into smaller transforms. Finally, differentiating each oscillation gives an algorithm for differentiating smooth periodic functions from their sampled values.
We consider discrete signals defined on a uniform periodic grid of \(n\) points. The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) expands a vector in the orthonormal basis of discrete complex exponentials.
For integer frequency \(k\), the vector with entries \(e^{2\pi i jk/n}\) samples one complex oscillation. Frequency zero is constant. Increasing \(k\) increases the number of turns made by the complex phase over one period. Taking inner products with these vectors measures the corresponding amplitudes. The minus sign in the forward transform comes from conjugating the basis vectors.

title: 21  Fourier Analysis
text:
NoteDefinition: Periodic Grid Signal



Let \(t_j=2\pi j/n\) for \(j=0,...,n-1\) be grid points in one period. A vector \(\bx\in\fC^n\) stores samples \(x_j=f(t_j)\). Extend its entries periodically by \(x_{j+n}=x_j\). The grid coordinates themselves satisfy \(t_{j+n}=t_j+2\pi\), so it is the sampled values that repeat.









NoteDefinition: DFT Matrix



Let \(\omega_n = e^{-2\pi i / n}\) denote the primitive \(n\)-th root of unity. The Discrete Fourier Transform matrix \(\bF \in \fC^{n \times n}\) has entries \[
\begin{align}
F_{jk} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{jk} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} e^{-2\pi i j k / n}, \qquad 0 \leq j, k \leq n-1.
\end{align}
\] The forward transform maps a spatial signal \(\bx \in \fC^n\) to its frequency representation \(\hat{\bx} = \bF\bx\).








NoteLemma: Unitarity of the DFT Matrix



The normalized DFT matrix \(\bF\) is unitary: \[
\begin{align}
\bF^* \bF = \bF \bF^* = \bI_n.
\end{align}
\] Consequently, the inverse transform is given by the conjugate transpose: \(\bF^{-1} = \bF^*\).








TipProof





We evaluate the \((j, \ell)\) entry of the Gram matrix product \(\bF^* \bF\). Because \((\bF^*)_{jk} = \overline{F_{kj}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{-jk}\), we have \[
\begin{align}
(\bF^* \bF)_{j\ell} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (\bF^*)_{jk} F_{k\ell} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \omega_n^{-jk} \omega_n^{k\ell} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \left( \omega_n^{\ell - j} \right)^k.
\end{align}
\] The complex conjugate reverses the sign in the exponent, so the product depends only on the difference of column indices. This is why the geometric sum appears, rather than a general sum with unrelated terms.
If \(j = \ell\), each term in the summation equals \(\omega_n^0 = 1\), yielding \(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} 1 = 1\). If \(j \neq \ell\), let \(r = \omega_n^{\ell - j}\). Because \(-(n-1) \leq \ell - j \leq n-1\) and \(j \neq \ell\), the base \(r \neq 1\), while \(r^n = (\omega_n^n)^{\ell - j} = 1^{\ell - j} = 1\). The finite geometric series sums to \[
\begin{align}
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} r^k = \frac{1 - r^n}{1 - r} = \frac{1 - 1}{1 - r} = 0.
\end{align}
\] Therefore, \((\bF^* \bF)_{j\ell} = \delta_{j\ell}\), which establishes \(\bF^* \bF = \bI_n\).
The Gram matrix is therefore the identity. Since \(\bF\) is square, \(\bF^*\bF=\bI\) makes \(\bF\) nonsingular and gives \(\bF^{-1}=\bF^*\). Multiplication in the reverse order then gives \(\bF\bF^*=\bI\) as well. This explains both asserted unitary identities.









WarningExercise



Unitary coordinates and geometric sums. Let \(\bF \in \fC^{4 \times 4}\) be the 4-point DFT matrix. Write out its sixteen numerical entries explicitly using powers of \(\omega_4 = -i\). Verify directly that columns 0 and 2 are orthogonal, and confirm that \(\bF^* \bF = \bI_4\).








NoteTheorem: Parseval’s Identity and Isometry



The Discrete Fourier Transform is an isometry on \(\fC^n\) with respect to the Euclidean norm: \[
\begin{align}
\|\bF\bx\|_2 = \|\bx\|_2 \qquad \text{for all } \bx \in \fC^n.
\end{align}
\] The inner product is likewise preserved: \(\langle \bF\bx, \bF\by \rangle = \langle \bx, \by \rangle\).








WarningExercise



Use \(\bF^*\bF=\bI\) to prove preservation of inner products, then set the two vectors equal to obtain Parseval’s identity. What factor appears if the forward transform is left unnormalized?








NoteDefinition: Frequency Bins and Nyquist Limit



For a signal sampled on \(n\) points with uniform spacing \(h = 2\pi / n\), integer frequency index \(k\) corresponds to the continuous Fourier mode \(e^{ikx}\). The distinct resolvable frequencies are ordered as \[
\begin{align}
0, 1, 2, ..., \lfloor n/2 \rfloor, -\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor, ..., -1.
\end{align}
\] The maximum resolvable frequency is the Nyquist frequency \(k_{\text{Nyq}} = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\). Any continuous mode with frequency \(|k| > k_{\text{Nyq}}\) aliases to a lower grid frequency satisfying \(k' \equiv k \pmod n\).








WarningExercise



On a grid of four points, write the sampled vectors for frequencies \(0\), \(1\), \(2\), and \(5\). Show that frequencies \(1\) and \(5\) give identical vectors. More generally, prove that adding \(n\) to an integer frequency leaves its samples unchanged. Why can samples alone not distinguish these frequencies?








TipRemark



(Normalization convention) Numerical libraries such as NumPy’s np.fft.fft define the forward transform without the factor \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so that \(\hat{\bx}_{\text{numpy}} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_j \omega_n^{jk}\), and place the full factor \(1/n\) in the inverse transform np.fft.ifft. This choice scales the entries by \(\sqrt{n}\) relative to the unitary operator \(\bF\) defined here.
