section: 21.2 Circulant Matrices and the Convolution Theorem
text:
21.2 Circulant Matrices and the Convolution Theorem
A linear system or filtering operation that commutes with spatial translation is represented by a circulant matrix. The Discrete Fourier Transform diagonalizes every circulant matrix.






NoteDefinition: Circulant Matrix



Let \(\bc = (c_0, c_1, ..., c_{n-1})^T \in \fC^n\). The circulant matrix \(\mathbf{C} = \operatorname{circ}(\bc) \in \fC^{n \times n}\) has entries \(C_{jk} = c_{(j - k) \pmod n}\): \[
\begin{align}
\mathbf{C} = \begin{pmatrix}
        c_0 & c_{n-1} & c_{n-2} & ... & c_1 \\
        c_1 & c_0 & c_{n-1} & ... & c_2 \\
        c_2 & c_1 & c_0 & ... & c_3 \\
        \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
        c_{n-1} & c_{n-2} & c_{n-3} & ... & c_0
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
\]








NoteTheorem: Spectral Diagonalization of Circulant Matrices



Every circulant matrix \(\mathbf{C} = \operatorname{circ}(\bc)\) is diagonalized by the unitary DFT matrix: \[
\begin{align}
\mathbf{C} = \bF^* \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bF,
\end{align}
\] where the diagonal eigenvalue matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_0, ..., \lambda_{n-1})\) has entries equal to the unnormalized DFT coefficients of the first column: \[
\begin{align}
\lambda_k = \sqrt{n} (\bF\bc)_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j \omega_n^{jk}.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Let \(\mathbf{S}\in\fR^{n\times n}\) have first column \((0,1,0,...,0)^T\) and be circulant (for \(n\geq2\)) be the cyclic permutation matrix that shifts coordinate indices forward by one: \(\mathbf{S}\bx = (x_{n-1}, x_0, x_1, ..., x_{n-2})^T\). Powers of \(\mathbf{S}\) shift indices by \(j\) positions, satisfying \(\mathbf{S}^n = \bI\). Every circulant matrix is a polynomial in \(\mathbf{S}\): \[
\begin{align}
\mathbf{C} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j \mathbf{S}^j.
\end{align}
\] The first column of \(\mathbf S^j\) is the coordinate vector with its one in cyclic position \(j\). Thus the first column of \(\sum_jc_j\mathbf S^j\) is \(\bc\). Both sides are circulant and a circulant is determined by its first column, proving the polynomial representation.
Let \(\bv_k\) denote the \(k\)-th column of \(\bF^*\), with entries \((\bv_k)_j = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{-jk}\). Multiplying by the shift matrix gives \[
\begin{align}
(\mathbf{S}\bv_k)_j = (\bv_k)_{(j-1) \pmod n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{-(j-1)k} = \omega_n^k \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega_n^{-jk} \right) = \omega_n^k (\bv_k)_j.
\end{align}
\] Thus \(\bv_k\) is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{S}\) with eigenvalue \(\omega_n^k\). Applying the polynomial representation of \(\mathbf{C}\) to \(\bv_k\) yields \[
\begin{align}
\mathbf{C}\bv_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j \mathbf{S}^j \bv_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j (\omega_n^k)^j \bv_k = \left( \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j \omega_n^{jk} \right) \bv_k = \lambda_k \bv_k.
\end{align}
\] Collecting all \(n\) eigenvector equations in matrix form gives \(\mathbf{C}\bF^* = \bF^* \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\). Multiplying on the right by \(\bF\) yields \(\mathbf{C} = \bF^* \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bF\).
The case \(n=1\) is the scalar identity and does not require a shift matrix. For larger \(n\), the factor \(\sqrt n\) in the eigenvalue formula appears because the chosen DFT is unitary, while the polynomial eigenvalue sum is unnormalized. It must not be dropped when using this normalization.









WarningExercise



Circulant spectral inversion for the periodic Poisson problem. Consider the discrete periodic Poisson equation \(-\frac{u_{j-1} - 2u_j + u_{j+1}}{h^2} = f_j\) on \(n\) points with periodic boundary conditions.

Express the coefficient matrix as a circulant matrix \(\mathbf{C} = \operatorname{circ}(\bc)\) and identify the entries of \(\bc\).
Compute the eigenvalues \(\lambda_k\) of \(\mathbf{C}\) using the referenced result. Show that \(\lambda_0 = 0\) and \(\lambda_k > 0\) for \(k = 1, ..., n-1\).
Explain why the system is solvable if and only if \(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j = 0\), and formulate an \(O(n \log n)\) solver using the FFT.









NoteTheorem: Discrete Convolution Theorem



Let \(\bc, \bx \in \fC^n\). The circular convolution \(\bz = \bc * \bx\) has components \[
\begin{align}
z_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} c_k x_{(j - k) \pmod n} = (\mathbf{C}\bx)_j, \qquad \mathbf{C} = \operatorname{circ}(\bc).
\end{align}
\] Applying the Discrete Fourier Transform converts convolution to entrywise multiplication: \[
\begin{align}
\bF(\bc * \bx) = \sqrt{n} (\bF\bc) \odot (\bF\bx),
\end{align}
\] where \(\odot\) denotes the Hadamard (entrywise) vector product.








WarningExercise



Write the convolution as \(\mathbf{C}\bx\) and substitute \(\mathbf{C}=\bF^*\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bF\). Apply \(\bF\) and use the formula for \(\lambda_k\). Account explicitly for the factor \(\sqrt n\).

title: 22  Linear Operators and the Poisson Equation
text:
22.1 Differential Operators and Discretization
To approximate a differential equation numerically, we replace its unknown function by values on a grid. A local difference formula then relates each value to its neighbors and produces a sparse linear system. We derive this system for \(-u''=f\) with prescribed endpoint values, then relate its eigenvalues to those of the differential operator.
The boundary conditions affect both solvability and the spectrum. Keeping them in the derivation will explain why this matrix is positive definite and why its condition number grows when the grid is refined.
At an interior node, the difference formula gives \(-u_{i-1}+2u_i-u_{i+1}=h^2f(x_i)\). The endpoint values \(u_0=u_{n+1}=0\) are known, so only \(u_1,...,u_n\) are unknowns. Writing one such equation per interior node gives the matrix below.
crumbs: 22  Linear Operators and the Poisson Equation

title: 22  Linear Operators and the Poisson Equation
text:
NoteDefinition: Linear Operator



A map \(\mathcal A:X\to Y\) between vector spaces is linear if \(\mathcal A(\alpha u+\beta v)=\alpha\mathcal A u+\beta\mathcal A v\) for all \(u,v\in X\) and scalars \(\alpha,\beta\). Here the vectors may be functions. Differentiation is a linear map from continuously differentiable functions to continuous functions. A matrix is the corresponding construction for finite lists of coordinates.








NoteDefinition: Dirichlet Poisson Problem



The one-dimensional Poisson problem with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary data is \[
\begin{align}
-u''(x)=f(x),\qquad 0<x<1,\qquad u(0)=u(1)=0.
\end{align}
\] The boundary conditions are part of the problem data.








NoteDefinition: Grid Function



For \(n\) interior grid points, let \(h=1/(n+1)\) and \(x_i=ih\), \(i=1,...,n\). A grid function is the vector \[
\begin{align}
\bu=(u_1,...,u_n)^T,\qquad u_i\approx u(x_i).
\end{align}
\] The boundary values are fixed separately by the boundary conditions.








NoteDefinition: Finite Difference Stencil



Approximating \(u''(x)\) on a grid with spacing \(h\): \[
\begin{align}
u''(x_k) \approx \frac{u(x_{k-1}) - 2u(x_k) + u(x_{k+1})}{h^2}.
\end{align}
\] For \(u\in C^4\), Taylor expansion gives a truncation error bounded by \(h^2\|u^{(4)}\|_\infty/12\).








WarningExercise




Taylor expand \(u(x+h)\) and \(u(x-h)\) about \(x\).
Add the two expansions.
Solve for \(u''(x)\).
Identify the leading error term and prove the \(O(h^2)\) claim in the referenced result.










WarningExercise



Write the three equations when there are three interior nodes. Next prescribe \(u(0)=\alpha\) and \(u(1)=\beta\). Show that the coefficient matrix stays the same and determine the changes in the first and last entries of the right-hand side.








NoteDefinition: 1-D Discrete Laplacian



Discretizing \(-d^2/dx^2\) on \([0,1]\) with \(u(0)=u(1)=0\) yields the tridiagonal system \(\bT \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{f}\): \[
\begin{align}
\bT = \frac{1}{h^2} \text{tridiag}(-1, 2, -1) \in \fR^{n \times n}.
\end{align}
\]








TipRemark



(Sparsity) Each row of \(\bT\) uses only the grid point and its two neighbors. This locality is why finite difference matrices are sparse.








NoteTheorem: Spectrum Convergence



Eigenvalues of \(\bT\) are \(\lambda_k = \frac{4}{h^2} \sin^2(\frac{k\pi}{2(n+1)})\). As \(n \to \infty\), \(\lambda_k \to k^2 \pi^2\) (eigenvalues of continuous \(-d^2/dx^2\)).








WarningExercise




Let \((\bv_k)_j=\sin(jk\pi h)\) with \(h=1/(n+1)\).
Compute the \(j\)-th entry of \(\bT\bv_k\).
Use \(\sin(A-B)+\sin(A+B)=2\sin A\cos B\).
Use \(1-\cos\theta=2\sin^2(\theta/2)\).
Derive the eigenvalue formula in the referenced result.
Let \(h\to 0\) with fixed \(k\) and recover \(k^2\pi^2\).









NoteTheorem: Discrete Poisson Structure



The matrix \(\bT\) in the referenced result is sparse, symmetric positive definite, and has condition number \[
\begin{align}
\kappa_2(\bT)=O(h^{-2}).
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Sparsity and symmetry follow directly from the tridiagonal stencil \(\bT = \frac{1}{h^2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1, 2, -1)\). For any grid vector \(\bu \in \fR^n\) with boundary conditions \(u_0 = u_{n+1} = 0\), the quadratic form expands as a sum of squared forward differences: \[
\begin{align}
\bu^T \bT \bu
    &= \frac{1}{h^2} \sum_{i=1}^n u_i (2u_i - u_{i-1} - u_{i+1}) \\
    &= \frac{1}{h^2} \sum_{i=1}^n (u_i^2 - u_i u_{i-1} + u_i^2 - u_i u_{i+1}) \\
    &= \frac{1}{h^2} \sum_{i=0}^n (u_{i+1} - u_i)^2.
\end{align}
\] In the sum of squared differences, each interior \(u_i^2\) occurs twice, and each neighbor product occurs with coefficient \(-2\). The endpoint squares vanish because both boundary values are zero. This reproduces exactly the expanded quadratic form and justifies the rearrangement.
Because \(u_0 = 0\), if \(\bu^T\bT\bu = 0\), then \(u_{i+1} - u_i = 0\) for all \(i\), forcing \(u_1 = ... = u_n = 0\). Hence \(\bu^T\bT\bu > 0\) for all \(\bu \neq \bzero\), proving that \(\bT\) is SPD.
By the referenced result, the extremal eigenvalues are \[
\begin{align}
\lambda_{\min} &= \lambda_1 = \frac{4}{h^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi h}{2}\right) = \frac{4}{h^2}\left(\frac{\pi h}{2} + O(h^3)\right)^2 = \pi^2 + O(h^2), \\
    \lambda_{\max} &= \lambda_n = \frac{4}{h^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{n\pi h}{2}\right) = \frac{4}{h^2}\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi h}{2}\right) = \frac{4}{h^2}(1 - O(h^2)).
\end{align}
\] The largest-mode identity uses \(n\pi h=\pi-\pi h\), so \(\sin(n\pi h/2)=\cos(\pi h/2)\). The smallest mode instead has angle tending to zero, where \(\sin z=z+O(z^3)\). These two different limits explain why one eigenvalue stays of constant size while the other grows like \(h^{-2}\).
The 2-norm condition number is therefore \[
\begin{align}
\kappa_2(\bT) = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}} = \frac{4/h^2 + O(1)}{\pi^2 + O(h^2)} = \frac{4}{\pi^2 h^2} + O(1) = O(h^{-2}).
\end{align}
\]









WarningExercise



Count the nonzero entries of \(\bT\). Then replace the Dirichlet boundary conditions by periodic conditions and form the analogous matrix for \(n\geq3\). Find a nonzero vector in its null space. Which step in the positive-definiteness proof fails, and what compatibility condition must the right-hand side satisfy?

title: 22  Linear Operators and the Poisson Equation
text:
22.2 Operator Norms and Conditioning






NoteDefinition: Boundedness



An operator is bounded if \(\|\mathcal{A}u\|_Y \leq C \|u\|_X\) for some \(C < \infty\).

Matrices are always bounded.
Boundedness of a differential operator depends on the domain and the norms. For a function on \([0,1]\), the \(L^2\) norm is \(\|u\|_{L^2}=(\int_0^1|u(x)|^2\,dx)^{1/2}\). The functions \(u_k(x)=\sin(2\pi kx)\) all have norm \(1/\sqrt2\), whereas their derivatives have norm \(2\pi k/\sqrt2\). Thus no fixed constant \(C\) can bound \(\|u_k'\|_{L^2}\) by \(C\|u_k\|_{L^2}\) for every \(k\).
  If instead we measure the input by $\|u\|_{H^1}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|u'\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$, then $\|u'\|_{L^2}\leq\|u\|_{H^1}$ directly. The space $H^1$ consists of square-integrable functions whose weak first derivative is also square-integrable. For the smooth functions considered here, that derivative is the ordinary derivative. Including it in the input norm makes differentiation bounded.









TipRemark



The condition-number estimate uses two separate facts: the smallest eigenvalue approaches the positive constant \(\pi^2\), whereas the largest grows like \(4h^{-2}\). Thus halving \(h\) approximately quadruples the condition number. This is consistent with the unboundedness of the differential operator in the \(L^2\) norm, but unboundedness alone is not a proof of the estimate for a discretization.








TipRemark



(Solver consequence) Dense Gaussian elimination ignores sparsity. For Poisson matrices, sparse Cholesky, CG with preconditioning, multigrid, or FFT-based solvers are the natural algorithms, depending on geometry and boundary conditions.

title: 23  Iterative Methods for Linear Systems
text:
23.1 Matrix Splittings and Stationary Iterations
A sparse matrix can have a factorization that is too expensive to store. Iterative methods instead improve an approximate solution through matrix–vector products and simpler solves. Their cost depends both on the cost of one correction and on how many corrections are needed.
For an approximation \(\bx\), compute the residual \(\br=\bb-\bA\bx\). The exact correction satisfies \(\bA\boldsymbol\delta=\br\). Solving that equation exactly would be the original task again. We instead solve \(\bM\boldsymbol\delta=\br\) with a matrix \(\bM\) that is cheap to use, and add the correction to \(\bx\).
The correction update is \(\bx^{(k+1)}=\bx^{(k)}+\bM^{-1}(\bb-\bA\bx^{(k)})\). The inverse here denotes a solve with \(\bM\), rather than a matrix to form. Rearranging this expression gives the traditional splitting \(\bA=\bM-\mathbf N\) and the recurrence below. The same \(\bM\) is used at every step, which explains the word stationary.
crumbs: 23  Iterative Methods for Linear Systems

title: 23  Iterative Methods for Linear Systems
text:
NoteDefinition: Stationary Iteration



Given a splitting \(\bA = \bM - \mathbf{N}\), the corresponding stationary iteration computes successive approximations via the fixed-point recurrence \[
\begin{align}
\bM\bx^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{N}\bx^{(k)} + \bb \iff \bx^{(k+1)} = \bT\bx^{(k)} + \bc,
\end{align}
\] where \(\bT = \bM^{-1}\mathbf{N} = \bI - \bM^{-1}\bA\) is the iteration matrix and \(\bc = \bM^{-1}\bb\) is the modified right-hand side vector.








WarningExercise



Consider the matrix \(\bA = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) and the splitting \(\bM = 4\bI\). Compute the iteration matrix \(\bT = \bI - \bM^{-1}\bA\), find its eigenvalues, and evaluate its spectral radius \(\rho(\bT)\).








TipRemark



The exact solution is a fixed point because its residual is zero. That fact establishes consistency of the iteration, but does not imply convergence to the fixed point. The correction must reduce every possible error direction. The following spectral-radius criterion states exactly when this occurs.
crumbs: 23  Iterative Methods for Linear Systems

title: 23  Iterative Methods for Linear Systems
section: 23.2 Convergence Theory and the Spectral Radius
text:
23.2 Convergence Theory and the Spectral Radius
The convergence of a linear stationary iteration is determined entirely by the spectral properties of the iteration matrix \(\bT\).






WarningExercise



For the scalar equation \(ax=b\) with \(a>0\), use the correction \(\delta=(b-ax)/m\) with \(m>0\). Derive the error relation \(e^{(k+1)}=(1-a/m)e^{(k)}\). Determine the values of \(a/m\) for which the errors decrease, alternate in sign, remain unchanged in magnitude, or grow. The matrix criterion extends this calculation to all eigenvector directions.








NoteDefinition: Spectral Radius



Let \(\bT \in \fR^{n \times n}\) with spectrum \(\sigma(\bT) \subset \fC\). The spectral radius of \(\bT\) is defined as the maximum modulus among all its eigenvalues: \[
\begin{align}
\rho(\bT) = \max \{ |\lambda| : \lambda \in \sigma(\bT) \}.
\end{align}
\]








NoteTheorem: Gelfand’s Spectral Radius Theorem



For any matrix norm \(\|\cdot\|\) induced by a vector norm on \(\fC^n\) and any matrix \(\bT \in \fR^{n \times n}\), \[
\begin{align}
\rho(\bT) = \lim_{k \to \infty} \|\bT^k\|^{1/k}.
\end{align}
\] In particular, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an induced matrix norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\) such that \(\|\bT\|_* \leq \rho(\bT) + \varepsilon\).








WarningExercise



The following construction proves the norm assertion and the limit. Use Schur form \(\bT=\bQ\bU\bQ^*\) and set \(\bD=\operatorname{diag}(1,\eta,...,\eta^{n-1})\). Show that every strictly upper triangular entry of \(\bD^{-1}\bU\bD\) tends to zero as \(\eta\to0\). Choose \(\eta\) so that its infinity norm is at most \(\rho(\bT)+\varepsilon\), and define \(\|\bx\|_*=\|\bD^{-1}\bQ^*\bx\|_\infty\). Finally use equivalence of norms to obtain \(\limsup_k\|\bT^k\|^{1/k}\leq\rho(\bT)+\varepsilon\) in any fixed norm, and an eigenvector to obtain the reverse bound. Let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).








NoteTheorem: Fundamental Convergence Criterion for Stationary Iterations



The stationary iteration \(\bx^{(k+1)} = \bT\bx^{(k)} + \bc\) converges to the unique solution \(\bx^* = \bA^{-1}\bb\) for every initial guess \(\bx^{(0)} \in \fR^n\) if and only if \[
\begin{align}
\rho(\bT) < 1.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Let \(\be^{(k)} = \bx^{(k)} - \bx^*\) denote the error vector at step \(k\). Subtracting the fixed-point identity \(\bx^* = \bT\bx^* + \bc\) from the iteration formula \(\bx^{(k+1)} = \bT\bx^{(k)} + \bc\): \[
\begin{align}
\be^{(k+1)}
    &= \bx^{(k+1)} - \bx^* \\
    &= (\bT\bx^{(k)} + \bc) - (\bT\bx^* + \bc) \\
    &= \bT(\bx^{(k)} - \bx^*)
    = \bT \be^{(k)}.
\end{align}
\] Applying this recurrence recursively yields \[
\begin{align}
\be^{(k)} = \bT^k \be^{(0)}.
\end{align}
\] The recurrence shows why the error, rather than the iterate itself, is the convenient object: the fixed right-hand side has cancelled. In particular, testing all initial guesses is equivalent to testing all initial errors, since any error vector can be realized by choosing \(\bx^{(0)}=\bx^*+\be^{(0)}\).
The error \(\be^{(k)} \to \bzero\) for all initial errors \(\be^{(0)} \in \fR^n\) if and only if \(\lim_{k\to\infty} \bT^k = \bzero\).
If \(\rho(\bT) < 1\), choose \(\varepsilon = \frac{1 - \rho(\bT)}{2} > 0\). By Gelfand’s theorem (the referenced result), there exists an induced matrix norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\) such that \[
\begin{align}
\|\bT\|_* \leq \rho(\bT) + \varepsilon = \frac{1 + \rho(\bT)}{2} < 1.
\end{align}
\] Then \(\|\bT^k\|_* \leq \|\bT\|_*^k \to 0\) as \(k \to \infty\), so \(\bT^k \to \bzero\) and \(\|\be^{(k)}\|_* \leq \|\bT\|_*^k \|\be^{(0)}\|_* \to 0\).
Conversely, suppose \(\bT^k \to \bzero\). If \(\lambda \in \sigma(\bT)\) with eigenvector \(\bv \neq \bzero\), then \(\bT^k \bv = \lambda^k \bv\). For this sequence to converge to \(\bzero\), we must have \(|\lambda|^k \to 0\), forcing \(|\lambda| < 1\). If an eigenvector is complex while the matrix is real, write it as \(\bv=\ba+i\bb\). Convergence of \(\bT^k\) on every real vector makes both \(\bT^k\ba\) and \(\bT^k\bb\) tend to zero, so convergence also holds for their complex combination. Thus the eigenvector test covers complex eigenvalues as well.
Because this holds for all eigenvalues, \(\rho(\bT) < 1\).









TipRemark



(Asymptotic convergence rate and iteration count) The quantity \(-\log_{10} \rho(\bT)\) represents the asymptotic rate of convergence, measuring the number of decimal digits of accuracy gained per iteration. To reduce the initial error by a relative tolerance factor \(\varepsilon\), the required number of iterations satisfies \[
\begin{align}
k \approx \frac{\ln(1/\varepsilon)}{-\ln \rho(\bT)}.
\end{align}
\] If \(\rho(\bT) = 0.99\), we have \(-\ln(0.99) \approx 0.01005\), which requires approximately \(230\) iterations to reduce the error by a factor of ten. As \(\rho(\bT) \to 1\), convergence slows drastically.

title: 23  Iterative Methods for Linear Systems
text:
23.3 Krylov Subspaces and Matrix-Free Solvers
A stationary method applies the same splitting at every step. A Krylov method instead chooses the iterate \(\bx^{(k)}\) from the affine space \(\bx^{(0)}+\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\br^{(0)})\), where \(\mathcal{K}_k\) is the Krylov subspace of the referenced result generated by the initial residual. The basis for this space is built by the Arnoldi process of the referenced section, or by the Lanczos recurrence when \(\bA\) is symmetric. The conjugate gradient and GMRES methods differ in the optimality criterion used to select \(\bx^{(k)}\).






NoteTheorem: Krylov Polynomial Representation



Let \(\bx^{(0)}\) be an initial guess with residual \(\br^{(0)} = \bb - \bA\bx^{(0)}\). Any iterate \(\bx^{(k)}\) belonging to the affine Krylov space \(\bx^{(0)} + \mathcal{K}_k(\bA, \br^{(0)})\) can be represented as \[
\begin{align}
\bx^{(k)} = \bx^{(0)} + p_{k-1}(\bA)\br^{(0)},
\end{align}
\] where \(p_{k-1}\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(k-1\). The corresponding residual vector satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\br^{(k)} = \bb - \bA\bx^{(k)} = q_k(\bA)\br^{(0)},
\end{align}
\] where \(q_k(t) = 1 - t p_{k-1}(t)\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(k\) satisfying the normalization constraint \(q_k(0) = 1\).








WarningExercise



Write a general correction as \(\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j\bA^j\br^{(0)}\) and subtract its image from \(\br^{(0)}\). Prove the polynomial representation. Conversely, if \(q_k(0)=1\), show that \((1-q_k(t))/t\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(k-1\).








TipRemark



(Matrix-free computation) Krylov subspace methods never require explicit access to the individual entries of \(\bA\). They interact with the linear operator exclusively by computing matrix–vector products \(\bv \mapsto \bA\bv\). Consequently, linear systems can be solved efficiently even when the matrix is defined implicitly as a differential operator or a numerical simulation routine.








NoteDefinition: Stopping Criteria for Iterative Solvers



Because the true error \(\be^{(k)} = \bx^{(k)} - \bx^*\) is unobservable, termination is determined using the computable residual vector \(\br^{(k)} = \bb - \bA\bx^{(k)}\). Common stopping criteria include:

Relative residual test: \(\frac{\|\br^{(k)}\|_2}{\|\bb\|_2} \leq `tol`\).
Preconditioned relative residual test: \(\frac{\|\bM^{-1}\br^{(k)}\|_2}{\|\bM^{-1}\bb\|_2} \leq `tol`\).
Step difference test: \(\frac{\|\bx^{(k+1)} - \bx^{(k)}\|_2}{\|\bx^{(k+1)}\|_2} \leq `tol`\).









WarningExercise



Prove that if \(\|\bT\| < 1\) for some induced matrix norm, then the error satisfies \(\|\be^{(k)}\| \leq \frac{\|\bT\|}{1 - \|\bT\|} \|\bx^{(k)} - \bx^{(k-1)}\|\).


Relative tests require a nonzero denominator; for \(\bb=\bzero\), use an absolute residual tolerance. A small step alone can also signal stagnation. Recompute the true residual before accepting convergence, and use the residual–error bound to interpret its size. The normwise backward-error denominator \(\|\bA\|\|\bx^{(k)}\|+\|\bb\|\) often gives a more useful scale than \(\|\bb\|\) alone.

title: 24  Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, and SOR Methods
text:
24.1 The Jacobi Method
Each row of a linear system can be solved for its diagonal unknown when that diagonal entry is nonzero. Jacobi uses the old values of every other unknown. Gauss–Seidel uses new values as soon as they are available. Relaxation changes how far each such update is taken. We derive these choices and then determine sufficient conditions for convergence.
For the matrix formulas we use \(\bA=\bD-\bL_A-\bU_A\), where \(\bD\) is diagonal and \(-\bL_A\), \(-\bU_A\) are the strictly lower and upper parts of \(\bA\). The minus signs are a convention. For example, if \(a_{21}=1\), then \((L_A)_{21}=-1\).
Jacobi uses the diagonal as an easily solved approximation to the matrix. Strict diagonal dominance is a sufficient convergence condition, but is not part of the definition. It computes the \((k+1)\)-th estimate of each unknown \(x_i\) exclusively from the \(k\)-th estimates of all other variables.

title: 25  The Conjugate Gradient Method
25  The Conjugate Gradient Method
text:
WarningExercise



What changes when \(a<0\)? When \(a=0\), consider \(b=0\) and \(b\neq0\) separately. Explain why setting a derivative to zero, by itself, does not establish that a point is a minimum.









NoteExample



For the system \[
\begin{align}
2x_1+x_2=4,\qquad x_1+2x_2=5,
\end{align}
\] we have \[
\begin{align}
\bA=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
    \qquad \bb=\begin{pmatrix}4\\5\end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
\] and \[
\begin{align}
\phi(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2+x_1x_2+x_2^2-4x_1-5x_2.
\end{align}
\] The solution is \((1,2)^T\). With \(e_1=x_1-1\) and \(e_2=x_2-2\), completing the square in two variables gives \[
\begin{align}
\phi(x_1,x_2)+7
    &=e_1^2+e_1e_2+e_2^2\\
    &=\frac12\bigl((e_1+e_2)^2+e_1^2+e_2^2\bigr).
\end{align}
\] Every square vanishes at the solution, and their sum is positive everywhere else. Thus the smallest energy is \(-7\), attained only at \((1,2)^T\).








WarningExercise



Expand the two translated expressions to verify the identity above. Next differentiate \(\phi(x_1,x_2)\) with respect to each variable, holding the other fixed. Show that setting the two partial derivatives to zero recovers the two original equations. Where does symmetry of \(\bA\) enter the coefficient of \(x_1x_2\)?









NoteTheorem: Energy and Solution Error



Let \(\bA\) be SPD and let \(\bx^*\) solve \(\bA\bx^*=\bb\). For every \(\bx\), \[
\begin{align}
\phi(\bx)-\phi(\bx^*)
    =\frac12(\bx-\bx^*)^T\bA(\bx-\bx^*)
    =\frac12\|\bx-\bx^*\|_{\bA}^2.
\end{align}
\] Consequently, \(\bx^*\) is the unique minimizer of \(\phi\).








TipProof





Let \(\be=\bx-\bx^*\), so \(\bx=\bx^*+\be\). We compare the two energies by substituting this expression into the definition.

Distribute the matrix product before collecting terms: \[
\begin{align}
(\bx^*+\be)^T\bA(\bx^*+\be)
  &=\bx^{*T}\bA\bx^*+\bx^{*T}\bA\be
    +\be^T\bA\bx^*+\be^T\bA\be.
\end{align}
\] Also \(\bb^T(\bx^*+\be)=\bb^T\bx^*+\bb^T\be\). Therefore \[
\begin{align}
\phi(\bx^*+\be)-\phi(\bx^*)
  =\tfrac12\bx^{*T}\bA\be+\tfrac12\be^T\bA\bx^*
   +\tfrac12\be^T\bA\be-\bb^T\be.
\end{align}
\] The terms containing only \(\bx^*\) have cancelled because they make up \(\phi(\bx^*)\).
A scalar equals its transpose. Symmetry of \(\bA\) consequently gives \[
\begin{align}
\bx^{*T}\bA\be
  =(\bx^{*T}\bA\be)^T
  =\be^T\bA^T\bx^*=\be^T\bA\bx^*.
\end{align}
\] The two half-weighted cross terms sum to \(\be^T\bA\bx^*\). Since \(\bA\bx^*=\bb\), this is \(\be^T\bb=\bb^T\be\), exactly the term that is subtracted. What remains is \(\tfrac12\be^T\bA\be\).
Positive definiteness says \(\be^T\bA\be>0\) for every \(\be\neq\bzero\), and the value is zero for \(\be=\bzero\). Thus \(\phi(\bx)>\phi(\bx^*)\) whenever \(\bx\neq\bx^*\). This proves uniqueness as well as minimality.

title: 25  The Conjugate Gradient Method
text:
25.2 Line Search and Steepest Descent
Let \(\bx\) be the current guess, and choose a nonzero direction \(\bp\). Points on the line through \(\bx\) in this direction have the form \(\bx+\alpha\bp\), where the scalar \(\alpha\) is the step length. Choosing the best point on this line is a one-variable problem, even when \(\bx\) has millions of entries.
Write \(\br=\bb-\bA\bx\) for the current residual. Expanding as in the preceding proof gives \[
\begin{align}
\phi(\bx+\alpha\bp)
    =\phi(\bx)-\alpha\bp^T\br
      +\frac{\alpha^2}{2}\bp^T\bA\bp.
\end{align}
\] The coefficient \(\bp^T\bA\bp\) is positive. This is an upward-opening quadratic in \(\alpha\), just like the scalar function with which we began. Differentiating with respect to \(\alpha\) gives \[
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{d\alpha}\phi(\bx+\alpha\bp)
    =-\bp^T\br+\alpha\bp^T\bA\bp.
\end{align}
\] Hence the unique minimizing step is \[
\begin{align}
\alpha=\frac{\bp^T\br}{\bp^T\bA\bp}.
\end{align}
\] This is called an exact line search: exact refers to minimizing along the chosen line, not to solving the whole linear system in one step.






WarningExercise



Substitute this step length into the quadratic to show that the energy decrease is \[
\begin{align}
\phi(\bx)-\phi(\bx+\alpha\bp)
    =\frac{(\bp^T\br)^2}{2\bp^T\bA\bp}.
\end{align}
\] When is there no improvement? Relate your answer to the slope at \(\alpha=0\). Explain why replacing \(\bp\) by a nonzero scalar multiple changes the step length but leaves the new point unchanged.


How should we choose \(\bp\)? The term linear in \(\alpha\) is \(-\alpha\bp^T\br\). Among directions of Euclidean length one, Cauchy–Schwarz shows that the largest initial decrease occurs at \(\bp=\br/\|\br\|_2\), provided \(\br\neq\bzero\). Thus the residual points in the locally steepest downhill direction. In the language of multivariable calculus, \(\nabla\phi(\bx)=\bA\bx-\bb=-\br\) is the gradient, and the residual is its negative.
Since scaling the direction does not change the line, we can simply take \(\bp=\br\). Repeating the line minimization in the current residual direction gives steepest descent: \[
\begin{align}
\alpha_k&=\frac{\br^{(k)T}\br^{(k)}}
                    {\br^{(k)T}\bA\br^{(k)}},\\
    \bx^{(k+1)}&=\bx^{(k)}+\alpha_k\br^{(k)}.
\end{align}
\] If the residual is zero, the system is already solved. Otherwise \(\alpha_k>0\) and the energy strictly decreases.






WarningExercise



Derive \(\br^{(k+1)}=\br^{(k)}-\alpha_k\bA\br^{(k)}\). Use the step-length formula to prove \(\br^{(k+1)T}\br^{(k)}=0\). Interpret this as saying that the energy has zero slope along the line just minimized. Does it imply orthogonality to every earlier residual?


Steepest descent makes the best local choice of direction, but a good local slope need not give rapid progress over many steps. If the energy level sets are elongated ellipses, the residual can point across the narrow part of the ellipse instead of along its long direction toward the minimum. Successive line searches can then alternate across this narrow valley. The following calculation shows this behavior without relying on a picture.






WarningExercise



Let \(\bA=\operatorname{diag}(1,9)\), \(\bb=\bzero\), and \(\bx^{(0)}=(9,1)^T\), so the solution is the origin.

Compute \(\br^{(0)}\) and show that \(\alpha_0=1/5\). Find \(\bx^{(1)}\) and \(\br^{(1)}\).
Take a second steepest-descent step. Show that \(\alpha_1=1/5\) and \(\bx^{(2)}=(16/25)\bx^{(0)}\).
Compare the directions of the two steps. Why did two exact line searches fail to reach the solution of this two-variable system?

title: 25  The Conjugate Gradient Method
25  The Conjugate Gradient Method
25  The Conjugate Gradient Method
text:
25.5 Convergence Rate and Preconditioning
Although CG terminates in \(n\) steps in exact arithmetic, its primary utility in scientific computing is as a rapid iterative solver for which \(k \ll n\).






NoteTheorem: Chebyshev Error Bound for Conjugate Gradient



Let \(\bA\) be symmetric positive definite with 2-norm condition number \(\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\). The error at step \(k\) satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\|\bx^{(k)} - \bx^*\|_\bA}{\|\bx^{(0)} - \bx^*\|_\bA} \leq 2 \left( \frac{\sqrt{\kappa} - 1}{\sqrt{\kappa} + 1} \right)^k.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Assume first that the initial error \(\be^{(0)}=\bx^{(0)}-\bx^*\) is nonzero. A zero initial error needs no iteration.

A Krylov correction is \(s(\bA)\br^{(0)}\), with \(\deg s\leq k-1\). Since \(\br^{(0)}=-\bA\be^{(0)}\), the corrected error is \[
\begin{align}
\be^{(0)}+s(\bA)\br^{(0)}
  =[\bI-\bA s(\bA)]\be^{(0)}=p(\bA)\be^{(0)},
\end{align}
\] where \(p(t)=1-ts(t)\) has degree at most \(k\) and \(p(0)=1\). Conversely, every polynomial with these properties has this form because \(1-p(t)\) is divisible by \(t\).
Expand \(\be^{(0)}=\sum_i c_i\bq_i\) in an orthonormal eigenbasis. Then \[
\begin{align}
\|p(\bA)\be^{(0)}\|_{\bA}^2
  &=\sum_i\lambda_i p(\lambda_i)^2c_i^2\\
  &\leq\left(\max_i|p(\lambda_i)|^2\right)
        \sum_i\lambda_i c_i^2.
\end{align}
\] CG minimizes the energy-norm error over these corrections. Taking square roots therefore bounds its relative error by \(\max_i|p(\lambda_i)|\) for every admissible \(p\).
Let \(a=\lambda_{\min}\) and \(b=\lambda_{\max}\). If \(a<b\), the affine map \((b+a-2t)/(b-a)\) takes \([a,b]\) to \([-1,1]\). Choose \[
\begin{align}
p(t)=\frac{T_k((b+a-2t)/(b-a))}{T_k((b+a)/(b-a))}.
\end{align}
\] At \(t=0\) the numerator equals the denominator, so \(p(0)=1\). On \([a,b]\), the numerator has magnitude at most one. Therefore the relative error is at most \(1/T_k(c)\), where \(c=(b+a)/(b-a)>1\).
Put \(\zeta=c+\sqrt{c^2-1}>1\). The Chebyshev recurrence, checked first at \(k=0,1\), gives \[
\begin{align}
T_k(c)=\tfrac12(\zeta^k+\zeta^{-k})\geq\tfrac12\zeta^k.
\end{align}
\] Writing \(\kappa=b/a\) and simplifying gives \[
\begin{align}
\zeta
  =\frac{b+a+2\sqrt{ab}}{b-a}
  =\frac{\sqrt b+\sqrt a}{\sqrt b-\sqrt a}
  =\frac{\sqrt\kappa+1}{\sqrt\kappa-1}.
\end{align}
\] Hence \(1/T_k(c)\leq2\zeta^{-k}\), which is the claimed bound.
If \(a=b\), the spectral theorem gives \(\bA=a\bI\). The first CG correction has step length \(1/a\) and gives the exact solution. Thus the stated conclusion also holds for every \(k\geq1\) when \(\kappa=1\).

This is the classical Chebyshev bound for CG (Saad 2003; Greenbaum 1997).









WarningExercise



Derive the expression for \(T_k(c)\) by checking its first two values and three-term recurrence. Then simplify \(c+\sqrt{c^2-1}\) in terms of \(b/a\). Explain why a polynomial that is small only at the eigenvalues can give a better CG estimate than one bounded on the whole interval.








NoteCorollary: Termination with Distinct Eigenvalues



If \(\bA\) has only \(m\) distinct eigenvalues, CG reaches the exact solution in at most \(m\) iterations in exact arithmetic.








TipProof





Let \(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_m\) be the distinct eigenvalues. Each is positive because \(\bA\) is SPD.

Define \[
\begin{align}
p_m(t)=\prod_{j=1}^m(1-t/\lambda_j).
\end{align}
\] It has degree \(m\), value one at zero, and value zero at every eigenvalue. The divisions are legitimate because no eigenvalue is zero.
In an orthonormal eigenbasis \(\bA=\bQ\boldsymbol\Lambda\bQ^T\), powers of \(\bA\) give \(p_m(\bA)=\bQ p_m(\boldsymbol\Lambda)\bQ^T\). Every diagonal entry of \(p_m(\boldsymbol\Lambda)\) is zero. Therefore \(p_m(\bA)=\bzero\).
As shown in the preceding proof, after \(m\) steps the admissible errors include every \(p(\bA)\be^{(0)}\) with \(\deg p\leq m\) and \(p(0)=1\). In particular they include \(p_m(\bA)\be^{(0)}=\bzero\). CG selects the smallest energy norm among these errors. A norm is nonnegative, so a zero candidate forces the minimum to be zero. Thus the iterate is the exact solution, or the algorithm has already terminated earlier.










WarningExercise



For a diagonal SPD matrix with three distinct eigenvalues, construct the polynomial in the referenced result and verify that it annihilates the matrix.








TipRemark



(The square root condition number advantage) The CG bound depends on \(\sqrt{\kappa}\). For comparison, the worst-case energy contraction factor for steepest descent with exact line searches is \((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1)\). General stationary iterations depend on their iteration matrices, not solely on \(\kappa(\bA)\). For an ill-conditioned system with \(\kappa = 10^4\), the reduction factor per iteration for steepest descent is approximately \((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1) \approx 0.9998\), whereas for CG it is \((\sqrt{\kappa}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa}+1) = 99/101 \approx 0.9802\), giving roughly one hundred times as large an asymptotic logarithmic reduction per step in these bounds. Actual rates also depend on the spectrum and initial error.








TipRemark



(Superlinear convergence) The Chebyshev bound is a worst-case guarantee for an arbitrary spectrum. When the eigenvalues of \(\bA\) are grouped into tight clusters with only a few isolated outliers, CG eliminates the outlying eigenmodes in the first few iterations and then converges at a rate governed by the clustered eigenvalues. This behavior is termed superlinear convergence.


The convergence bound suggests changing coordinates so that different directions have more comparable scales. An SPD matrix \(\bM\) supplies such a change through its factorization \(\bM=\bC\bC^T\). We analyze CG in the transformed coordinates, but implement it using solves with \(\bM\). The construction below explains why those solves preserve the required symmetry.






NoteDefinition: Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (PCG)



Let \(\bM\) be a symmetric positive definite preconditioner. Write \(\bM=\bC\bC^T\). PCG is ordinary CG applied to the SPD system \(\bC^{-1}\bA\bC^{-T}\by=\bC^{-1}\bb\), with \(\bx=\bC^{-T}\by\). This is essential because \(\bM^{-1}\bA\) need not be symmetric in the Euclidean inner product. Initialize \(\bz^{(0)}\) by solving \(\bM\bz^{(0)}=\br^{(0)}\) and set \(\bp^{(0)}=\bz^{(0)}\). Use the usual solution and residual updates, then solve for the new \(\bz\) and set \(\bp^{(k+1)}=\bz^{(k+1)}+\beta_k\bp^{(k)}\). At each step, a linear system \(\bM\bz^{(k)} = \br^{(k)}\) is solved, and the step lengths and direction updates become \[
\begin{align}
\alpha_k = \frac{\br^{(k)T}\bz^{(k)}}{\bp^{(k)T}\bA\bp^{(k)}}, \qquad \beta_k = \frac{\br^{(k+1)T}\bz^{(k+1)}}{\br^{(k)T}\bz^{(k)}}.
\end{align}
\] The convergence bound applies to the SPD matrix \(\bC^{-1}\bA\bC^{-T}\). A useful preconditioner improves its eigenvalue distribution while remaining inexpensive to solve with. The cost of constructing and applying the preconditioner must be included in the comparison.

title: 26  The Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) Method
text:
26.1 Reduction to Hessenberg Least Squares
For a nonsymmetric matrix, the SPD energy argument no longer supplies an objective to minimize. The residual norm remains meaningful: we can choose the available correction that best satisfies the equations. GMRES applies this choice to an expanding Krylov subspace (Saad and Schultz 1986).
Arnoldi provides orthonormal coordinates for the corrections and their images under \(\bA\). In those coordinates, the minimization becomes a small least-squares problem. We derive that reduction, update its solution with plane rotations, and examine what is lost when the stored basis is discarded at a restart.
Let \(\br^{(0)}=\bb-\bA\bx^{(0)}\) be nonzero and let \(\beta=\|\br^{(0)}\|_2\). We run the Arnoldi iteration of the referenced result from \(\bv_1=\br^{(0)}/\beta\). By the referenced result, after \(k\) steps the columns of \(\bV_k\) form an orthonormal basis of \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\br^{(0)})\) and \(\bA\bV_k=\bV_{k+1}\bar{\bH}_k\). These two facts reduce the residual minimization in \(\fR^n\) to a small least-squares problem.
At the first step, the correction has the form \(\alpha\br^{(0)}\). We therefore minimize \(\|\br^{(0)}-\alpha\bA\br^{(0)}\|_2\). The next exercise solves this scalar problem. Later steps allow more correction directions, but apply the same least-squares principle.

title: 26  The Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) Method
text:
26.2 Givens Rotations






NoteTheorem: Incremental QR Factorization of the Hessenberg Matrix



At step \(k\), applying the previously accumulated Givens rotations \(\bG_1, ..., \bG_{k-1}\) transforms the first \(k-1\) entries of the new column of \(\bar{\bH}_k\). The subdiagonal entry at position \((k+1, k)\) is then eliminated using a new Givens rotation \(\bG_k\) defined by \[
\begin{align}
\bG_k = \begin{pmatrix} c_k & s_k \\ -s_k & c_k \end{pmatrix}, \qquad c_k = \frac{h_{kk}^{(k-1)}}{\sqrt{(h_{kk}^{(k-1)})^2 + h_{k+1,k}^2}}, \quad s_k = \frac{h_{k+1,k}}{\sqrt{(h_{kk}^{(k-1)})^2 + h_{k+1,k}^2}}.
\end{align}
\] Applying \(\bG_k ... \bG_1\) transforms \(\bar{\bH}_k\) into an upper triangular matrix \(\bR_k\) with a zero final row, and transforms the right-hand side vector \(\beta \be_1\) into \(\bg_{k+1} = (\gamma_1, ..., \gamma_k, \gamma_{k+1})^T\). The residual norm at iteration \(k\) is obtained without forming \(\bx^{(k)}\): \[
\begin{align}
\|\br^{(k)}\|_2 = |\gamma_{k+1}|.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Each plane rotation acts as an orthogonal matrix on the full \((k+1)\)-dimensional space by leaving the other coordinates unchanged. Their product \(\bQ_k=\bG_k\cdots\bG_1\) is therefore orthogonal and preserves Euclidean norms.
The first \(k-1\) rotations are already known from the preceding step. Applying them to the new column leaves only one possible subdiagonal entry. The new rotation removes it. Thus \[
\begin{align}
\bQ_k\bar{\bH}_k=\begin{pmatrix}\bR_k\\\bzero^T\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \bQ_k(\beta\be_1)=\begin{pmatrix}\bg_{1:k}\\\gamma_{k+1}\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
\] Here \(\bR_k\) is \(k\times k\). It is nonsingular because rotations preserve rank and \(\bar{\bH}_k\) has full column rank before breakdown.
For any coefficient vector \(\by\), preserve the norm by applying \(\bQ_k\), then separate the last coordinate: \[
\begin{align}
\|\beta\be_1-\bar{\bH}_k\by\|_2^2
&=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}\bg_{1:k}-\bR_k\by\\\gamma_{k+1}\end{pmatrix}\right\|_2^2\\
&=\|\bg_{1:k}-\bR_k\by\|_2^2+|\gamma_{k+1}|^2.
\end{align}
\] The last summand does not depend on \(\by\), so it is a lower bound for the squared residual. Solve the triangular system \(\bR_k\by=\bg_{1:k}\) to make the first summand zero. Hence that lower bound is attained, and the minimum residual norm is exactly \(|\gamma_{k+1}|\).
Only the transformed right-hand side is needed to read this norm. Forming the full iterate \(\bx^{(0)}+\bV_k\by\) can wait until the stopping test is satisfied.









TipRemark



(Happy breakdown vs. stagnation) If the subdiagonal entry \(h_{k+1,k}\) vanishes, the referenced result shows that the Krylov subspace is invariant under \(\bA\). When \(\bA\) is nonsingular, its restriction to this invariant subspace is nonsingular, so the GMRES least-squares problem has residual zero and \(\bx^{(k)}\) is the exact solution. Termination for this reason is called happy breakdown. Stagnation is a different phenomenon. The Krylov space may continue to grow while its image under \(\bA\) contributes no useful correction to the residual. Non-normality, an unfavorable polynomial approximation problem, or a poor preconditioner can all cause this behavior, and the residual history alone does not identify which one is responsible.

title: 26  The Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) Method
text:
26.3 Restarted GMRES and Practical Considerations






NoteDefinition: Restarted GMRES(\(m\))



Full GMRES requires storing \(k\) basis vectors of length \(n\), incurring \(O(kn)\) memory storage and \(O(k^2 n)\) orthogonalization flops. To avoid memory exhaustion on large systems, the algorithm is restarted every \(m\) steps:

Run \(m\) steps of GMRES starting from \(\bx^{(0)}\) to produce \(\bx^{(m)}\).
Compute the residual \(\br^{(m)} = \bb - \bA\bx^{(m)}\).
Clear the Krylov basis vectors, set \(\bx^{(0)} \leftarrow \bx^{(m)}\), and repeat.









WarningExercise



(Left versus right preconditioning) Compare left preconditioning (\(\bM^{-1}\bA\bx = \bM^{-1}\bb\)) and right preconditioning (\(\bA\bM^{-1}\by = \bb\), \(\bx = \bM^{-1}\by\)). Show that right-preconditioned GMRES minimizes the true residual \(\|\bb-\bA\bx\|_2\), whereas left-preconditioned GMRES minimizes \(\|\bM^{-1}(\bb-\bA\bx)\|_2\). Explain why a code that uses left preconditioning may need to monitor both quantities.








TipRemark



(The trade-off of restarting) Restarted GMRES(\(m\)) bounds memory usage to \(O(mn)\) and bounds orthogonalization cost per cycle. However, restarting discards the accumulated Krylov subspace and destroys the global optimality property. If \(m\) is chosen too small, the algorithm may stagnate completely.

26.4 Further Exercises






WarningExercise



(Arnoldi factorization by hand) For the matrix and initial residual \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \br^{(0)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
\] perform two steps of the Arnoldi iteration by hand.

Compute \(\bv_1\) and \(\bw_1 = \bA\bv_1\). Find \(h_{11}, h_{21}\) and \(\bv_2\).
Compute \(\bw_2 = \bA\bv_2\). Find \(h_{12}, h_{22}, h_{32}\) and \(\bv_3\).
Explicitly assemble the matrices \(\bV_2\) and the \(3 \times 2\) upper Hessenberg matrix \(\bar{\bH}_2\).









WarningExercise



(Hessenberg QR and residual norm via Givens) Using the \(3 \times 2\) matrix \(\bar{\bH}_2\) from the preceding Arnoldi exercise:

Form the Givens rotation \(\bG_1\) that eliminates \(h_{21}\), and the rotation \(\bG_2\) that eliminates \(h_{32}\).
Apply these rotations to the right-hand side vector \(\beta \be_1 = (\sqrt{2}, 0, 0)^T\).
Read off the residual norm \(\|\br^{(2)}\|_2\) from the transformed vector without computing \(\bx^{(2)}\).









WarningExercise



(GMRES polynomial minimax on an ellipse) Suppose the eigenvalues of \(\bA\) are enclosed within an ellipse in the complex plane centered at \(c > 0\) with focal distance \(d < c\) that does not contain the origin.

Using the scaled Chebyshev polynomial \(p(z) = T_k((c - z)/d) / T_k(c/d)\), show that \(p(0) = 1\).
Apply the referenced result to derive an explicit upper bound for \(\|\br^{(k)}\|_2 / \|\br^{(0)}\|_2\) in terms of the semi-axes of the ellipse.









WarningExercise



(Exact stagnation for a cyclic permutation) Let \(\bA\) be the cyclic permutation matrix defined by \(\bA\be_j=\be_{j+1}\) for \(j<n\) and \(\bA\be_n=\be_1\). Take \(\bx^{(0)}=\bzero\) and \(\bb=\be_1\).

Prove that \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bb)=\operatorname{span}\{\be_1,...,\be_k\}\) for \(k<n\).
Show that \(\bA\mathcal{K}_k=\operatorname{span}\{\be_2,...,\be_{k+1}\}\) is orthogonal to \(\bb\). Conclude that \(\|\br^{(k)}\|_2=1\) for every \(k<n\).
Show that \(\bx=\be_n\) becomes available at step \(n\) and gives zero residual. Construct the degree-\(n\) residual polynomial that vanishes on the spectrum of \(\bA\), and explain why no polynomial of smaller degree can do so.







Saad, Yousef. 2003. Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems. 2nd ed. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718003.


Saad, Yousef, and Martin H. Schultz. 1986. “GMRES: A Generalized Minimal Residual Algorithm for Solving Nonsymmetric Linear Systems.” SIAM Journal on Scientific and Statistical Computing 7 (3): 856–69. https://doi.org/10.1137/0907058.

title: 27  Multigrid Methods
text:
27.1 Oscillating Error and the Smoothing Property
A local iteration can quickly remove oscillations from an error while barely changing a smooth error. A coarse grid represents that smooth part with fewer unknowns. Multigrid combines the inexpensive local updates with corrections computed on successively coarser grids. We first analyze the updates, then derive the equation that the coarse correction must solve.
Weighted Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel converge slowly as stand-alone solvers because smooth error components decay slowly. Their value as smoothers is that they reduce oscillatory error in a few sweeps. Unweighted Jacobi has a high-frequency exception, derived below. A Fourier analysis of the error makes this asymmetry precise, and multigrid is built on it. The smoother removes the oscillatory error components, and the remaining smooth error is passed to a coarser grid, where it becomes oscillatory and cheap to resolve.
Frequency-Dependent Error Decay in Jacobi Iteration For the 1D model problem, the Jacobi update reads \[
\begin{align}
x_i^{(k+1)} = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(x_{i-1}^{(k)} + x_{i+1}^{(k)}\bigr) + \tfrac{1}{2}b_i.
\end{align}
\] Each new value is the average of its two neighbors plus a source term. Consider two extreme error profiles at some iteration:
Jacobi acts as a local averaging filter that pulls each value toward the mean of its neighbors. Oscillations cancel in that average, whereas smooth trends do not. Starting from a random initial guess, the error spans all frequencies. With weighted Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel, the oscillatory error is reduced first. The remaining smooth error motivates a correction on a coarser grid. Error and residual have different spectral weights, so both should be interpreted through the operator.

title: 27  Multigrid Methods
text:
Oscillatory error: neighboring values often have opposite signs, so averaging damps many high-frequency modes rapidly. The exact alternating mode is an exception for unweighted Jacobi: its sign flips without shrinking. Weighted Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel supplies the smoothing used in multigrid.
Smooth error (\(e_i \propto \sin(ij\pi h)\) for small mode index \(j\)): neighbors of node \(i\) carry nearly the same value as \(e_i\) itself, so their average barely moves things. The error barely changes per sweep.








WarningExercise



(Observing oscillating error) Set \(n = 63\), \(\bb = \bzero\), and \(\bx^* = \bzero\), so the error equals the iterate exactly. Run Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel from the same random initial vector \(\bx^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \bI)\).

Plot the error profile \(\be^{(k)} = \bx^{(k)}\) at iterations \(k = 0, 1, 3, 10, 20\). Describe how the spectral composition of the error changes. Observe the behavior of the high-frequency components.
Decompose \(\be^{(k)}\) into Fourier mode amplitudes \(\hat{e}_j^{(k)} = \langle \be^{(k)}, \phi^{(j)}\rangle / \|\phi^{(j)}\|^2\) and plot \(|\hat{e}_j^{(k)}|\) vs. \(j\) at the same iterations. Which modes decay fast, which persist?
The Jacobi iteration matrix has eigenvalues \(\mu_j = \cos(j\pi h)\). Use this to predict the amplitude of mode \(j\) after \(k\) sweeps as a function of the initial amplitude \(|\hat{e}_j^{(0)}|\). Does your plot match the prediction?
After 20 sweeps, what does the remaining error look like? Argue, using the eigenvalue formula, why no fine-grid iteration alone can efficiently eliminate it, necessitating a coarse-grid correction.









NoteDefinition: Fourier Modes on a Uniform Grid



Consider the 1D model problem with the \(n \times n\) tridiagonal matrix \(\bA\) having \(2\) on the main diagonal and \(-1\) on the off-diagonals (the finite-difference discretization of \(-u'' = f\) on \([0,1]\) scaled by \(h^2\)). Let \(h = 1/(n+1)\). For the nested grids below take \(n=2m+1\). The Fourier modes are the vectors \[
\begin{align}
\phi^{(k)}_j = \sin(kj\pi h), \quad j = 1,...,n, \quad k = 1,...,n.
\end{align}
\] These form an orthogonal basis for \(\fR^n\) (by discrete sine orthogonality) and diagonalize \(\bA\): \[
\begin{align}
\bA\phi^{(k)} = \lambda_k\,\phi^{(k)}, \qquad \lambda_k = 2 - 2\cos(k\pi h) = 4\sin^2\!\Bigl(\frac{k\pi h}{2}\Bigr).
\end{align}
\] Small \(k\) yields long-wavelength (smooth) modes, while large \(k\) yields short-wavelength (oscillatory) modes.








NoteTheorem: Eigenvalues of the Jacobi Iteration Matrix



For the 1D model problem, the Jacobi iteration matrix \(\bT_J = \bI - \tfrac{1}{2}\bA\) has eigenvalues \[
\begin{align}
\mu_k = \cos(k\pi h), \quad k = 1, ..., n,
\end{align}
\] with eigenvectors \(\phi^{(k)}\). After \(\nu\) Jacobi sweeps, mode \(k\) of the error is scaled by \(\mu_k^\nu = \cos^\nu(k\pi h)\).








TipProof





Since \(\bD = 2\bI\), the Jacobi iteration matrix is \(\bT_J = \bI - \frac{1}{2}\bA\). Applying \(\bT_J\) to the eigenvector \(\phi^{(k)}\): \[
\begin{align}
\bT_J\phi^{(k)}
  &= \left(\bI - \frac{1}{2}\bA\right)\phi^{(k)}
  = \phi^{(k)} - \frac{1}{2}\bA\phi^{(k)} \\
  &= \phi^{(k)} - \frac{1}{2}\lambda_k\phi^{(k)}
  = \left(1 - \frac{\lambda_k}{2}\right)\phi^{(k)}.
\end{align}
\] This calculation uses a general fact: if \(\bA\bv=\lambda\bv\), then \((\bI-c\bA)\bv=(1-c\lambda)\bv\). The eigenvector is unchanged, and only its eigenvalue changes. Here \(c=1/2\).
Substituting \(\lambda_k = 2 - 2\cos(k\pi h)\) yields \[
\begin{align}
1 - \frac{\lambda_k}{2}
  = 1 - (1 - \cos(k\pi h))
  = \cos(k\pi h).
\end{align}
\] For an initial error \(\be^{(0)}=\sum_k c_k\phi^{(k)}\), applying the iteration \(\nu\) times gives \(\be^{(\nu)}=\sum_k c_k\mu_k^\nu\phi^{(k)}\). This follows by applying the matrix to each basis vector separately and using linearity. It justifies the statement about each mode after repeated sweeps.
Therefore \(\bT_J\phi^{(k)} = \cos(k\pi h)\phi^{(k)}\).









NoteDefinition: Low- and High-Frequency Modes



With respect to a grid of mesh size \(h = 1/(n+1)\), partition the \(n\) Fourier modes by frequency:

Low-frequency (smooth) modes: \(k = 1, ..., \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\), where \(k\pi h \in (0, \pi/2)\). These satisfy \(\mu_k = \cos(k\pi h) \in (0,1)\), and for small \(k\), \(\mu_k \approx 1 - (k\pi h)^2/2 \approx 1\), so these modes decay slowly.
High-frequency (oscillatory) modes: \(k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1, ..., n\), where \(k\pi h \in [\pi/2, \pi)\).









TipRemark



Standard Jacobi (\(\omega = 1\)) is a poor smoother, because the highest-frequency mode (\(k = n\)) satisfies \(\mu_n = \cos(n\pi h) = \cos(\pi n/(n+1)) \approx -1\), so the iterate oscillates in sign rather than decaying. Weighted (damped) Jacobi with \(\omega = 2/3\) fixes this by controlling the entire high-frequency band.








NoteDefinition: Weighted Jacobi Iteration



The weighted Jacobi method introduces a damping parameter \(\omega \in (0,1)\): \[
\begin{align}
\bx^{(k+1)} = \bx^{(k)} + \omega\bD^{-1}\bigl(\bb - \bA\bx^{(k)}\bigr),
\end{align}
\] with iteration matrix \(\bT_\omega = \bI - \omega\bD^{-1}\bA\) and eigenvalues \[
\begin{align}
\mu_k(\omega) = 1 - \omega(1 - \cos(k\pi h)).
\end{align}
\] The standard multigrid choice is \(\omega = 2/3\).








NoteTheorem: Smoothing Property of Weighted Jacobi



For the 1D model problem with \(\omega = 2/3\), the smoothing factor \[
\begin{align}
\bar{\mu} = \max_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor < k \leq n}\,|\mu_k(2/3)| \leq \frac{1}{3}.
\end{align}
\] That is, every high-frequency component of the error is reduced by at least \(2/3\) in a single weighted Jacobi step.








TipProof





The weighted Jacobi error matrix is \[
\begin{align}
\bT_\omega=\bI-\omega\bD^{-1}\bA.
\end{align}
\] For this matrix \(\bD=2\bI\). A sine mode of index \(k\) has eigenvalue \(2-2\cos(k\pi h)\) under \(\bA\). Substituting it into the error matrix gives its amplification factor \[
\begin{align}
\mu_k(\omega)
&=1-\tfrac\omega2[2-2\cos(k\pi h)]\\
&=1-\omega+\omega\cos(k\pi h).
\end{align}
\] For \(\omega=2/3\), this is \(1/3+(2/3)\cos(k\pi h)\).
Because \(n=2m+1\) and \(h=1/(n+1)\), a high-frequency index satisfies \(k\geq m+1\). Hence \(k\pi h\in[\pi/2,\pi)\) and \(-1<\cos(k\pi h)\leq0\). It follows that \[
\begin{align}
-\tfrac13<\mu_k(2/3)\leq\tfrac13,
\qquad |\mu_k(2/3)|\leq\tfrac13.
\end{align}
\] After \(\nu\) sweeps, the coefficient of this mode is multiplied by \(\mu_k(2/3)^\nu\), whose magnitude is at most \(3^{-\nu}\). The sine modes form an orthogonal basis, so the same norm contraction holds for any combination restricted to this high-frequency band. No such bound is being asserted here for the low-frequency band.









TipRemark



After \(\nu\) weighted Jacobi sweeps, every high-frequency error component is reduced by \((1/3)^\nu\). The remaining error is dominated by smooth modes, which are nearly constant on the scale of \(h\). This smooth, slowly-varying error is the target of the coarse-grid correction in multigrid.








NoteExample



Eigenvalue spectrum of \(\bT_{2/3}\) for \(n = 15\), \(h = 1/16\).
The eigenvalues \(\mu_k = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1 - \cos(k\pi/16))\) for selected \(k\):

\(k = 1\) (smoothest): \(\mu_1 \approx 0.981\) (minimal decay per sweep).
\(k = 4\): \(\mu_4 = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1 - \cos(\pi/4)) \approx 0.804\) (slow decay).
\(k = 8\): \(\mu_8 = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1 - \cos(\pi/2)) = 1/3 \approx 0.333\).
\(k = 12\): \(\mu_{12} = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1 - \cos(3\pi/4)) \approx -0.138\) (rapid decay).
\(k = 15\) (most oscillatory): \(\mu_{15} \approx -0.330\) (magnitude bounded by \(1/3\)).

Modes \(k \geq 8\) all satisfy \(|\mu_k| \leq 1/3\), confirming the smoothing property. Modes \(k \leq 7\) range from \(0.63\) to \(0.98\) and are essentially untouched by the smoother.

title: 27  Multigrid Methods
text:
27.2 The Two-Grid Correction Scheme
A smooth error on a fine grid of mesh size \(h\) looks oscillatory on a coarser grid of mesh size \(2h\). More precisely, the smooth fine-grid modes (\(k < n/2\)) oscillate at wavelength \(> 2h\) and are well-represented on the coarse grid. Once the high-frequency components have been attenuated by the smoother, the remaining error lives in a low-dimensional smooth subspace that a direct solve on a coarse grid of size \(n/2\) can eliminate efficiently.






NoteDefinition: Prolongation Operator



The prolongation (or interpolation) operator \(\bP: \fR^{m} \to \fR^{n}\) (where \(m = (n-1)/2\) for grids satisfying \(n = 2m+1\)) transfers a coarse-grid vector to the fine grid by linear interpolation. For a coarse-grid vector \(\bv \in \fR^m\), the fine-grid vector \(\bP\bv \in \fR^n\) is defined by \[
\begin{align}
(\bP\bv)_{2j} = v_j, \qquad (\bP\bv)_{2j-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(v_{j-1} + v_j), \quad j = 1, ..., m,
\end{align}
\] with boundary conventions \(v_0 = v_{m+1} = 0\) and the final midpoint value \((\bP\bv)_{2m+1}=v_m/2\). In matrix form, \(\bP\) is \(n \times m\) with entries \(1\) at coarse-grid points and \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) weights at fine-grid midpoints.








NoteDefinition: Restriction Operator



The restriction operator \(\bR: \fR^{n} \to \fR^{m}\) transfers a fine-grid vector to the coarse grid. The standard full-weighting restriction averages each coarse point with its fine-grid neighbors: \[
\begin{align}
(\bR\bw)_j = \tfrac{1}{4}w_{2j-1} + \tfrac{1}{2}w_{2j} + \tfrac{1}{4}w_{2j+1}, \quad j = 1, ..., m.
\end{align}
\] In matrix form, \(\bR = \tfrac{1}{2}\bP^T\). This choice ensures that the Galerkin coarse-grid operator \(\bA_c = \bR\bA\bP\) is SPD whenever \(\bA\) is SPD.








TipRemark



The relationship \(\bR = \tfrac{1}{2}\bP^T\) is called the variational principle and preserves symmetry and positive definiteness of \(\bA_c\), since \(\bP\) has full column rank. Accuracy of the coarse space requires a separate approximation argument. For the physical scaling \(\bA=h^{-2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1)\), \(\bA_c\) is the natural \(2h\) finite-difference matrix. If the factor \(h^{-2}\) is omitted on the fine grid, the inherited coarse matrix is \(\tfrac14\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1)\). This special property simplifies analysis but does not hold in general for variable-coefficient or higher-dimensional problems.


Let \(\boldsymbol\epsilon=\bx^*-\tilde{\bx}\) be the correction we would like to make. Although it is unknown, its equation is known: \(\bA\boldsymbol\epsilon=\br\). Approximate the correction by a prolongated coarse vector \(\bP\be_c\), and require the restricted residual of this equation to vanish. This gives \[
\begin{align}
\bR(\br-\bA\bP\be_c)=\bzero,
\qquad (\bR\bA\bP)\be_c=\bR\br.
\end{align}
\] This derives both the coarse matrix and its right-hand side. We transfer the residual because it supplies an equation for the unknown error.






NoteDefinition: Two-Grid Correction Scheme



Given \(\bA\bx = \bb\) on the fine grid, one step of the two-grid (TG) method from an iterate \(\bx^{(0)}\) is:

Pre-smoothing: Apply \(\nu_1 \geq 0\) smoother steps to get \(\tilde{\bx}\).
Residual: Compute \(\br = \bb - \bA\tilde{\bx}\).
Restrict: Form the coarse residual \(\br_c = \bR\br \in \fR^m\).
Coarse solve: Solve \(\bA_c\be_c = \br_c\) exactly for \(\be_c \in \fR^m\).
Prolong and correct: Set \(\hat{\bx} = \tilde{\bx} + \bP\be_c\).
Post-smoothing: Apply \(\nu_2 \geq 0\) smoother steps to \(\hat{\bx}\) to get \(\bx^{(1)}\).

The coarse-grid system \(\bA_c\be_c = \br_c\) solves the residual equation: if \(\bx^* - \tilde{\bx}\) is smooth and lies in the range of \(\bP\), this recovers the error exactly.








NoteTheorem: Ideal Coarse-Grid Correction



If the error \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \bx^* - \tilde{\bx}\) lies in the range of \(\bP\) (i.e., \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \bP\boldsymbol{\delta}\) for some \(\boldsymbol{\delta} \in \fR^m\)), then the two-grid correction recovers the exact solution: \(\hat{\bx} = \bx^*\).








TipProof





Suppose the error before correction has the form \(\boldsymbol\epsilon=\bx^*-\tilde{\bx}=\bP\boldsymbol\delta\). The vector \(\boldsymbol\delta\) need not be known. We show that the coarse equations recover it.
Use the exact equation \(\bA\bx^*=\bb\) to express the computable residual as \[
\begin{align}
\br=\bb-\bA\tilde{\bx}
=\bA(\bx^*-\tilde{\bx})
=\bA\boldsymbol\epsilon=\bA\bP\boldsymbol\delta.
\end{align}
\] Restriction gives \[
\begin{align}
\br_c=\bR\br=\bR\bA\bP\boldsymbol\delta
=\bA_c\boldsymbol\delta.
\end{align}
\] By definition the algorithm solves \(\bA_c\be_c=\br_c\). Thus \(\be_c\) and \(\boldsymbol\delta\) satisfy the same coarse linear system. The coarse matrix is nonsingular, so the solution is unique and \(\be_c=\boldsymbol\delta\).
Now prolongate and add: \[
\begin{align}
\hat{\bx}=\tilde{\bx}+\bP\be_c
=\tilde{\bx}+\bP\boldsymbol\delta
=\tilde{\bx}+(\bx^*-\tilde{\bx})=\bx^*.
\end{align}
\] This proves exact correction for errors in the range of \(\bP\). It does not claim that an arbitrary smooth error is exactly in that range. Approximation of other errors is a separate part of multigrid convergence theory (Briggs et al. 2000).









WarningExercise



Take \(n=7\), \(\bA=\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1)\), \(\bb=\mathbf1\), and \(\bx^{(0)}=\bzero\). Write out \(\bP\) and \(\bR\), and compute \(\bA_c=\bR\bA\bP\). Compare the true residual norms after four weighted Jacobi sweeps and after a two-grid step with two pre- and two post-sweeps. Count the coarse solve as well as the smoothing work. Does a lower residual alone establish a lower total cost?

title: 27  Multigrid Methods
text:
27.3 The Multigrid V-Cycle
The two-grid method replaces the fine-grid iteration matrix with one that damps all error components, at the cost of an exact coarse-grid solve. For large problems the coarse grid may itself be large. Multigrid applies the idea recursively. Instead of solving the coarse-grid problem exactly, it applies the two-grid scheme again at the coarser level, and so on, until the coarsest grid is trivially small (a single unknown). This gives the V-cycle.






NoteDefinition: Multigrid Grid Hierarchy



For \(n = 2^L - 1\), define \(L\) nested grids with mesh sizes \(h_\ell = 2^{-\ell}\), giving \(n_\ell = 2^\ell - 1\) interior points at level \(\ell = 1, ..., L\). The finest grid is \(\ell = L\) (mesh size \(h\)) and the coarsest is \(\ell = 1\) (a single point). At each level \(\ell\) we have a system matrix \(\bA_\ell\) (built via Galerkin: \(\bA_{\ell-1} = \bR_\ell\bA_\ell\bP_\ell\)), restriction \(\bR_\ell: \fR^{n_\ell} \to \fR^{n_{\ell-1}}\), and prolongation \(\bP_\ell: \fR^{n_{\ell-1}} \to \fR^{n_\ell}\).








NoteDefinition: Multigrid V-Cycle



\(\mathtt{MG}(\ell,\, \bx,\, \bb)\): one multigrid V-cycle at level \(\ell\), returning an improved approximation to \(\bA_\ell\bx = \bb\):

Base case (\(\ell = 1\)): return \(\bA_1^{-1}\bb\) (exact solve on a \(1 \times 1\) system).
Pre-smoothing: \(\bx \leftarrow S_\ell^{\nu_1}(\bx,\,\bb)\) (\(\nu_1\) steps of the smoother at level \(\ell\)).
Restrict residual: \(\br_{\ell-1} \leftarrow \bR_\ell(\bb - \bA_\ell\bx)\).
Coarse-grid correction: \(\be_{\ell-1} \leftarrow \mathtt{MG}(\ell-1,\,\bzero,\,\br_{\ell-1})\).
Correct: \(\bx \leftarrow \bx + \bP_\ell\be_{\ell-1}\).
Post-smoothing: \(\bx \leftarrow S_\ell^{\nu_2}(\bx,\,\bb)\) (\(\nu_2\) steps of the smoother).
Return \(\bx\).

Calling \(\mathtt{MG}\) once as the coarse-grid solver in step 4 gives the V-cycle. Calling it twice gives the W-cycle, which is more robust on difficult problems at higher cost.








TipRemark



A single V-cycle descends from the finest level \(L\) to the coarsest level \(1\) (the down stroke'') applying pre-smoothing and restriction, then ascends back (theup stroke’’) applying prolongation and post-smoothing. Typical choices are \(\nu_1 = \nu_2 = 1\) or \(2\). The W-cycle replaces the single recursive call in step 4 with two calls, more aggressively correcting smooth error with work governed by \(W(n)=2W(n/2)+O(n)\) in one dimension, hence \(O(n\log n)\). In two or three dimensions, geometric coarsening gives a smaller recursion ratio and a W-cycle can still cost \(O(n)\).








TipRemark



(Mesh-independent convergence) For the standard Dirichlet Poisson problem, suitable smoothing and coarse-grid approximation give a V-cycle contraction in the energy norm with a factor \(q<1\) independent of mesh size. This is a convergence theorem about the whole cycle, not a consequence of the smoothing estimate alone. Its proof is beyond the present development; see (Briggs et al. 2000). For a new discretization, transfer rule, or smoother, uniform convergence needs to be established again. The complexity estimate below is independent of that convergence question.








WarningExercise



Let \(\bC=\bI-\bP(\bR\bA\bP)^{-1}\bR\bA\). Prove that \(\bC\bP=\bzero\) and \(\bC^2=\bC\). For \(\bR=c\bP^T\) with \(c>0\), show that \(\bP^T\bA\bC=\bzero\) and that \(\bC\) is an orthogonal projection in the energy inner product. Deduce \(\|\bC\be\|_{\bA}\leq\|\be\|_{\bA}\). Why does this only give a nonexpansive map, rather than a mesh-independent strict contraction?








TipRemark



For classical iterations on the 1D Poisson problem, \(\rho(\bT_J) = \cos(\pi h) \approx 1 - \pi^2h^2/2 \to 1\) as \(h \to 0\), requiring \(O(h^{-2})=O(n^2)\) Jacobi iterations for a fixed reduction of the slowest mode. With the V-cycle, the number of iterations to reach a fixed tolerance is bounded by a constant independent of \(n\). The cost per V-cycle is \(O(n)\) (geometric series over levels), making the total cost \(O(n)\), which is the optimal asymptotic complexity for this class of problems.








NoteTheorem: \(O(n)\) Complexity of the V-Cycle



Assume a fixed number of smoothing sweeps, \(O(n_\ell)\) work for smoothing, residuals, and transfers at level \(\ell\), and geometric coarsening. For \(L\) levels with \(n=n_L\) unknowns on the finest level, each V-cycle requires \(O(n)\) floating-point operations, independent of the number of levels \(L\).








TipProof





Let \(n=n_L\) denote the number of unknowns on the finest level. The fixed number of sweeps means there is a constant \(C\), independent of level and problem size, such that all local work at level \(\ell\) is at most \(Cn_\ell\). This includes residuals and transfers as assumed in the statement.
In a V-cycle there is only one recursive call to the next coarser level. Thus every level is visited once on descent and ascent, with that work already included in \(C\). The nested-grid sizes satisfy \[
\begin{align}
n_\ell+1=2^\ell
=\frac{2^L}{2^{L-\ell}}
=\frac{n+1}{2^{L-\ell}}.
\end{align}
\] Consequently \(n_\ell\leq(n+1)2^{-(L-\ell)}\). Summing the local bounds and the constant coarsest solve gives \[
\begin{align}
W(n)&\leq C\sum_{\ell=1}^L n_\ell+C_0\\
&\leq C(n+1)\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}2^{-j}+C_0\\
&\leq2C(n+1)+C_0.
\end{align}
\] For \(n\geq1\), \(n+1\leq2n\), so this is bounded by a constant times \(n\). This proves the work bound for one V-cycle. A linear bound for the complete solution additionally requires a number of cycles bounded independently of the mesh.









NoteExample



Multigrid vs. classical iterations on the 2D Poisson problem.
Discretize \(-\Delta u = f\) on the unit square with an \(n \times n\) grid (\(h = 1/(n+1)\)), giving \(N = n^2\) unknowns. Approximate iteration counts to reduce the residual by \(10^{-8}\), and total work in units of \(N\) multiplications:
The table states asymptotic work for a fixed tolerance under the model assumptions. Actual cycle counts depend on the right-hand side, initial error, norm, and stopping test; measure them in the implementation exercises below.








WarningExercise



(Smoothing property) For the \(n = 15\) 1D model problem:

Compute the eigenvalues \(\mu_k\) of the standard Jacobi (\(\omega = 1\)) and weighted Jacobi (\(\omega = 2/3\)) iteration matrices. Plot \(|\mu_k|\) as a function of \(k\) on a single figure.
Starting from a random initial error \(\be^{(0)} \in \fR^{15}\), apply 3 steps of each method. Plot the initial and final errors, and describe qualitatively how each method reshapes the error.
Identify the ``worst-case’’ mode (largest \(|\mu_k|\)) for each method over the high-frequency range \(k > 7\). Why is the standard Jacobi smoother inadequate for multigrid?









WarningExercise



(Two-grid implementation) Implement the two-grid correction scheme for the 1D model problem with \(n = 2^m - 1\) interior points.

Write restrict(r) using the full-weighting formula and prolongate(e) using linear interpolation for transferring between a fine grid and the next coarser grid.
Implement two\_grid(A, b, x0, nu1, nu2) with \(\nu_1\) pre-smoothing and \(\nu_2\) post-smoothing steps of weighted Jacobi (\(\omega = 2/3\)) and an exact coarse-grid solve via np.linalg.solve.
For \(m = 6\) (\(n = 63\)), plot residual norm versus iteration count for: (a) weighted Jacobi alone, (b) repeated two-grid cycling. Use a semi-log scale. Estimate the per-cycle convergence factor \(\rho\) for the two-grid method.









WarningExercise



(Multigrid V-cycle) Extend the two-grid implementation to a full V-cycle.

Implement vcycle(x, b, A\_list, level, nu1, nu2) recursively. At level 1 (a single unknown), solve exactly. Test first on the two-grid case to verify it matches your two-grid implementation.
Run the V-cycle on the 1D Poisson problem with \(n = 2^{10} - 1 = 1023\) and \(\nu_1 = \nu_2 = 1\). Measure the empirical convergence factor \(\rho_k = \|\br^{(k)}\| / \|\br^{(k-1)}\|\) for \(k = 1, ..., 15\). Is it approximately constant (mesh-independent)?
Repeat for \(n = 2^{12} - 1 = 4095\). Compare the convergence factors. Then vary \(\nu_1 = \nu_2 \in \{1, 2, 3\}\) and report the convergence factor versus the extra cost per cycle.









TipRemark



(Choosing a solver) The structure of the coefficient matrix determines the method. The following summary collects the recommendations of the preceding sections.

Dense symmetric positive definite. Cholesky factorization (the referenced result), with \(n^3/3\) flops and no pivoting.
Large sparse symmetric positive definite. Preconditioned conjugate gradients (the referenced section) or multigrid, with \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA))\) work per iteration.
Dense general square. Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting (the referenced result), with \(2n^3/3\) flops and the backward error of the referenced result.
Large sparse general square. Preconditioned GMRES (the referenced section).
Overdetermined with full column rank. Householder QR (the referenced result), which avoids the squared condition number of the normal equations.
Rank-deficient or nearly rank-deficient. The SVD (the referenced result), which determines the numerical rank and the minimum-norm solution.









NoteFurther reading



Saad and Greenbaum give complementary treatments of Krylov methods and preconditioning (Saad 2003; Greenbaum 1997). The original conjugate-gradient and GMRES papers remain readable (Hestenes and Stiefel 1952; Saad and Schultz 1986). For multigrid, the tutorial by Briggs, Henson, and McCormick is a natural next step (Briggs et al. 2000).






Briggs, William L., Van Emden Henson, and Steve F. McCormick. 2000. A Multigrid Tutorial. 2nd ed. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898719505.


Greenbaum, Anne. 1997. Iterative Methods for Solving Linear Systems. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611970937.


Hestenes, Magnus R., and Eduard Stiefel. 1952. “Methods of Conjugate Gradients for Solving Linear Systems.” Journal of Research of the National Bureau of Standards 49 (6): 409–36. https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.049.044.


Saad, Yousef. 2003. Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems. 2nd ed. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718003.


Saad, Yousef, and Martin H. Schultz. 1986. “GMRES: A Generalized Minimal Residual Algorithm for Solving Nonsymmetric Linear Systems.” SIAM Journal on Scientific and Statistical Computing 7 (3): 856–69. https://doi.org/10.1137/0907058.

title: 28  Randomized Methods in Linear Algebra
text:
28.1 Trace and Diagonal Estimation
A calculation may require only a sum of matrix entries or a few dominant directions. Computing an entire inverse or a full SVD can then do much more work than is needed. Random vectors let us estimate selected quantities through products and solves. We must specify what is random and how its error is measured.
We first estimate traces and diagonals from random probe vectors. We then compute low-rank approximations from the range of \(\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) for a random matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\). Finally, we show how random sampling limits fill during Gaussian elimination on graph Laplacians, which produces a preconditioner for the conjugate gradient method.
The trace of \(\bA^{-1}\) and the diagonal of \(\bA^{-1}\) appear as sums of variances in statistics, as effective resistances in graphs, and as sensitivities of linear models. Computing \(\operatorname{diag}(\bA^{-1})\) exactly requires solving \(\bA\bx=\be_i\) for every \(i\). The estimators below use only products \(\bz\mapsto\bA\bz\), or solves with \(\bA\), applied to a few random vectors \(\bz\).
For independent signs \(z_i=\pm1\) with equal probability, \(z_i^2=1\) whereas \(\mathbb E[z_iz_j]=0\) for \(i\neq j\). In a quadratic form, the diagonal contributions therefore survive averaging and the off-diagonal contributions cancel in expectation. A finite average still has random error. Unbiased means its expectation is correct, not that every sample is accurate.
Averaging \(k\) independent samples divides the variance by \(k\). For a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix, \(\|\bA\|_F^2=\sum_i\lambda_i^2\leq(\sum_i\lambda_i)^2=\operatorname{tr}(\bA)^2\), so with Gaussian probes the relative standard deviation of the averaged estimate is at most \(\sqrt{2/k}\). The error decreases like \(k^{-1/2}\), independently of \(n\), which is the usual Monte Carlo rate. One hundred probes therefore give a relative standard deviation of at most about fourteen percent, and the estimator is most useful when this accuracy is sufficient or when \(\|\bA\|_F\) is much smaller than \(\operatorname{tr}(\bA)\) (Hutchinson 1990).
To estimate \(\operatorname{diag}(\bA^{-1})\), we replace \(\bA\bz_l\) by \(\bA^{-1}\bz_l\) (Bekas et al. 2007). One sparse factorization of \(\bA\) is computed once, and each probe then costs one pair of triangular solves. For \(k\ll n\), this replaces \(n\) solves by \(k\) solves. Bekas, Kokiopoulou, and Saad also use structured probe vectors that are orthogonal on blocks of the matrix, which removes the error from entries within those blocks.

title: 28  Randomized Methods in Linear Algebra
text:
28.2 Randomized Low-Rank Approximation
By the referenced result, the best rank-\(k\) approximation of \(\bA\) is given by its truncated SVD. Computing the full SVD of a large matrix in order to keep a few singular triplets wastes almost all of the work. If the singular values decay, the dominant left singular vectors span most of the range of \(\bA\). A product \(\bA\boldsymbol{\omega}\) with a random vector \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) is a random combination of the columns of \(\bA\), and it lies mostly in that dominant subspace. A few such products therefore span most of the dominant range.






NoteDefinition: Randomized SVD



Let \(\bA\in\fR^{m\times n}\), let \(k\) be the target rank, and let \(p\geq2\) be an oversampling parameter with \(k+p\leq\min(m,n)\). If the sample matrix is rank deficient, retain only its independent orthonormal columns and adjust the reduced dimensions below.

Draw \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\in\fR^{n\times(k+p)}\) with independent standard normal entries.
Form \(\bY=\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) and compute its thin QR factorization \(\bY=\bQ\bR\).
Form \(\bB=\bQ^T\bA\in\fR^{(k+p)\times n}\) and compute its SVD \(\bB=\tilde{\bU}\bsigma\bV^T\).
Return the approximate SVD \(\bA\approx(\bQ\tilde{\bU})\bsigma\bV^T\), truncated to rank \(k\) if required.









WarningExercise



Assume \(\bA\) has rank exactly \(k\) and the columns of \(\bY\) span its range. Show that \(\bQ\bQ^T\bA=\bA\), so the reduced SVD recovers the matrix exactly in exact arithmetic. For a matrix of larger rank, derive \(\bA-\bQ\bB=(\bI-\bQ\bQ^T)\bA\). What error remains before any singular values of \(\bB\) are discarded?


The algorithm touches \(\bA\) only through the two products \(\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) and \(\bQ^T\bA\). For a dense matrix these cost \(O(mn(k+p))\) flops, and for a sparse matrix \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(\bA)(k+p))\). The QR factorization and the small SVD cost \(O((m+n)(k+p)^2)\). Before the final truncation, the approximation error is \(\|\bA-\bQ\bQ^T\bA\|\), because \(\bQ\tilde{\bU}\bsigma\bV^T=\bQ\bQ^T\bA\). Halko, Martinsson, and Tropp prove that \[
\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}\,\|\bA-\bQ\bQ^T\bA\|_F
    \leq\Big(1+\frac{k}{p-1}\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2\Big)^{1/2}
\end{align}
\] for Gaussian \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) (Halko et al. 2011). The second factor is the error of the truncated SVD, so the randomized method loses at most the first factor in expectation. With \(p=k+1\), that factor is \(\sqrt2\).






TipRemark



(Slowly decaying singular values) When the singular values decay slowly, the range of \(\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) contains significant components from the trailing singular vectors. Replacing \(\bY=\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) by \(\bY=(\bA\bA^T)^q\bA\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) multiplies the \(j\)th singular direction by \(\sigma_j^{2q+1}\) and suppresses the trailing directions, exactly as in power iteration (the referenced result). In floating-point arithmetic, the columns are orthonormalized after each multiplication, because the powers otherwise become numerically dependent (Halko et al. 2011).

title: 29  Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations
text:
29.1 Initial Value Problems and Well-Posedness
A differential equation gives the rate of change of a state. To compute a trajectory, we must turn that rate into a finite step. We begin with the simplest construction, then distinguish the error made in one step from the error accumulated over an interval.
Accuracy as the step size tends to zero does not settle how large a step we can use. A numerical solution can grow even when the exact solution decays. We study this restriction through a scalar test equation, then consider higher-order methods and the behavior of oscillating mechanical systems.
Before analyzing a method, we need an exact solution to compare it with. The next theorem gives a sufficient existence and uniqueness condition. Its global Lipschitz assumption is stronger than the local assumptions often used in ODE theory, but guarantees a solution throughout the stated finite interval.
