title: 29  Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations
text:
29.2 Time-Stepping Methods
The exact increment satisfies \(\by(t_{n+1})-\by(t_n)=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol f(t,\by(t))\,dt\). Approximating this integral by its left endpoint, right endpoint, or trapezoidal rule gives three basic methods. The right-endpoint methods contain the unknown new state on both sides, so each step requires solving equations.






NoteDefinition: Forward Euler, Backward Euler, and Trapezoidal Methods



For time step \(h = t_{n+1} - t_n\):

Forward Euler (explicit): \(\by_{n+1} = \by_n + h \boldsymbol{f}(t_n, \by_n)\).
Backward Euler (implicit): \(\by_{n+1} = \by_n + h \boldsymbol{f}(t_{n+1}, \by_{n+1})\).
Trapezoidal Rule (implicit Crank–Nicolson): \[
\begin{align}
\by_{n+1} = \by_n + \frac{h}{2} \left[ \boldsymbol{f}(t_n, \by_n) + \boldsymbol{f}(t_{n+1}, \by_{n+1}) \right].
\end{align}
\]

text:
29.5 Runge–Kutta Methods
Runge–Kutta methods achieve high orders of accuracy without storing historical steps by evaluating intermediate stages within each time step.






WarningExercise



A first improvement on Euler is to estimate the derivative halfway through the step. Form the provisional value \(\by_{n+1/2}=\by_n+(h/2)\boldsymbol f(\by_n)\) and then set \(\by_{n+1}=\by_n+h\boldsymbol f(\by_{n+1/2})\). For a smooth autonomous vector field, expand this update to order \(h^2\) and compare it with the exact Taylor expansion. What is its one-step defect? This two-stage construction illustrates why intermediate stages can improve the order.








NoteDefinition: Classical Fourth-Order Runge–Kutta Method (RK4)



For an autonomous ODE \(\by' = \boldsymbol{f}(\by)\), the classical RK4 method computes four stages: \[
\begin{align}
\boldsymbol{k}_1 &= \boldsymbol{f}(\by_n), \\
    \boldsymbol{k}_2 &= \boldsymbol{f}\left( \by_n + \frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{k}_1 \right), \\
    \boldsymbol{k}_3 &= \boldsymbol{f}\left( \by_n + \frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{k}_2 \right), \\
    \boldsymbol{k}_4 &= \boldsymbol{f}\left( \by_n + h\boldsymbol{k}_3 \right),
\end{align}
\] and sets the update \[
\begin{align}
\by_{n+1} = \by_n + \frac{h}{6} \left( \boldsymbol{k}_1 + 2\boldsymbol{k}_2 + 2\boldsymbol{k}_3 + \boldsymbol{k}_4 \right).
\end{align}
\] The one-step defect is \(O(h^5)\). With the normalization in the referenced result, the local truncation error and the global error are both \(O(h^4)\).








NoteTheorem: RK4 Stability Polynomial



Applied to the scalar linear test equation \(y' = \lambda y\), the stability function of RK4 is \[
\begin{align}
R(z) = 1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{6} + \frac{z^4}{24} = \sum_{k=0}^4 \frac{z^k}{k!}, \qquad z = h\lambda.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



Substitute \(f(y)=\lambda y\) into the four stages. Express each stage as \(\lambda y_n\) times a polynomial in \(z=h\lambda\), and collect terms in the update. Why does matching the exponential on this scalar test problem alone not prove order four for a nonlinear ODE?

title: 29  Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations
text:
29.6 Symplectic Integrators and Geometric Mechanics
For the oscillator \(q'=v\), \(v'=-q\), the exact energy \(H=(q^2+v^2)/2\) is constant. Forward Euler instead multiplies this energy by \(1+h^2\) at every step. A small local error can therefore accumulate into a qualitatively wrong orbit over many periods. We now construct an update from simple motions that preserve the geometry of position and momentum. The matrix identity below defines precisely the property called symplecticity.






NoteDefinition: Velocity Verlet Algorithm



For a potential \(V\) with continuous second derivatives and a separable Hamiltonian \(H(\bq, \bv) = \frac{1}{2}\|\bv\|_2^2 + V(\bq)\) with equations of motion \(\bq' = \bv\) and \(\bv' = \bF(\bq) = -\nabla V(\bq)\), the Velocity Verlet method is: \[
\begin{align}
\bv_{n+1/2} &= \bv_n + \frac{h}{2} \bF(\bq_n), \\
    \bq_{n+1} &= \bq_n + h \bv_{n+1/2}, \\
    \bv_{n+1} &= \bv_{n+1/2} + \frac{h}{2} \bF(\bq_{n+1}).
\end{align}
\]


Velocity Verlet first changes velocity with position held fixed, then changes position with velocity held fixed, and finally completes the velocity change. In one position dimension these are shears of the \((q,v)\) plane. Each preserves area. In higher dimensions, symplecticity requires the stronger matrix identity \(\bJ^T\boldsymbol\Omega\bJ=\boldsymbol\Omega\), where \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) pairs positions with their corresponding momenta. Volume preservation alone would not establish it.






NoteTheorem: Symplecticity and Area Preservation of Velocity Verlet



The one-step Velocity Verlet map \(\Psi_h: (\bq_n, \bv_n) \mapsto (\bq_{n+1}, \bv_{n+1})\) preserves the canonical symplectic structure. In particular, the Jacobian matrix \(\bJ = \frac{\partial(\bq_{n+1}, \bv_{n+1})}{\partial(\bq_n, \bv_n)}\) satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\det(\bJ) = 1.
\end{align}
\] The full symplectic assertion is that its Jacobian satisfies \(\bJ^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bJ=\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) for the canonical symplectic matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\). Symplecticity implies \(\det(\bJ)=1\), so Velocity Verlet also preserves phase-space volume.








TipProof





Decompose the Velocity Verlet step into the composition of three elementary shears: \[
\begin{align}
\Psi_h = \psi_3 \circ \psi_2 \circ \psi_1,
\end{align}
\] where: \[
\begin{align}
\psi_1(\bq, \bv) &= \left( \bq,\, \bv + \frac{h}{2}\bF(\bq) \right), \\
    \psi_2(\bq, \bv) &= (\bq + h\bv,\, \bv), \\
    \psi_3(\bq, \bv) &= \left( \bq,\, \bv + \frac{h}{2}\bF(\bq) \right).
\end{align}
\] Evaluating the Jacobian of each shear map: \[
\begin{align}
\bJ_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ \frac{h}{2}\nabla\bF(\bq) & \bI \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
    \bJ_2 = \begin{pmatrix} \bI & h\bI \\ \bzero & \bI \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
    \bJ_3 = \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ \frac{h}{2}\nabla\bF(\bq_{n+1}) & \bI \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
\] Here \(\nabla\bF\) denotes the Jacobian of the force, the matrix of its first partial derivatives. Since the force is the negative gradient of a potential with continuous second derivatives, that Jacobian is the negative Hessian of \(V\). Equality of mixed partial derivatives makes it symmetric. This symmetry is essential for the symplectic calculation.
Because \(\bF=-\nabla V\), the Hessian block \(\bS = \frac{h}{2}\nabla\bF = -\frac{h}{2}\nabla^2V\) is symmetric (\(\bS^T = \bS\)). With canonical symplectic matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix}\), evaluating the quadratic form for \(\bJ_1\): \[
\begin{align}
\bJ_1^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_1 &= \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bS \\ \bzero & \bI \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ \bS & \bI \end{pmatrix} \\
    &= \begin{pmatrix} -\bS & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ \bS & \bI \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\bS + \bS & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix} = \boldsymbol{\Omega}.
\end{align}
\] Similarly, for the translation shear \(\bJ_2\): \[
\begin{align}
\bJ_2^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_2 &= \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ h\bI & \bI \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bI & h\bI \\ \bzero & \bI \end{pmatrix} \\
    &= \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & h\bI \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bI & h\bI \\ \bzero & \bI \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & -h\bI + h\bI \end{pmatrix} = \boldsymbol{\Omega}.
\end{align}
\] The third shear \(\bJ_3\) has the same form as \(\bJ_1\) and satisfies \(\bJ_3^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_3 = \boldsymbol{\Omega}\). The canonical matrix \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) records the pairing of each position coordinate with its corresponding momentum coordinate. The displayed calculations verify the full symplectic matrix identity for each individual shear, rather than checking its determinant alone.
By the chain rule, \(\bJ = \bJ_3 \bJ_2 \bJ_1\), so \[
\begin{align}
\bJ^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ = \bJ_1^T \bJ_2^T \left( \bJ_3^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_3 \right) \bJ_2 \bJ_1 = \bJ_1^T \left( \bJ_2^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_2 \right) \bJ_1 = \bJ_1^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_1 = \boldsymbol{\Omega}.
\end{align}
\] Each shear has unit determinant: \(\det(\bJ_1) = \det(\bJ_2) = \det(\bJ_3) = 1\). Therefore \[
\begin{align}
\det(\bJ) = \det(\bJ_3)\det(\bJ_2)\det(\bJ_1) = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1.
\end{align}
\]
The product in the chain rule evaluates each Jacobian at the corresponding intermediate state. The identity for each factor holds at every such state, so the cancellations remain valid even for nonlinear forces. A unit determinant follows separately from their triangular block forms. This establishes both claims in the theorem.









WarningExercise



Symplectic geometry of the harmonic oscillator. Consider the harmonic oscillator \(q' = v\), \(v' = -q\) with exact energy \(E(q, v) = \frac{1}{2}(q^2 + v^2)\).

Compute the one-step update matrix \(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{FE}}\) for Forward Euler and show that \(\det(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{FE}}) = 1 + h^2 > 1\).
Compute the one-step update matrix \(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Verlet}}\) for Velocity Verlet. Confirm that \(\det(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Verlet}}) = 1\).
For \(0<h<2\), show that Velocity Verlet conserves the positive definite quadratic form \(\tilde{H}(q, v) = \frac{1}{2}(q^2 + v^2) - \frac{h^2}{8}q^2 = H(q, v) + O(h^2)\).

title: 29  Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations
text:
29.7 Further Exercises






WarningExercise



The discrete Gronwall lemma and Forward Euler convergence.

Let \(\by(t)\) solve \(\by' = \boldsymbol{f}(t, \by)\) with \(\|\boldsymbol{f}(t, \bu) - \boldsymbol{f}(t, \bv)\| \leq L\|\bu - \bv\|\). Use Taylor’s theorem to show that the one-step defect of Forward Euler satisfies \(\|\by(t_{n+1}) - (\by(t_n) + h\boldsymbol{f}(t_n, \by(t_n)))\| \leq \frac{h^2}{2} M_2\), where \(M_2 = \max \|\by''(t)\|\).
Derive the error recurrence \(\|\be_{n+1}\| \leq (1 + Lh)\|\be_n\| + \frac{h^2}{2}M_2\).
Apply the referenced result to establish the rigorous global error bound \(\|\be_n\| \leq \frac{M_2}{2L}(e^{L(t_n - t_0)} - 1)h\).









WarningExercise



Adaptive step size control via embedded Runge–Kutta pairs.

An embedded pair computes a lower-order approximation \(\by_{n+1}^{[p]}\) and a higher-order approximation \(\by_{n+1}^{[p+1]}\) sharing stages. Show that the difference \(\be_{n+1} = \by_{n+1}^{[p+1]} - \by_{n+1}^{[p]}\) satisfies \(\|\be_{n+1}\| = C h^{p+1} + O(h^{p+2})\).
Given error tolerance \(\varepsilon\) and current step size \(h_{\mathrm{old}}\), derive the optimal step size formula \(h_{\mathrm{new}} = s h_{\mathrm{old}} (\varepsilon / \|\be_{n+1}\|)^{1/(p+1)}\) with safety factor \(s \in (0, 1)\).
Explain why adaptive solvers reject a step and repeat with smaller \(h\) when \(\|\be_{n+1}\| > \varepsilon\), and why an implementation may cap the growth factor, for example by \(h_{\mathrm{new}}\leq5h_{\mathrm{old}}\). Explain why the numerical cap is a design choice.









WarningExercise



Stiffness in chemical cascades and BDF methods. Consider the singularly perturbed initial value problem \(\varepsilon y' = -y + \cos(t)\) with \(y(0) = 0\) and \(\varepsilon = 10^{-4}\).

Find the exact solution and identify the fast boundary layer transient \(e^{-t/\varepsilon}\) and the slow quasi-steady state \(\cos(t) + \varepsilon \sin(t)\).
Explain why explicit RK4 requires \(h \lesssim 2.8 \times 10^{-4}\) throughout the entire simulation, even after the transient has decayed to zero.
Formulate the BDF2 update \(\frac{3\by_{n+1} - 4\by_n + \by_{n-1}}{2h} = \boldsymbol{f}(t_{n+1}, \by_{n+1})\) and show that it allows time steps \(h = 0.1\) in the smooth regime.

Dahlquist’s paper is the classical source for the stability barrier for linear multistep methods (Dahlquist 1963). Quarteroni, Sacco, and Saleri provide a broader numerical-analysis reference (Quarteroni et al. 2007).

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
30.1 Definitions and Preprocessing
An observation with \(p\) measured features is a point in \(\fR^p\). A collection of observations may vary strongly along a few directions and very little along the others. Principal component analysis chooses orthogonal directions that retain as much of this variation as possible.
We first subtract the mean observation so that variation is measured about the origin. We then express the variance along a direction as a Rayleigh quotient. The SVD identifies the directions and gives the error caused by retaining only some of them.

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
NoteDefinition: Data Centering



Data matrix \(\bX \in \fR^{n\times p}\) (\(n\geq2\) samples, \(p\) features) is first centered: \[
\begin{align}
X_{ij} \leftarrow X_{ij} - \bar{x}_j, \quad \bar{x}_j = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}.
\end{align}
\] Throughout this section, \(\bX\) is assumed centered, and singular values beyond \(\min(n,p)\) are understood to be zero. A variance ratio is defined only when \(\|\bX\|_F>0\).








NoteDefinition: Sample Covariance Matrix



The matrix \(\bS = \frac{1}{n-1}\bX^T\bX \in \fR^{p\times p}\).

Diagonal: \(S_{jj}\) is the variance of feature \(j\).
Off-diagonal: \(S_{ij}\) is the covariance between features \(i\) and \(j\).
Property: \(\bS\) is symmetric positive semidefinite (SPSD).









WarningExercise




Show that centering makes each column of \(\bX\) have mean zero.
Prove that the diagonal entries of \(\bS\) are sample variances.
Prove that \(\bS\) is symmetric positive semidefinite by computing \(\bz^T\bS\bz\).

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
30.2 Principal Directions and Scores
For a unit direction \(\bv\in\fR^p\), the projected observations are the entries of \(\bX\bv\). Their mean is zero because the columns of \(\bX\) are centered. Their sample variance is therefore \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\|\bX\bv\|_2^2}{n-1}=\bv^T\bS\bv.
\end{align}
\] The first principal direction maximizes this variance. By the spectral theorem, it is an eigenvector for the largest eigenvalue of \(\bS\). Subsequent directions maximize variance subject to orthogonality to the preceding ones.






WarningExercise



Take centered observations \((2,0)\), \((-2,0)\), \((0,1)\), and \((0,-1)\) as rows of \(\bX\). Compute the variance along \(\bv=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^T\) and find its maximum. Identify the first and second principal directions. What changes if every second coordinate is multiplied by three?








NoteTheorem: Principal Directions and Scores



Let \(\bX = \bU\bsigma\bV^T\) be the SVD of the centered data matrix.

Principal Directions (Loadings): Columns of \(\bV\) (eigenvectors of \(\bS\)).
Principal Components (Scores): \(\bZ = \bX\bV = \bU\bsigma\).
Variances: \(\lambda_i = \text{Var}(\bz_i) = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}\).









TipProof





Substituting the SVD \(\bX = \bU\bsigma\bV^T\) into the sample covariance matrix \(\bS\): \[
\begin{align}
\bS &= \frac{1}{n-1} \bX^T\bX \\
    &= \frac{1}{n-1} \left( \bV\bsigma^T\bU^T \right) \left( \bU\bsigma\bV^T \right) \\
    &= \frac{1}{n-1} \bV \bsigma^T (\bU^T\bU) \bsigma \bV^T \\
    &= \bV \left( \frac{\bsigma^T\bsigma}{n-1} \right) \bV^T.
\end{align}
\] Because \(\bV\) is orthogonal and \(\frac{\bsigma^T\bsigma}{n-1}\) is diagonal with non-negative entries \(\frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}\), this is the spectral decomposition of \(\bS\). The columns \(\bv_i\) are eigenvectors of \(\bS\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2 / (n-1)\). The covariance eigenvalues are therefore squared singular values divided by \(n-1\). This division is positive because the sample-size assumption is \(n\geq2\). If a singular value is zero, the corresponding direction has zero measured sample variance.
The principal component score matrix is \[
\begin{align}
\bZ = \bX\bV = \left( \bU\bsigma\bV^T \right) \bV = \bU\bsigma (\bV^T\bV) = \bU\bsigma.
\end{align}
\] The sample covariance matrix of the scores is \[
\begin{align}
\bS_{\bZ} = \frac{1}{n-1} \bZ^T\bZ = \frac{1}{n-1} (\bsigma^T\bU^T)(\bU\bsigma) = \frac{\bsigma^T\bsigma}{n-1} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, ..., \lambda_p),
\end{align}
\] confirming that distinct score columns \(\bz_i, \bz_j\) have sample covariance zero for \(i \neq j\).
Because the centered columns of \(\bX\) have zero sums, \(\mathbf1^T\bZ=\mathbf1^T\bX\bV=\bzero^T\). Thus the score columns are centered too, making \(\bZ^T\bZ/(n-1)\) their sample covariance without an additional centering step. Its diagonal form proves that distinct score columns are uncorrelated. It does not imply statistical independence, which is a stronger claim. See Jolliffe (2002) for the statistical interpretation.









TipRemark



(PCA stability) Forming \(\bX^T\bX\) squares the 2-norm condition number: \(\kappa_2(\bX^T\bX)=\kappa_2(\bX)^2\) when \(\bX\) has full column rank. Compute the singular vectors directly from an SVD when small singular values or numerical rank matter.








WarningExercise



Show that centering is left multiplication by \(\bC=\bI-\mathbf1\mathbf1^T/n\). Prove that \(\bC^2=\bC=\bC^T\), deduce \(\operatorname{rank}(\bX)\leq n-1\), and explain why at most \(n-1\) principal components can have positive variance even when \(p>n\).

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
30.3 Variance and Dimensionality Reduction






NoteDefinition: Proportion of Variance Explained (PVE)



For the first \(k\) components: \[
\begin{align}
\text{PVE}_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^p \sigma_i^2}.
\end{align}
\]








NoteTheorem: Optimal Approximation



The rank-\(k\) matrix \[
\begin{align}
\bX_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i \bu_i \bv_i^T
\end{align}
\] is the optimal \(k\)-dimensional linear approximation of the data in the Frobenius norm, by the Eckart–Young theorem.








WarningExercise




Use the referenced result to prove the referenced result.
Show that \(\|\bX-\bX_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2\).
Show that \(\text{PVE}_k=1-\|\bX-\bX_k\|_F^2/\|\bX\|_F^2\).
Explain why a PVE threshold is a modeling choice, not a theorem.

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
30.4 Implementation Details






TipRemark



(Standardization) If features have different units, PCA will be dominated by large-scale features. When equal feature weighting is intended, standardize nonconstant columns by their standard deviations: \(X_{ij} \leftarrow (X_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)/s_j\).








TipRemark



(Interpretation) Principal components are directions of large variance. A large loading identifies a direction of variation in the data matrix. It does not by itself explain why that variation occurs.








NoteDefinition: Dual PCA for \(p \gg n\)



When the number of features greatly exceeds the number of samples, we may diagonalize the \(n\times n\) Gram matrix \(\mathbf{K}=\bX\bX^T\) instead of the \(p\times p\) covariance matrix. For each nonzero singular value, the feature-space principal direction is recovered from \(\bv_i=\bX^T\bu_i/\sigma_i\). Kernel PCA replaces this linear Gram matrix by a centered nonlinear kernel matrix.

title: 30  Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
text:
30.5 Further Exercises






WarningExercise



Center \(\bX = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \\ -1 & -4 \end{pmatrix}\) and compute \(\bS\). Find the PVE for \(k=1\).








WarningExercise



If two largest singular values are equal, show that any orthonormal basis of their right singular subspace gives the same variance and reconstruction error. Explain which PCA subspace is determined and which individual directions are not uniquely determined.








WarningExercise



Load the Iris dataset. Plot the data in the basis of the first two PCs. Do species cluster?








WarningExercise



Verify that the sum of variances \(\sum \lambda_i\) equals the total variance \(\text{Tr}(\bS)\).








NoteFurther reading



Jolliffe is a standard statistical reference for principal component analysis (Jolliffe 2002). The Golub–Kahan paper gives the bidiagonalization behind modern large-scale SVD calculations (Golub and Kahan 1965).






Golub, Gene H., and William Kahan. 1965. “Calculating the Singular Values and Pseudo-Inverse of a Matrix.” Journal of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics, Series B: Numerical Analysis 2 (2): 205–24. https://doi.org/10.1137/0702016.


Jolliffe, Ian T. 2002. Principal Component Analysis. 2nd ed. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/b98835.

title: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians
text:
31.1 Graph Matrices and the Laplacian
A graph records which pairs of vertices interact and how strongly. A scalar value at each vertex can describe a temperature, a signal, or a quantity attached to an observation. The graph Laplacian compares each value with those of its neighbors.
Its quadratic form adds the squared differences across edges. This connects eigenvalues to connectivity and suggests ways to partition a graph. We then normalize edge weights to obtain a random walk and use its probabilities to compare data points.
crumbs: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians

title: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians
text:
NoteDefinition: Adjacency and Degree Matrices



For a weighted undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n\geq2\) vertices, take \(E\) to contain exactly the edges of positive weight:

Adjacency \(\bA\): \(A_{ij} = w_{ij} \geq 0\) if \((i,j) \in E\), and \(A_{ij} = 0\) otherwise. We assume \(w_{ij} = w_{ji}\) and \(A_{ii} = 0\).
Degree \(\bD\): Diagonal matrix with entries \(D_{ii} = d_i = \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}\).









NoteExample



For the path \(1\)–\(2\)–\(3\) with unit weights, the middle vertex has two neighbors and the endpoints have one. Its Laplacian is \[
\begin{align}
\bL=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
\] For values \(\bx=(a,b,c)^T\), its quadratic form is \((a-b)^2+(b-c)^2\). A constant signal has zero energy. A jump across either edge has positive energy.








WarningExercise



Derive this quadratic form by multiplying out \(\bx^T\bL\bx\). Replace the second edge weight by \(\varepsilon>0\) and repeat. Evaluate the form on \((1,1,-2)^T\). How does the energy change as the second edge becomes weak?








NoteDefinition: Unnormalized Graph Laplacian



The unnormalized graph Laplacian is \[
\begin{align}
\bL = \bD - \bA.
\end{align}
\] For any signal \(\bx \in \fR^n\) on the vertices, the action of \(\bL\) acts as a discrete Laplace operator: \[
\begin{align}
(\bL \bx)_i = \sum_{j \sim i} w_{ij} (x_i - x_j).
\end{align}
\] The associated quadratic form satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\bx^T \bL \bx = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2 = \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2.
\end{align}
\]








NoteProposition: Laplacian Positive Semidefinite



For an undirected graph with nonnegative weights, \(\bL\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, and \(\bL\mathbf{1}=\bzero\).








TipProof





Symmetry follows from \(w_{ij} = w_{ji}\), so \(\bA = \bA^T\) and \(\bL = \bD - \bA = \bL^T\). Expanding the quadratic form algebraically from definitions: \[
\begin{align}
\bx^T \bL \bx &= \bx^T (\bD - \bA) \bx = \sum_{i=1}^n d_i x_i^2 - \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i x_j \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij} \right) x_i^2 - \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i x_j \\
    &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_j^2 - \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i x_j \\
    &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2 = \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2.
\end{align}
\] To obtain the middle equality, interchange the indices in one copy of the degree sum and use \(w_{ij}=w_{ji}\). The term \(-2x_ix_j\) then combines with \(x_i^2+x_j^2\) to form a square. The factor \(1/2\) removes the duplicate ordered pairs \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\).
Because \(w_{ij} \geq 0\) and \((x_i - x_j)^2 \geq 0\), each term is non-negative, so \(\bx^T \bL \bx \geq 0\) for all \(\bx \in \fR^n\), proving positive semidefiniteness. For \(\bx = \mathbf{1}\), every coordinate satisfies \((\bL\mathbf{1})_i = d_i - \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij} = 0\), so \(\bL\mathbf{1} = \bzero\).
The quadratic-form inequality is the definition of positive semidefiniteness. It is not strict positive definiteness, because the nonzero constant vector has zero quadratic form and is annihilated by the matrix.









NoteTheorem: Spectral Properties of the Graph Laplacian



Let the eigenvalues of \(\bL\) be ordered as \(0 = \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq ... \leq \lambda_n\).

\(\lambda_1 = 0\) with eigenvector \(\bv_1 = \mathbf{1}\).
The multiplicity of eigenvalue \(0\) equals the number of connected components of \(G\).
The second smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\) is the algebraic connectivity (Fiedler value). It satisfies \(\lambda_2 > 0\) if and only if \(G\) is connected.









TipProof





the referenced result shows that all eigenvalues of \(\bL\) are nonnegative and that \(\mathbf{1}\in\ker(\bL)\), so \(\lambda_1=0\).
It remains to identify the entire nullspace. If \(\bx\in\ker(\bL)\), then \[
\begin{align}
0=\bx^T\bL\bx=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2.
\end{align}
\] Every term is nonnegative. Hence \(x_i=x_j\) across every edge with positive weight, and therefore \(\bx\) is constant on each connected component. Conversely, a vector that is constant on each connected component has zero difference across every edge and belongs to \(\ker(\bL)\). A constant on one connected component may be chosen independently of the constants on the other components, because there are no edges between them. The vector equal to one on a given component and zero elsewhere is therefore in the null space.
The indicator vectors of the connected components form a basis for this nullspace, so the multiplicity of eigenvalue zero equals the number of components.
In particular, \(G\) is connected exactly when \(\ker(\bL)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}\}\). In that case zero is a simple eigenvalue, so \(\lambda_2>0\). If \(G\) is disconnected, the nullspace has dimension at least two and \(\lambda_2=0\).
These indicator vectors are independent because their supports are disjoint and nonempty. They span every vector constant on components by assigning its component-wise constants as coefficients. This supplies both halves of the basis assertion and the exact dimension count.









WarningExercise



(Path graph Laplacian spectrum) For a three-node unweighted path graph \(1-2-3\), write down \(\bA\) and \(\bL\). Compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(\bL\) by hand. Verify that \(\lambda_1 = 0\) with \(\bv_1 = (1, 1, 1)^T\), and compute the algebraic connectivity \(\lambda_2\).








NoteCorollary: Rayleigh Characterization of Algebraic Connectivity



For a connected undirected graph, \[
\begin{align}
\lambda_2
    =\min_{\bx\perp\mathbf{1},\,\bx\neq\bzero}
    \frac{\bx^T\bL\bx}{\bx^T\bx}
    =\min_{\bx\perp\mathbf{1},\,\bx\neq\bzero}
    \frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2}{\sum_i x_i^2}.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





For a connected graph, the null space is spanned by the constant vector. Normalize it as \(\bq_1=\mathbf1/\sqrt n\) and complete an orthonormal eigenbasis \(\bq_1,...,\bq_n\), with \(0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\).
Expand a vector perpendicular to \(\mathbf1\) in this basis. Its first coefficient is \(\bq_1^T\bx=\mathbf1^T\bx/\sqrt n=0\), so \(\bx=\sum_{i=2}^nc_i\bq_i\). For a nonzero such vector, at least one remaining coefficient is nonzero. Therefore \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\bx^T\bL\bx}{\bx^T\bx}
&=\frac{\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum_{i=2}^n c_i^2}\\
&\geq\frac{\lambda_2\sum_{i=2}^nc_i^2}{\sum_{i=2}^n c_i^2}
=\lambda_2.
\end{align}
\] The lower bound is attained by \(\bx=\bq_2\), which is perpendicular to the constant vector. Hence it is the minimum over the entire allowed subspace.
Finally, substitute the graph energy identity \(\bx^T\bL\bx=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2\) and \(\bx^T\bx=\sum_i x_i^2\). This gives the second expression in the statement. The orthogonality constraint removes the constant direction, whose quotient would otherwise give the uninformative minimum zero.









WarningExercise



(Rayleigh quotient for algebraic connectivity) For the path graph in the preceding exercise, minimize the quotient in the referenced result over vectors of the form \((a,b,-a-b)^T\). Verify that the minimum equals the computed value of \(\lambda_2\). Then evaluate the numerator on a two-level vector that is constant on each side of a proposed cut and explain how weak cross-cut weights lower its energy.








NoteDefinition: Normalized Laplacians



Assume every vertex has positive degree. Normalized Laplacians account for high-degree vertices:

Symmetric Normalized Laplacian: \(\bL_{\text{sym}} = \bD^{-1/2} \bL \bD^{-1/2} = \bI - \bD^{-1/2} \bA \bD^{-1/2}\). Its spectrum lies in the interval \([0, 2]\).
Random Walk Laplacian: \(\bL_{\text{rw}} = \bD^{-1} \bL = \bI - \bD^{-1} \bA\). It is similar to \(\bL_{\text{sym}}\) and shares its eigenvalues.









WarningExercise



Write \(\by=\bD^{-1/2}\bx\) and use \((y_i-y_j)^2\leq2y_i^2+2y_j^2\) to prove \(0\leq\bx^T\bL_{\mathrm{sym}}\bx\leq2\|\bx\|_2^2\). Deduce the spectral interval \([0,2]\), and verify the similarity between the two normalized Laplacians. What definition must be added if isolated vertices are allowed?

title: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians
text:
31.2 Spectral Clustering
A cut divides the vertices into nonempty sets \(A\) and \(B\). Let \(\operatorname{cut}(A,B)=\sum_{i\in A,j\in B}w_{ij}\) and \(\operatorname{vol}(A)=\sum_{i\in A}d_i\). The normalized cut divides the cross-edge weight by the volume on each side and adds the two results: \[
\begin{align}
\operatorname{Ncut}(A,B)
=\operatorname{cut}(A,B)
\left(\frac1{\operatorname{vol}(A)}+\frac1{\operatorname{vol}(B)}\right).
\end{align}
\] The denominators discourage cutting off a set with tiny total degree. The discrete problem selects vertex sets. A relaxation permits real-valued assignments and gives a lower bound on the best discrete value. Assume positive degrees and a connected graph in the following construction.






NoteTheorem: Spectral Relaxation of Graph Cuts



Partitioning a graph into two disjoint sets \(A\) and \(B\) to minimize the normalized cut is NP-hard. Relaxing the discrete indicator vector to a continuous vector subject to an orthogonality constraint yields the Rayleigh quotient problem \[
\begin{align}
\min_{\bx \perp \bD\mathbf{1},\, \bx \neq \bzero} \frac{\bx^T \bL \bx}{\bx^T \bD \bx}.
\end{align}
\] The optimal solution is the Fiedler eigenvector \(\bv_2\) of the generalized eigenvalue problem \(\bL \bv = \lambda \bD \bv\), or equivalently the second eigenvector of \(\bL_{\text{rw}}\). Spectral clustering embeds vertices in \(\fR^k\) using the first \(k\) nontrivial eigenvectors, then partitions the coordinates using \(k\)-means.








WarningExercise



For a cut \(A,B\), let \(v_A=\sum_{i\in A}d_i\) and \(v_B=\sum_{i\in B}d_i\). Set \(x_i=1/v_A\) on \(A\) and \(x_i=-1/v_B\) on \(B\). Show that \(\bx^T\bD\mathbf1=0\) and that its generalized Rayleigh quotient is \(\operatorname{cut}(A,B)(1/v_A+1/v_B)\). Then set \(\bz=\bD^{1/2}\bx\) and use the spectral theorem to derive the relaxed minimizer stated above. Explain why converting that vector back into a cut is a separate step.

text:
31.4 Permutation Invariance and Graph Spectra






TipRemark



(Comparing configurations of identical particles) In molecular systems and particle clusters with \(N\) identical atoms, the state is specified by atomic positions in \(\fR^{3N}\). Comparing coordinate vectors requires deciding which atom in one configuration corresponds to which in the other, as well as accounting for rotations and translations. An exhaustive assignment search has \(N!\) candidates and becomes expensive quickly. Distance-based graph quantities avoid choosing a coordinate alignment, although a graph spectrum does not uniquely identify every configuration.








NoteTheorem: Permutation Invariance of Graph Spectra



Let \(\bD \in \fR^{N \times N}\) be the pairwise interatomic distance matrix with entries \(D_{ij} = \|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\|_2\). Under any atom permutation \(\sigma \in S_N\), the distance matrix transforms by an orthogonal permutation matrix \(\bP_\sigma\): \[
\begin{align}
\bD_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bD \bP_\sigma^T.
\end{align}
\] Let \(\bL\) be any graph Laplacian constructed from edge weights \(w_{ij} = f(D_{ij})\). Then the permuted Laplacian is \[
\begin{align}
\bL_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bL \bP_\sigma^T.
\end{align}
\] Because \(\bP_\sigma\) is orthogonal, \(\bL_\sigma\) is orthogonally similar to \(\bL\). Therefore, the eigenvalue spectrum \[
\begin{align}
\operatorname{spec}(\bL) = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, ..., \lambda_N)
\end{align}
\] is invariant under all atomic permutations \(\sigma \in S_N\) and all rigid Euclidean isometries \(\mathrm{SE}(3)\).








TipProof





Because rigid rotations and translations preserve pairwise distances \(\|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\|_2\), the matrix \(\bD\) is invariant under \(\mathrm{SE}(3)\).
For a rigid transformation \(\br_i\mapsto\bR\br_i+\boldsymbol t\) with \(\bR^T\bR=\bI\), the difference transforms as \(\bR(\br_i-\br_j)\). Its squared length is \((\br_i-\br_j)^T\bR^T\bR(\br_i-\br_j)\), equal to its old squared length. Translation cancels in the difference. Any affinity built only from these distances is therefore unchanged.
Under a permutation \(\sigma \in S_N\), vertex \(i\) maps to \(\sigma(i)\), so the permuted affinity matrix has entries \(W_{\sigma(i), \sigma(j)} = W_{ij}\). In matrix notation, \(\bW_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bW \bP_\sigma^T\). Similarly, the degree matrix transforms as \(\bD_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bD \bP_\sigma^T\). Thus \[
\begin{align}
\bL_\sigma = \bD_\sigma - \bW_\sigma = \bP_\sigma (\bD - \bW) \bP_\sigma^T = \bP_\sigma \bL \bP_\sigma^T.
\end{align}
\] Because permutation matrices are orthogonal (\(\bP_\sigma^{-1} = \bP_\sigma^T\)), the characteristic polynomial satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\det(\bL_\sigma - \lambda \bI)
    =
    \det(\bP_\sigma (\bL - \lambda \bI) \bP_\sigma^T)
    =
    \det(\bP_\sigma)\det(\bL - \lambda \bI)\det(\bP_\sigma^T)
    =
    \det(\bL - \lambda \bI).
\end{align}
\] The roots of the characteristic polynomial are identical. Thus the eigenvalue multiset \(\operatorname{spec}(\bL)\) is invariant under any relabeling of identical particles.
Similarity preserves the multiset of roots, including multiplicity. Sorting these eigenvalues therefore removes the arbitrary vertex ordering. This is an invariance statement, not a uniqueness statement: two different graphs or configurations can still have the same spectrum.

title: 31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians
text:
31.5 Affinity Scaling and Bandwidth Selection






TipRemark



(Sigmoidal behavior of the affinity sum) The Gaussian affinity kernel \(K_{ij} = \exp(-\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2 / (2\delta^2))\) requires selecting the bandwidth parameter \(\delta\). If \(\delta\) is too small, points are isolated and \(K_{ij} \approx 0\) for \(i \neq j\). If \(\delta\) is too large, points are fully connected and \(K_{ij} \approx 1\).
Define the total affinity sum \[
\begin{align}
S(\delta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N \exp\left(-\frac{\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2}{2\delta^2}\right).
\end{align}
\] For distinct data points, the log-affinity sum passes between two limiting plateaus. Under adequate sampling of a smooth manifold, an intermediate range may exhibit the scaling below:

As \(\delta \to 0\), \(K_{ij} \to 0\) for \(i \neq j\), so \(S(\delta) \to N\) and \(\ln S(\delta) \to \ln N\).
As \(\delta \to \infty\), \(K_{ij} \to 1\) for all \(i,j\), so \(S(\delta) \to N^2\) and \(\ln S(\delta) \to 2\ln N\).
In an intermediate range where the continuum approximation dominates the diagonal terms, \(S(\delta)\) can scale approximately as \(\delta^d\), where \(d\) is the intrinsic manifold dimension. The slope \(\frac{d\ln S(\delta)}{d\ln \delta} \approx d\) estimates dimension.

An intermediate scaling regime is a useful diagnostic for choosing \(\delta\), but does not guarantee recovery of manifold geometry. Sampling density, finite sample size, and connectivity must also be checked.

WarningExercise



(Permutation invariance of graph spectra) Consider a cluster of four identical atoms in \(\fR^3\).

Let the coordinates be arranged in a vector \(\bx \in \fR^{12}\). Explain why a direct search over all assignments of identical atoms has \(4!=24\) candidate permutations. What information would be lost by comparing the coordinate vectors without allowing relabeling?
Construct the interatomic distance matrix \(\bD\) and form the graph Laplacian \(\bL\). Prove that for any permutation \(\sigma \in S_4\), \(\bL_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bL \bP_\sigma^T\).
Explain how sorting the eigenvalues \(\operatorname{spec}(\bL) = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3, \lambda_4)\) produces a coordinate-free, permutation-invariant fingerprint for molecular structure.

(Diffusion time as a geometric low-pass filter) Let a diffusion operator on a data manifold have leading eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = 0.98\) and \(\lambda_2 = 0.80\).

Compute the ratio of modal contributions \((\lambda_2 / \lambda_1)^{2t}\) for diffusion times \(t = 1\), \(t = 5\), and \(t = 20\).
Explain why increasing \(t\) contracts local high-frequency fluctuations while preserving macroscopic manifold geometry.
What happens to the diffusion distance \(D_t(\bx_i, \bx_j)\) as \(t \to \infty\)?

(Sigmoidal bandwidth selection) Let \(N = 100\) data points be sampled uniformly from a circle of radius \(R = 1\) in \(\fR^2\).

Write down the formula for the affinity sum \(S(\delta) = \sum_{i,j} \exp(-\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2 / (2\delta^2))\).

For \(\delta\in[0.1,0.5]\), estimate the slope numerically. Identify where it is near one and where diagonal contributions or the curvature of the circle affect it. Repeat for two sample sizes and explain why a finite interval of exact scaling is not guaranteed.

title: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions
text:
32.1 The Exponential and Its Algebraic Properties
The scalar equation \(u'=au\) has solution \(u(t)=e^{ta}u(0)\). For the system \(\bu'=\bA\bu\), we seek a matrix that advances every initial vector in the same way. Replacing scalar powers by matrix powers in the exponential series produces that matrix.
For a large sparse matrix, the full exponential can be dense even though applying \(\bA\) to a vector is cheap. If only one initial state \(\bv\) is given, our computational objective is the vector \(e^{t\bA}\bv\). We construct an approximation in a Krylov subspace and use the defect in the differential equation to assess its error. The later sensitivity and logarithm constructions extend this calculation to estimating model parameters.
$$ \[\begin{align}

\bu'(t)=\bA\bu(t),\qquad\bu(0)=\bv,\\

\bu(t)=e^{t\bA}\bv.
\end{align}\] $$
crumbs: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions

title: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions
text:
NoteDefinition: The Matrix Exponential



For any square matrix \(\bA \in \fC^{n \times n}\), the matrix exponential is defined by the convergent power series \[
\begin{align}
e^{\bA} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{\bA^k}{k!} = \bI + \bA + \frac{1}{2}\bA^2 + \frac{1}{6}\bA^3 + ...
\end{align}
\] For any scalar \(t \in \fR\), the matrix function \(e^{t\bA}\) satisfies \(\frac{d}{dt} e^{t\bA} = \bA e^{t\bA} = e^{t\bA}\bA\).








WarningExercise



Use \(\|\bA^k\|\leq\|\bA\|^k\) to compare the defining series with a scalar exponential and prove absolute convergence. On a bounded interval of \(t\), justify termwise differentiation to verify the differential equation and initial value. Compute the exponential of \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) directly from the series. Why does this example not require diagonalization?








NoteTheorem: Algebraic Properties of the Matrix Exponential



Let \(\bA, \bB \in \fC^{n \times n}\).

If \(\bA\) and \(\bB\) commute (\(\bA\bB = \bB\bA\)), then \(e^{\bA+\bB} = e^\bA e^\bB\). If they do not commute, this equality fails in general.
The matrix exponential is always nonsingular, with inverse \((e^\bA)^{-1} = e^{-\bA}\).
For any nonsingular similarity transform \(\bS\), \(e^{\bS\bA\bS^{-1}} = \bS e^\bA \bS^{-1}\). In particular, if \(\bA = \bQ\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bQ^{-1}\) is diagonalizable, then \(e^\bA = \bQ \operatorname{diag}(e^{\lambda_1}, ..., e^{\lambda_n}) \bQ^{-1}\).
The determinant satisfies Jacobi’s formula: \(\det(e^\bA) = e^{\operatorname{trace}(\bA)}\).









TipProof





The exponential series is absolutely convergent in a matrix norm, since \(\|\bA^k/k!\|\leq\|\bA\|^k/k!\) and the scalar exponential series converges. This permits the regrouping of products used below.
When \(\bA\) and \(\bB\) commute, the product of the two series can be grouped by total degree: \[
\begin{align}
e^{\bA}e^{\bB}
&=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\sum_{j=0}^k\frac{\bA^j\bB^{k-j}}{j!(k-j)!}\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac1{k!}
   \sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}\bA^j\bB^{k-j}\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(\bA+\bB)^k}{k!}=e^{\bA+\bB}.
\end{align}
\] Commutativity is needed for the matrix binomial theorem in the last step. Without it, terms such as \(\bA\bB\) and \(\bB\bA\) cannot be collected as though they were equal.
Set \(\bB=-\bA\). These matrices commute, and \(e^{\bzero}=\bI\), so both \(e^{\bA}e^{-\bA}\) and \(e^{-\bA}e^{\bA}\) equal the identity. This proves nonsingularity and the inverse formula.
For similarity, induction gives \((\bS\bA\bS^{-1})^k=\bS\bA^k\bS^{-1}\): the adjacent factors \(\bS^{-1}\bS\) cancel when one more factor is multiplied. The case \(k=0\) also holds because \(\bS\bI\bS^{-1}=\bI\). Substituting into the convergent series gives \[
\begin{align}
e^{\bS\bA\bS^{-1}}
=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{\bS\bA^k\bS^{-1}}{k!}
=\bS e^{\bA}\bS^{-1}.
\end{align}
\] For diagonal \(\bA\), each power and then each exponential entry is computed diagonally. This proves the diagonalizable-matrix formula.
For the determinant, use Schur form \(\bA=\bQ\bT\bQ^*\). Similarity invariance gives \(e^{\bA}=\bQ e^{\bT}\bQ^*\). Every power of an upper triangular matrix is upper triangular, and its \(i\)th diagonal entry is \(t_{ii}^k\). Therefore \(e^{\bT}\) is upper triangular with diagonal entries \(e^{t_{ii}}\). Its determinant is their product: \[
\begin{align}
\det(e^{\bA})=\det(e^{\bT})
=\prod_i e^{t_{ii}}=e^{\sum_i t_{ii}}
=e^{\operatorname{tr}(\bA)}.
\end{align}
\] Trace and determinant are unchanged by similarity. This establishes the final property without assuming diagonalizability. These are standard matrix-exponential identities (Higham 2008).









WarningExercise



Use \(\bB=-\bA\) to prove the inverse formula. Prove \((\bS\bA\bS^{-1})^k=\bS\bA^k\bS^{-1}\) by induction and substitute it into the series to prove similarity invariance. Finally, use Schur form and the diagonal entries of powers of a triangular matrix to show \(\det(e^{\bA})=e^{\operatorname{tr}(\bA)}\).








TipRemark



(Storage and the exponential action) Classical methods for computing the full \(n \times n\) matrix \(e^{\bA}\) rely on scaling and squaring with rational Padé approximants. Evaluating an \([m/m]\) Padé approximant requires computing matrix powers and solving matrix linear systems, incurring \(O(n^3)\) operations. More critically, even when \(\bA\) is sparse, the exponential \(e^{t\bA}\) is typically dense. Storing \(e^{t\bA}\) for \(n = 10^6\) requires eight terabytes of memory in double precision. Many evolution calculations require only the action \(e^{t\bA}\bv\), which can be approximated without forming the full exponential.

title: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions
text:
32.3 The Continuous-Adjoint Sensitivity Formula
In parameter inference, we estimate unknown coefficients in an evolution model from discrete observations. Consider an affine generator family $$ \[\begin{align}

    \bA(\btheta) = \bA_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{M_{\mathrm{lib}}} \theta_j \bA_j,
\end{align}\] $$ where \(\bA_0\) is a baseline operator, the matrices \(\bA_j\) represent candidate physical mechanisms, and \(\btheta = (\theta_1, ..., \theta_{M_{\mathrm{lib}}})^T\) is a vector of unknown rate parameters.
Suppose the prediction \(\by\) is compared with observed data through a real scalar function \(\ell\). To adjust a parameter, we need the derivative of that comparison with respect to the parameter. Differentiating the ODE gives one possible calculation for each parameter. An adjoint rearranges the chain rule so that all parameters share the same backward propagation. Parameters are real, and the initial vector is fixed. For complex states we use the real differential convention \(d\ell=\operatorname{Re}[(\nabla_{\by}\ell)^*d\by]\).






NoteTheorem: Adjoint Gradient Formula for Exponential Actions



Let \(\by = e^{h\bA(\btheta)}\bv\) denote the state propagated across an interval of length \(h\). Let \(\ell(\by)\) be a differentiable scalar loss with endpoint gradient \(\nabla_{\by}\ell\). Then the derivative of the loss with respect to coefficient \(\theta_j\) is \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta_j} = h \operatorname{Re} \int_0^1 \blambda(s)^* \bA_j \bm{f}(s)\,ds,
\end{align}
\] where the forward path \(\bm{f}(s)\) and adjoint path \(\blambda(s)\) are defined by \[
\begin{align}
\bm{f}(s) = e^{sh\bA}\bv, \qquad \blambda(s) = e^{(1-s)h\bA^*} \nabla_{\by}\ell, \qquad 0 \leq s \leq 1.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Let \(\bm{f}(s)\) satisfy the ODE \(\bm{f}'(s) = h\bA(\btheta)\bm{f}(s)\) with \(\bm{f}(0) = \bv\) and \(\by = \bm{f}(1)\). Let \(\bg_j(s)=\partial\bm f(s)/\partial\theta_j\). The product rule applied to \(\bA(\btheta)\bm f(s)\) gives two terms: one differentiates the matrix and the other the state. Since the family is affine, \(\partial\bA/\partial\theta_j=\bA_j\). The initial state is fixed, so \(\bg_j(0)=\bzero\).
Differentiating this initial-value problem with respect to \(\theta_j\) yields the tangent equation \[
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{ds} \left( \frac{\partial \bm{f}}{\partial \theta_j} \right) = h\bA \left( \frac{\partial \bm{f}}{\partial \theta_j} \right) + h\bA_j \bm{f}(s), \qquad \frac{\partial \bm{f}(0)}{\partial \theta_j} = \bzero.
\end{align}
\] Applying variation of constants at the endpoint \(s = 1\) gives \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial \by}{\partial \theta_j} = h \int_0^1 e^{(1-s)h\bA} \bA_j \bm{f}(s)\,ds.
\end{align}
\] Applying the chain rule to the scalar loss \(\ell(\by)\) and taking the real part produces \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta_j} &= \operatorname{Re}\left( (\nabla_{\by}\ell)^* \frac{\partial \by}{\partial \theta_j} \right)
    = h \operatorname{Re} \int_0^1 (\nabla_{\by}\ell)^* e^{(1-s)h\bA} \bA_j \bm{f}(s)\,ds \\
    &= h \operatorname{Re} \int_0^1 \left( e^{(1-s)h\bA^*} \nabla_{\by}\ell \right)^* \bA_j \bm{f}(s)\,ds
    = h \operatorname{Re} \int_0^1 \blambda(s)^* \bA_j \bm{f}(s)\,ds.
\end{align}
\]
The identity \((e^{(1-s)h\bA^*})^*=e^{(1-s)h\bA}\) follows by conjugate-transposing the power series term by term. This is the step that moves propagation from the state derivative to the loss gradient. In a real problem the conjugations and real-part operation reduce to ordinary transposes and the usual chain rule.









WarningExercise



Check the formula when \(A(\theta)=\theta\) is scalar, \(v=1\), and \(\ell(y)=\tfrac12(y-y_{\rm obs})^2\). Differentiate \(y=e^{h\theta}\) directly, then evaluate the adjoint integral. Why does its integrand become independent of \(s\) in this example?








TipRemark



(The adjoint sharing principle) Evaluating a separate directional Fréchet derivative \(L_{\exp}(h\bA, h\bA_j)\) for each candidate matrix \(\bA_j\) repeats the forward exponential propagation \(M_{\mathrm{lib}}\) times. The adjoint identity separates propagation from the candidate directions. We compute the forward path \(\bm{f}\) and adjoint path \(\blambda\) once per observation interval, and evaluate their contractions against \(\bA_j\) via numerical quadrature.

title: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions
text:
32.4 Shared Krylov Spaces and Quadrature
To evaluate the bilinear integral numerically, we approximate both paths using independent forward and adjoint Krylov spaces, and integrate the contraction using Gauss–Legendre quadrature.






NoteTheorem: Bilinear Quadrature Evaluation



Let \(\mathcal{K}_{m_f}(\bA, \bv)\) have basis \(\bV_f\) and projected Hessenberg matrix \(\bH_f\), with \(\beta_f = \|\bv\|_2\). Let \(\mathcal{K}_{m_a}(\bA^*, \nabla_{\by}\ell)\) have basis \(\bV_a\) and projected matrix \(\bH_a\), with \(\beta_a = \|\nabla_{\by}\ell\|_2\). At any Gauss–Legendre node \(s_q \in [0, 1]\) with quadrature weight \(w_q\), the path approximations are \[
\begin{align}
\bm{f}^{(q)} = \beta_f \bV_f e^{s_q h \bH_f}\be_1, \qquad \blambda^{(q)} = \beta_a \bV_a e^{(1-s_q) h \bH_a}\be_1.
\end{align}
\] The coefficient gradient evaluates to \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta_j} \approx h \sum_{q=1}^{n_q} w_q \operatorname{Re}\left[ (\blambda^{(q)})^* \bA_j \bm{f}^{(q)} \right].
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



One-Sided Termination: Construct a \(3 \times 3\) example where \(\bv\) is an exact eigenvector of \(\bA\), yielding forward residual \(\rho_f = 0\) at step 1, while the adjoint starting vector is not an eigenvector. Explain why product heuristics fail in this setting.








TipRemark



(One-sided termination in refinement heuristics) A common stopping diagnostic tests the product of forward and adjoint residuals \(\rho_f \rho_a\). If the forward path reaches an invariant subspace, \(\rho_f = 0\), causing the product to vanish even when the adjoint path is at depth \(m_a = 2\) and completely unresolved. Reliable stopping criteria require monitoring forward and adjoint convergence separately.
crumbs: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions

title: 32  Matrix Exponentials and Krylov Subspace Actions
text:
32.5 Matrix Logarithms and Generator Recovery
A discrete observation map records evolution over a fixed interval. In the scalar case, recovering a decay rate from a positive multiplier uses \(a=h^{-1}\log k\). For oscillations, the exponential loses integer multiples of \(2\pi\) in phase. The principal matrix logarithm chooses one branch, but recovering the actual generator also requires that its frequencies fall within that branch.






NoteDefinition: The Matrix Logarithm



Let \(\bK \in \fC^{n \times n}\) have no eigenvalues on the closed negative real axis \((-\infty, 0]\). The principal matrix logarithm \(\log(\bK)\) is the unique matrix \(\bA\) such that \(e^\bA = \bK\) and all eigenvalues of \(\bA\) satisfy \(|\operatorname{Im}(\lambda)| < \pi\).








WarningExercise



Logarithm Branch Cuts: Let an evolution operator have oscillatory eigenvalue \(\lambda = -\gamma + i\omega\) with \(\omega = 50\pi\). Determine the maximum observation interval \(h\) that avoids branch-cut crossing in the principal matrix logarithm.








TipRemark



(Projection and finite-time closure bias) If \(P\) denotes the orthogonal projection onto a subspace of observables \(\calF\), the projected generator obtained from finite-time observations satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\widehat{\bA}_h = h^{-1}\log\left( P e^{h\calA} |_{\calF} \right) \neq P\calA|_{\calF}.
\end{align}
\] Unless \(\calF\) is invariant under \(\calA\), projection and exponentiation do not commute. The resulting finite-time closure bias can be expanded in powers of \(h\), but its leading order depends on which terms leave the observable space. Any rate such as \(O(h^r)\) therefore requires a separately defined closure depth and corresponding assumptions.

WarningExercise



Dense vs. Action Complexity: A sparse matrix \(\bA \in \fR^{10^6 \times 10^6}\) has 10 nonzero entries per row. Compute the memory required to store \(e^{h\bA}\) as a dense array. Compare this with storing \(m=30\) Arnoldi basis vectors.








WarningExercise



Adjoint Sharing: Let an overcomplete library contain \(M_{\mathrm{lib}} = 200\) candidate directions. Let each forward and adjoint Krylov construction use \(m\) products, and count products with \(\bA\) or \(\bA^*\) separately from contractions with candidate matrices. Compare rebuilding a forward and adjoint path separately for each of the 200 coefficients with sharing the two paths across all coefficients at five quadrature nodes. State the cost model for a candidate contraction, and explain why the number of candidates and nodes alone does not determine the cost of directional Fréchet derivatives.








WarningExercise



Taylor vs. Krylov Convergence: For the 1D discrete Laplacian \(\bA\) with \(\|\bA\|_2 = 4 \times 10^4\) and \(t = 10^{-2}\), compare the polynomial degrees suggested by a direct Taylor remainder bound and by Krylov projection. State every estimate you use, since neither degree is determined by \(\|\bA\|_2\) alone.








NoteFurther reading



Higham gives the general theory of matrix functions (Higham 2008). Moler and Van Loan explain why apparently reasonable methods for the matrix exponential can fail, and Al-Mohy and Higham develop a modern action method that avoids forming the exponential (Moler and Van Loan 2003; Al-Mohy and Higham 2011).






Al-Mohy, Awad H., and Nicholas J. Higham. 2011. “Computing the Action of the Matrix Exponential, with an Application to Exponential Integrators.” SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 33 (2): 488–511. https://doi.org/10.1137/100788860.


Higham, Nicholas J. 2008. Functions of Matrices: Theory and Computation. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717778.


Hochbruck, Marlis, and Christian Lubich. 1997. “On Krylov Subspace Approximations to the Matrix Exponential Operator.” SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 34 (5): 1911–25. https://doi.org/10.1137/S0036142995280572.


Moler, Cleve, and Charles F. Van Loan. 2003. “Nineteen Dubious Ways to Compute the Exponential of a Matrix, Twenty-Five Years Later.” SIAM Review 45 (1): 3–49. https://doi.org/10.1137/S00361445024180.

title: 33  Markov Chains, Continuous Generators, and the CME
text:
33.1 Discrete-Time Markov Chains
A finite random system has a probability of occupying each possible state. A Markov model specifies how these probabilities change using only the current state. We first use a matrix of transition probabilities for a discrete step, then a matrix of transition rates for continuous time.
The matrix conventions matter: throughout this section, probabilities are columns, so column \(j\) describes transitions out of state \(j\). We derive conservation and positivity, then assemble reaction models and examine the error introduced by retaining only a finite set of states.
crumbs: 33  Markov Chains, Continuous Generators, and the CME

title: 33  Markov Chains, Continuous Generators, and the CME
text:
NoteDefinition: Probability Vector



A vector \(\bx\in\fR^n\) is a probability vector if \[
\begin{align}
x_i\geq 0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1.
\end{align}
\] The entry \(x_i\) represents the probability of occupying state \(i\).








NoteDefinition: Column-Stochastic Matrix



A matrix \(\bP \in \fR^{n \times n}\) is column-stochastic if:

\(P_{ij} \geq 0\) for all \(i,j\).
\(\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij} = 1\) for each column \(j\).









NoteExample



For two states, take \(\bP=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.1\\0.2&0.9\end{pmatrix}\). Starting in state one gives distribution \((0.8,0.2)^T\) after one step. Starting from probabilities \((0.6,0.4)^T\) gives a mixture of the two columns, namely \((0.52,0.48)^T\).








WarningExercise



Compute the second step for each initial distribution. Prove that multiplying any probability vector by a column-stochastic matrix produces another probability vector. Identify separately where you use nonnegative entries and where you use the column sums.








TipRemark



(Column convention) Column \(j\) of \(\bP\) contains the transition probabilities from state \(j\) to all destination states \(i\). The update rule for a probability distribution is \(\bx^{(k+1)} = \bP \bx^{(k)}\).








NoteTheorem: Spectrum of a Stochastic Matrix



If \(\bP\) is column-stochastic, then \(\lambda=1\) is an eigenvalue, and every eigenvalue satisfies \(|\lambda|\leq 1\).








TipProof





The column-sum condition can be written \(\mathbf1^T\bP=\mathbf1^T\). Taking transposes gives \(\bP^T\mathbf1=\mathbf1\), so one is an eigenvalue of \(\bP^T\). The characteristic polynomials of a matrix and its transpose agree, because \[
\begin{align}
\det(\bP^T-z\bI)=\det((\bP-z\bI)^T)=\det(\bP-z\bI).
\end{align}
\] Hence one is also an eigenvalue of \(\bP\). The constant vector need not be its right eigenvector under the column convention.
To bound any eigenvalue, use an eigenvector \(\bv\neq\bzero\) of \(\bP^T\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Choose \(j\) where \(|v_j|=\max_i|v_i|>0\). Its scalar eigenvalue equation is \[
\begin{align}
\lambda v_j=\sum_i P_{ij}v_i.
\end{align}
\] Since the entries are nonnegative, \[
\begin{align}
|\lambda||v_j|
&\leq\sum_iP_{ij}|v_i|\\
&\leq\sum_iP_{ij}|v_j|
=|v_j|\sum_iP_{ij}=|v_j|.
\end{align}
\] Divide by the positive number \(|v_j|\) to get \(|\lambda|\leq1\). The argument also covers complex eigenvectors because it uses absolute values. Equality of characteristic polynomials transfers this bound to every eigenvalue of \(\bP\).









NoteDefinition: Stationary Distribution



A probability vector \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is stationary if \(\bP \boldsymbol{\pi} = \boldsymbol{\pi}\). It is a right eigenvector of \(\bP\) associated with \(\lambda=1\), normalized so that \(\mathbf{1}^T\boldsymbol{\pi}=1\).








WarningExercise



The matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) moves deterministically between two states. Find a stationary distribution, then start from \(\be_1\) and show that the distributions do not converge. A stationary distribution can exist without attracting every initial distribution. Which hypothesis of the following theorem rules out this example?








NoteTheorem: Perron–Frobenius for Markov Chains



If \(\bP\) is irreducible (every state can be reached from any other state in finitely many steps) and primitive (aperiodic, so \(\bP^k > 0\) elementwise for some \(k \geq 1\)), then:

\(\lambda_1 = 1\) is an algebraically and geometrically simple eigenvalue.
\(|\lambda_i| < 1\) for all other eigenvalues \(\lambda_i \neq 1\).
The stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is strictly positive in every entry.
For any initial probability vector \(\bx^{(0)}\), \(\lim_{k\to\infty} \bP^k \bx^{(0)} = \boldsymbol{\pi}\).









NoteDefinition: Spectral Gap and Mixing Time



For a primitive chain with eigenvalues ordered as \(1 = \lambda_1 > |\lambda_2| \geq ... \geq |\lambda_n|\), the spectral gap is \[
\begin{align}
\delta = 1 - |\lambda_2|.
\end{align}
\] For a diagonalizable matrix, the error \(\|\bx^{(k)} - \boldsymbol{\pi}\|_2\) decays asymptotically as \(\mathcal{O}(|\lambda_2|^k)\). The number of steps \(k_\varepsilon\) required to reach error tolerance \(\varepsilon\) satisfies \[
\begin{align}
k_\varepsilon \approx \frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\delta}.
\end{align}
\]








WarningExercise



(Discrete spectrum and mixing) Under the column-stochastic convention, let \(\bP=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.1\\0.2&0.9\end{pmatrix}\). Find its stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), its second eigenvalue, and the spectral gap \(\delta\). Starting from \(\bx^{(0)}=\be_1\), derive the exact formula for \(\|\bP^k\bx^{(0)}-\boldsymbol{\pi}\|_2\). Compare the first \(k\) for which this error is at most \(10^{-3}\) with the estimate \(\log(10^3)/\delta\), and explain why the latter is only an asymptotic rule.








NoteDefinition: Detailed Balance (Reversibility)



A Markov chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) if \[
\begin{align}
P_{ij} \pi_j = P_{ji} \pi_i \qquad \text{for all } i, j.
\end{align}
\] A chain satisfying detailed balance is reversible.








NoteTheorem: Real Spectrum of Reversible Chains



Let \(\bP\) satisfy detailed balance with stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi} > 0\). Define \(\bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}} = \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\pi})\). Then the matrix \[
\begin{align}
\bS = \bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1/2} \bP \bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{1/2}
\end{align}
\] is symmetric. Consequently, all eigenvalues of \(\bP\) are real, and \(\bP\) has an orthogonal basis of eigenvectors in the inner product weighted by \(\bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1}\).








TipProof





Let \(\bD_{\boldsymbol\pi}\) have the positive stationary probabilities on its diagonal. Positivity makes its square root and inverse square root well defined. Entry \((i,j)\) of the transformed matrix is \[
\begin{align}
S_{ij}=\pi_i^{-1/2}P_{ij}\pi_j^{1/2}
=\frac{P_{ij}\pi_j}{\sqrt{\pi_i\pi_j}}.
\end{align}
\] Detailed balance changes the numerator to \(P_{ji}\pi_i\), giving \[
\begin{align}
S_{ij}=\frac{P_{ji}\pi_i}{\sqrt{\pi_i\pi_j}}
=\pi_j^{-1/2}P_{ji}\pi_i^{1/2}=S_{ji}.
\end{align}
\] Thus \(\bS\) is real symmetric and has a real orthonormal eigenbasis \(\bq_i\) with real eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\).
Undo the similarity. The vectors \(\bv_i=\bD_{\boldsymbol\pi}^{1/2}\bq_i\) satisfy \[
\begin{align}
\bP\bv_i
=\bD_{\boldsymbol\pi}^{1/2}\bS\bq_i
=\lambda_i\bv_i.
\end{align}
\] The invertible change of coordinates preserves their independence, so they form a basis. In the claimed weighted inner product their pairings are \[
\begin{align}
\bv_i^T\bD_{\boldsymbol\pi}^{-1}\bv_j
=\bq_i^T\bD_{\boldsymbol\pi}^{1/2}
   \bD_{\boldsymbol\pi}^{-1}\bD_{\boldsymbol\pi}^{1/2}\bq_j
=\bq_i^T\bq_j=\delta_{ij}.
\end{align}
\] This proves the weighted orthonormality assertion in addition to reality of the spectrum.

text:
33.2 Continuous-Time Markov Chains and the CME
A rate differs from a probability. If the transition rate from \(j\) to \(i\) is \(A_{ij}\), then over a small time \(\Delta t\) the corresponding transition probability is \(A_{ij}\Delta t+o(\Delta t)\). The probability of remaining in \(j\) is one minus the total exit rate times \(\Delta t\), to first order. Thus the transition matrix has expansion \(\bI+\Delta t\bA+o(\Delta t)\), which explains the signs and column sums of a generator.






WarningExercise



For two states with rates \(1\to2\) equal to \(a>0\) and \(2\to1\) equal to \(b>0\), write the generator and derive both equations for \(p_1'\) and \(p_2'\). Show that \(p_1+p_2\) remains constant and find the stationary probabilities. Check the units of each matrix entry.








NoteDefinition: Continuous-Time Infinitesimal Generator



A continuous-time Markov jump process on a discrete state space evolves according to \[
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}\bp(t) = \bA \bp(t),
\end{align}
\] where \(\bp(t)\) is the probability distribution vector and \(\bA\) is an infinitesimal generator matrix satisfying:

\(A_{ij} \geq 0\) for all \(i \neq j\) (transition rates between distinct states are nonnegative).
\(\sum_{i} A_{ij} = 0\) for every column \(j\) (column sums vanish).
\(A_{jj} = -\sum_{i \neq j} A_{ij} \leq 0\) (diagonal entries equal the negative total exit rate from state \(j\)).









WarningExercise



Choose \(\nu\geq\max_j(-A_{jj})\) with \(\nu>0\) and set \(\bP=\bI+\bA/\nu\). Prove that \(\bP\) is column-stochastic and that \[
\begin{align}
e^{t\bA}=e^{-\nu t}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}\bP^k.
\end{align}
\] Deduce positivity, conservation of total mass, and \(\|e^{t\bA}\|_1=1\) for \(t\geq0\). Repeat the argument for a finite subgenerator whose column sums are nonpositive and prove that its exponential is substochastic. This construction is called uniformization.


A reaction model applies the same balance to molecule counts. Each term adds probability arriving from one neighboring count and subtracts probability leaving the current count. We take the propensity of an infeasible reaction to be zero, and terms involving states outside the nonnegative count space to be zero. For an infinite state space, conservation requires a nonexplosive process: only finitely many jumps occur in a finite time almost surely. The infinite-state statements below assume a well-defined conservative process and the summability needed for the displayed equations.






NoteDefinition: Chemical Master Equation (CME)



Consider a chemically reacting system with \(S\) molecular species and \(R\) reaction channels. The discrete state \(\bx \in \mathbb{N}_0^S\) records the copy number of each species. Each reaction channel \(k \in \{1,...,R\}\) is characterized by a stoichiometric change vector \(\bnu_k \in \mathbb{Z}^S\) and a propensity function \(\alpha_k(\bx; \bc) \geq 0\) parameterized by rate constants \(\bc\).
The Chemical Master Equation governs the probability \(p(\bx, t)\) of occupying state \(\bx\) at time \(t\): \[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial p(\bx, t)}{\partial t}
    =
    \sum_{k=1}^R \Big[ \alpha_k(\bx - \bnu_k; \bc)\, p(\bx - \bnu_k, t) - \alpha_k(\bx; \bc)\, p(\bx, t) \Big].
\end{align}
\] Enumerating the reachable states yields the linear system of ordinary differential equations \[
\begin{align}
\dot{\bp}(t) = \bA(\bc) \bp(t), \qquad \bp(0) = \bp_0,
\end{align}
\] whose exact formal solution is the matrix exponential action \(\bp(t) = \exp(t\bA(\bc)) \bp_0\).








WarningExercise



For births at constant rate \(\lambda\) and deaths at rate \(\mu x\), write the equation for \(p_x'(t)\). Treat \(x=0\) separately. Identify which terms represent arrivals and departures, and explain why a death term from state zero must vanish. Write the first three columns of the infinite generator.

text:
33.3 Generator Assembly and Stochastic Simulation
Two computations start from the list of reactions. The first builds the generator \(\bA(\bc)\) on a finite set of states and evolves the whole distribution. The second samples individual trajectories of the jump process and never enumerates the state space. The generator is needed for the finite state projection below. Sampled trajectories provide the data for the Koopman estimators of the referenced section, and their histograms give an independent check on computed distributions.






NoteDefinition: Generator Assembly by Forward Enumeration



Let \(\mathcal S\) be a finite set of \(n\) states, stored in a hash table that maps each state \(\bx\) to its index \(\iota(\bx)\in\{1,...,n\}\). For each \(\bx\in\mathcal S\) and each reaction \(k\) with \(\alpha_k(\bx;\bc)>0\):

Compute the destination \(\by=\bx+\bnu_k\).
If \(\by\in\mathcal S\), append the triplet \(\big(\iota(\by),\iota(\bx),\alpha_k(\bx;\bc)\big)\).

Finally, append the diagonal triplet \(\big(\iota(\bx),\iota(\bx),-\sum_k\alpha_k(\bx;\bc)\big)\) for each \(\bx\), and convert the triplets to CSR format by the referenced result.


The diagonal entry contains the total exit rate, including the rates of reactions whose destination lies outside \(\mathcal S\). Column \(\iota(\bx)\) therefore sums to minus the rate at which probability leaves \(\mathcal S\) from \(\bx\), which is the leakage measured by the finite state projection bound. Assembly visits each pair of a state and a reaction once and performs one expected constant-time hash lookup for each, so it costs \(O(nR)\) operations and produces at most \(n(R+1)\) nonzero entries. Searching all pairs of states for possible transitions would cost \(O(n^2)\) instead.






NoteDefinition: Stochastic Simulation Algorithm



Let the process be in state \(\bx\) at time \(t\). Gillespie’s direct method advances it as follows (Gillespie 1977).

Compute the propensities \(\alpha_k(\bx;\bc)\) and their sum \(a_0(\bx)=\sum_{k=1}^R\alpha_k(\bx;\bc)\). If \(a_0(\bx)=0\), stop.
Draw independent \(u_1,u_2\) uniformly from \((0,1)\).
Set \(\tau=-\ln(u_1)/a_0(\bx)\), and choose the smallest \(k\) with \(\sum_{l=1}^k\alpha_l(\bx;\bc)\geq u_2\,a_0(\bx)\).
Replace \(t\) by \(t+\tau\) and \(\bx\) by \(\bx+\bnu_k\).









NoteTheorem: Exactness of the Stochastic Simulation Algorithm



Assume \(a_0(\bx)>0\), with zero-rate channels unable to fire. Suppose that from state \(\bx\) each positive-rate reaction \(k\) fires after an independent exponential waiting time with rate \(\alpha_k(\bx;\bc)\), and that the first reaction to fire determines the next state. Then the time to the next reaction is exponential with rate \(a_0(\bx)\), the next reaction is \(k\) with probability \(\alpha_k(\bx;\bc)/a_0(\bx)\), and these two events are independent. The waiting time and reaction index produced by the referenced result have exactly this joint distribution.








TipProof





Fix the current state and abbreviate its positive reaction rates by \(\alpha_k\), with \(a_0=\sum_k\alpha_k>0\). A rate-zero channel never fires and may be omitted. Let \(T_k\) be the independent exponential waiting time of channel \(k\), let \(T=\min_kT_k\), and let \(K\) be the first channel to fire. Ties have probability zero because these distributions are continuous.
For channel \(k\) to fire first at time \(s\), its waiting-time density contributes \(\alpha_ke^{-\alpha_ks}\), and every other waiting time must exceed \(s\). Independence multiplies their survival probabilities. Thus the joint density in time is \[
\begin{align}
\Pr(K=k,\ T\in ds)/ds
=\alpha_ke^{-\alpha_ks}\prod_{l\neq k}e^{-\alpha_ls}
=\alpha_ke^{-a_0s}.
\end{align}
\] Integrate for \(s>\tau\): \[
\begin{align}
\Pr(K=k,T>\tau)
=\int_\tau^\infty\alpha_ke^{-a_0s}\,ds
=\frac{\alpha_k}{a_0}e^{-a_0\tau}.
\end{align}
\] Setting \(\tau=0\) gives \(\Pr(K=k)=\alpha_k/a_0\). Summing over \(k\) gives \(\Pr(T>\tau)=e^{-a_0\tau}\). The joint expression is the product of these marginals, proving independence.
The algorithm reproduces both marginals. For \(u_1\) uniform on \((0,1)\), \[
\begin{align}
\Pr(-\ln u_1/a_0>\tau)=\Pr(u_1<e^{-a_0\tau})=e^{-a_0\tau}.
\end{align}
\] The interval assigned to channel \(k\) by the cumulative sums has length \(\alpha_k\) in an interval of length \(a_0\). A uniform \(u_2a_0\) lands there with probability \(\alpha_k/a_0\). Independent uniforms preserve independence of the two selections. This proves exactness of this single jump, which can be repeated at each new state (Gillespie 1977).



Recomputing all propensities and selecting a reaction by linear search costs \(O(R)\) per event. A tree reduces the selection cost to \(O(\log R)\), but the total event cost also includes updating every propensity affected by the reaction. The number of steps up to time \(T\) is about \(\int_0^Ta_0(\bX(t))\,dt\), which is large when some reactions are fast. An expected value \(\mathbb{E}[f(\bX(T))]\) is estimated by averaging \(f\) over \(N\) independent trajectories. By the central limit theorem, the error of this average has standard deviation \(\sigma_f/\sqrt N\), where \(\sigma_f\) is the standard deviation of \(f(\bX(T))\). Each additional digit of accuracy therefore requires a hundred times more trajectories. The finite state projection below computes an approximation to the distribution instead. Its cost depends on the number of retained states and the accuracy required of both truncation and time propagation.

text:
33.4 Finite State Projection (FSP)






TipRemark



(Truncating the state space) The CME generator \(\bA(\bc)\) is defined over an infinite or very large discrete state space \(\mathbb{N}_0^S\). A finite computation therefore requires truncation, aggregation, or another representation that avoids enumerating the full state space.


Truncating the state space removes paths after they leave the retained set. It should not redirect an outgoing transition back into that set. We therefore keep the original negative diagonal entries while dropping the off-diagonal entries for omitted destinations. The resulting loss of total probability measures the discrepancy caused by truncation. Renormalizing the remaining probabilities would conceal that loss.






NoteDefinition: Finite State Projection (FSP)



Let the discrete state space be partitioned into a finite retained index set \(J \subset \mathbb{N}_0^S\) with \(|J| = K\), and an infinite or omitted complement set \(J^c\). Permuting states so that \(J\) appears first partitions the full generator: \[
\begin{align}
\bA = \begin{pmatrix} \bA_J & \bA_{J, J^c} \\ \bA_{J^c, J} & \bA_{J^c} \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
\] The Finite State Projection of Munsky and Khammash (Munsky and Khammash 2006) approximates the true marginal probability on \(J\) by solving the isolated subgenerator system \[
\begin{align}
\dot{\bp}_J(t) = \bA_J \bp_J(t), \qquad \bp_J(0) = \bp_0|_J.
\end{align}
\] Here \(\bA_J\) has nonpositive diagonal entries and nonnegative off-diagonal entries, but its column sums are nonpositive because transitions into \(J^c\) act as probability leaks.








NoteTheorem: FSP 1-Norm Leakage Bound



Let \(\bp(t)\) be the exact probability distribution solving \(\dot{\bp} = \bA\bp\) with initial condition supported on \(J\), so that \(\mathbf{1}^T\bp(t) = 1\). Let \(\bp_J(t) = \exp(t\bA_J)\bp_0|_J\) be the FSP solution. Then:

Pointwise underestimation: \(\bzero \leq \bp_J(t) \leq \bp|_J(t)\) for all \(t \geq 0\).
The full-space error of the zero-padded FSP approximation equals the leaked mass: \[
\begin{align}
\|\bp(t) - \widetilde{\bp}_J(t)\|_1 = 1 - \mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t),
\end{align}
\] where \(\widetilde{\bp}_J(t)\) is \(\bp_J(t)\) padded with zeros on \(J^c\). The retained-state error satisfies \[
\begin{align}
\|\bp|_J(t)-\bp_J(t)\|_1
         =\mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t)-\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t)
         \leq 1-\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t).
\end{align}
\]









TipProof





The exact retained dynamics satisfy the non-autonomous subgenerator ODE \[
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}\bp|_J(t) = \bA_J\bp|_J(t) + \bA_{J,J^c}\bp|_{J^c}(t), \qquad \bp|_J(0) = \bp_0|_J.
\end{align}
\] The FSP approximation satisfies \(\frac{d}{dt}\bp_J(t) = \bA_J\bp_J(t)\) with the same initial condition \(\bp_J(0) = \bp_0|_J\). Subtracting the two equations gives the defect ODE for the difference \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_J(t) = \bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t)\): \[
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{\delta}_J(t) = \bA_J \boldsymbol{\delta}_J(t) + \bA_{J,J^c}\bp|_{J^c}(t), \qquad \boldsymbol{\delta}_J(0) = \bzero.
\end{align}
\] The two retained trajectories have exactly the same initial data. Their difference therefore starts at zero. The only forcing in its equation is probability returning from omitted states, represented by the nonnegative coupling term.
By Duhamel’s formula (variation of constants): \[
\begin{align}
\boldsymbol{\delta}_J(t) = \bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t) = \int_0^t e^{(t-s)\bA_J}\bA_{J,J^c}\bp|_{J^c}(s)\,ds.
\end{align}
\] For the finite retained matrix, nonnegativity of its exponential follows from the uniformization construction already given: shift its diagonal by a sufficiently large positive multiple of the identity and expand the resulting nonnegative matrix in powers. Every term of that exponential series is nonnegative.
Because \(\bA_J\) has non-negative off-diagonal entries, it is a Metzler matrix, and its matrix exponential \(e^{\tau\bA_J}\) is entrywise non-negative for all \(\tau \geq 0\). Furthermore, the coupling matrix \(\bA_{J, J^c} \geq \bzero\) and exact probabilities \(\bp|_{J^c}(s) \geq \bzero\) are non-negative. Consequently, the integrand is entrywise non-negative, proving that \[
\begin{align}
\bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t) \geq \bzero \implies \bzero \leq \bp_J(t) \leq \bp|_J(t) \quad \text{for all } t \geq 0.
\end{align}
\]
Because \(\bp_J(t) \leq \bp|_J(t)\), the marginal 1-norm difference on \(J\) simplifies without absolute value signs: \[
\begin{align}
\|\bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t)\|_1
    =
    \sum_{i \in J} \big( p_i(t) - [\bp_J(t)]_i \big)
    =
    \mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t) - \mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t).
\end{align}
\] The total probability across the full space satisfies \(\mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t) + \mathbf{1}^T\bp|_{J^c}(t) = 1\). The omitted probability mass on \(J^c\) is exactly \(1 - \mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t)\). Adding the unmodeled mass on \(J^c\) gives \[
\begin{align}
\|\bp(t) - \widetilde{\bp}_J(t)\|_1
    &=
    \|\bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t)\|_1 + \|\bp|_{J^c}(t)\|_1 \\
    &=
    \big(\mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t) - \mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t)\big) + \big(1 - \mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t)\big) \\
    &=
    1 - \mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t).
\end{align}
\] The zero-padded FSP approximation is a subprobability vector, so the familiar identity between total variation distance and half the \(1\)-norm for two probability vectors does not apply directly. With the convention \(d(\mu,\nu)=\sup_B|\mu(B)-\nu(B)|\), its discrepancy from the exact distribution is the full leaked mass. A comparison of two probability distributions requires specifying how the missing mass is represented, for example by an absorbing sink.
The certificate concerns the exact solution of the finite subgenerator equation. A numerical approximation to that solution introduces an additional propagation error. If that error is bounded by \(\varepsilon_{\rm num}\) in the \(1\)-norm, the triangle inequality adds it to the truncation discrepancy. The truncation certificate should therefore not be presented as a complete error bound for an arbitrary numerical propagator (Munsky and Khammash 2006).









WarningExercise



(FSP 1-norm leakage bound derivation) Consider a CTMC with generator \(\bA\) partitioned into retained set \(J\) and complement \(J^c\).

Prove that \(\mathbf{1}^T\bA_J \leq \bzero^T\) elementwise, with strict inequality for at least one entry if transitions from \(J\) to \(J^c\) exist.
Show that \(\frac{d}{dt}\big(\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t)\big) \leq 0\), confirming that total modeled probability mass decreases monotonically over time.
Let \(\varepsilon=1-\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(T)\). Verify from the referenced result that the zero-padded FSP error is exactly \(\varepsilon\) in the \(1\)-norm. Explain what additional identification of omitted states would be needed before comparing an absorbing sink with the exact distribution.
