section: 33.5 Truncation Strategy: Probability Flux versus Probability Mass
text:
33.5 Truncation Strategy: Probability Flux versus Probability Mass






TipRemark



(Failure of instantaneous mass truncation) A naive heuristic for expanding or pruning states in the FSP retains states where the instantaneous probability \(p_i(t)\) exceeds a threshold \(\varepsilon\). In multiscale or stiff reaction networks, this heuristic can discard a low-mass intermediate that carries substantial probability flux and thereby produce an order-one error.








NoteDefinition: Probability Flux



For a transition from state \(j\) to state \(i\) with rate \(A_{ij} > 0\), the instantaneous probability flux at time \(t\) is \[
\begin{align}
\Phi_{ij}(t) = A_{ij} p_j(t).
\end{align}
\] The cumulative probability flux entering state \(i\) over the time interval \([0, T]\) is \[
\begin{align}
F_i(T) = \int_0^T \sum_{j \neq i} A_{ij} p_j(s)\, ds.
\end{align}
\]








TipRemark



(Transient intermediate states) Consider a reaction cascade \(S_1 \xrightarrow{k_1} S_2 \xrightarrow{k_2} S_3\) with \(k_2 \gg k_1\). State \(S_2\) has a rapid exit rate, so its instantaneous probability is tiny: \(p_2(t) \approx \frac{k_1}{k_2} p_1(t) \ll 1\). Pruning based on instantaneous mass \(p_2(t) < \varepsilon\) deletes \(S_2\) from the state space. However, every reaction producing \(S_3\) must pass through \(S_2\). Deleting \(S_2\) severs the probability flow entirely, causing an \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) error in \(p_3(T)\).
Robust adaptive FSP algorithms monitor cumulative probability flux rather than instantaneous probability mass. A state may have negligible instantaneous mass yet carry substantial probability flux across the network.

text:
33.6 Further Exercises






WarningExercise



(Simulation of a birth–death process) Consider the reactions \(\emptyset\to X\) with propensity \(k_1\) and \(X\to\emptyset\) with propensity \(k_2x\), started from \(x=0\). Implement the referenced result, and compare the histogram of \(X(T)\) over \(10^4\) trajectories with the Poisson distribution of mean \((k_1/k_2)(1-e^{-k_2T})\). Then assemble the generator on the states \(0,...,n_{\max}\) by the referenced result, compute \(e^{T\bA}\be_1\), and compare all three distributions.








WarningExercise



(Detailed balance) Consider the column-stochastic matrix \[
\begin{align}
\bP=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.2&0\\0.4&0.5&0.1\\0&0.3&0.9\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
\] Find its stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), verify detailed balance on each edge, and compute \(\bS = \bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1/2}\bP\bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{1/2}\). Verify directly that \(\bS\) is symmetric and that the eigenvalues of \(\bP\) are real.








WarningExercise



(Probability mass versus cumulative flux in stiff cascades) Consider the three-state continuous-time Markov chain \[
\begin{align}
X_1 \xrightarrow{k_1} X_2 \xrightarrow{k_2} X_3
\end{align}
\] with \(k_1 = 1\), \(k_2 = 10^4\), and initial condition \(\bp(0) = (1, 0, 0)^T\).

Solve the system analytically for \(p_1(t), p_2(t), p_3(t)\).
Show that \(\max_{t \geq 0} p_2(t) \approx 10^{-4}\). If a threshold \(\varepsilon = 10^{-3}\) is used to prune states by instantaneous mass, state \(X_2\) is discarded at all times.
Compute the cumulative flux \(\int_0^T k_1 p_1(s)\, ds\) entering \(X_2\) for \(T = 3\). Show that over \(95\%\) of the total system probability passes through \(X_2\) despite its negligible instantaneous mass.
Explain why adaptive truncation based on cumulative probability flux preserves state \(X_2\) while mass-based thresholding disconnects the state space.









WarningExercise



(Birth–death process and infinite generator truncation) For a simple birth–death process with birth rate \(\lambda\) and death rate \(\mu x\), write down the tridiagonal subgenerator \(\bA_J\) for copy numbers \(x \in \{0, 1, ..., N\}\). Formulate the exit rate from boundary state \(N\) and derive the leakage rate \(\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t)\) as a function of \(p_N(t)\).








NoteFurther reading



The finite-state projection method and its error certificate originate with Munsky and Khammash (Munsky and Khammash 2006). Higham’s treatment of matrix functions is useful background for the exponential calculations used here (Higham 2008).






Gillespie, Daniel T. 1977. “Exact Stochastic Simulation of Coupled Chemical Reactions.” The Journal of Physical Chemistry 81 (25): 2340–61.


Higham, Nicholas J. 2008. Functions of Matrices: Theory and Computation. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717778.


Munsky, Brian, and Mustafa Khammash. 2006. “The Finite State Projection Algorithm for the Solution of the Chemical Master Equation.” The Journal of Chemical Physics 124 (4): 044104. https://doi.org/10.1063/1.2145882.

title: 34  Koopman Theory, EDMD, and Continuous Generators
text:
34.1 Koopman Operator Theory
An observation of a dynamical system may be a function of its state, such as position, energy, or a molecule count. Instead of asking how the state changes, we can ask how each such function changes after one step. Composition with the state update defines the Koopman operator.
This operator is linear in the observed function even when the state update is nonlinear. Its function space may be infinite dimensional. We first examine that distinction, then fit matrices on selected functions using least squares. For reaction models, the same construction relates the evolution of expected observations to the master equation.

title: 34  Koopman Theory, EDMD, and Continuous Generators
text:
34.2 Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) and EDMD
Suppose a scalar state is observed in pairs \((x_m,y_m)\). Fitting one multiplier asks for \(\min_a\sum_m(y_m-ax_m)^2\). Provided not all \(x_m\) vanish, the answer is \(a=\sum_mx_my_m/\sum_mx_m^2\). DMD applies this least-squares calculation to vectors, placing each observation in a column. This orientation differs from PCA, where observations were rows.






NoteDefinition: Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD)



Given snapshot matrices \(\bX, \bY \in \fR^{n \times M}\) where \(\bY\) advances \(\bX\) by time step \(h\): \[
\begin{align}
\bX = [\bx_1, \bx_2, ..., \bx_M], \qquad \bY = [\by_1, \by_2, ..., \by_M], \qquad \by_m = \mathbf{F}(\bx_m),
\end{align}
\] DMD seeks the best-fit linear map \(\bA \approx \bY \bX^\dagger\) in the Frobenius norm.
To compute the reduced model:

Compute the rank-\(r\) truncated SVD \(\bX \approx \bU_r \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_r \bV_r^T\).
Project onto the span of the retained left singular vectors (often called the proper orthogonal decomposition, or POD, subspace): \(\widetilde{\bA} = \bU_r^T \bY \bV_r \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_r^{-1} \in \fR^{r \times r}\).
Compute eigendecomposition \(\widetilde{\bA} \bw_i = \mu_i \bw_i\).
The DMD modes are \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_i = \bY \bV_r \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_r^{-1} \bw_i\).









NoteProposition: DMD as a Least-Squares Fit



The minimum-Frobenius-norm solution of \[
\begin{align}
\min_{\bA}\|\bY-\bA\bX\|_F
\end{align}
\] is \(\bA_*=\bY\bX^\dagger\). If \(\bX=\bU_r\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_r\bV_r^T\) is a rank-\(r\) SVD, the representation of this map on \(\mathcal{R}(\bU_r)\) is \[
\begin{align}
\widetilde{\bA}=\bU_r^T\bA_*\bU_r
    =\bU_r^T\bY\bV_r\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_r^{-1}.
\end{align}
\]








TipProof





Let row \(i\) of \(\bA\) be \(\ba_i^T\) and row \(i\) of \(\bY\) be \(\by_i^T\). The squared Frobenius residual is \[
\begin{align}
\|\bY-\bA\bX\|_F^2
=\sum_i\|\by_i^T-\ba_i^T\bX\|_2^2
=\sum_i\|\by_i-\bX^T\ba_i\|_2^2.
\end{align}
\] Different rows of \(\bA\) appear in different summands. Hence we may minimize each summand independently. The pseudoinverse least-squares theorem gives its unique minimum-norm solution \[
\begin{align}
\ba_i=(\bX^T)^\dagger\by_i=(\bX^\dagger)^T\by_i.
\end{align}
\] Transposing back and collecting the rows gives \(\bA_*=\bY\bX^\dagger\). Among all residual minimizers, the squared Frobenius norm is \(\sum_i\|\ba_i\|_2^2\). Choosing the minimum norm independently in every row therefore gives the minimum-Frobenius-norm matrix.
For a rank-\(r\) SVD, \(\bX^\dagger=\bV_r\boldsymbol\Sigma_r^{-1}\bU_r^T\). Its diagonal inverse is defined because the retained singular values are positive. Substitute into the reduced representation: \[
\begin{align}
\bU_r^T\bA_*\bU_r
&=\bU_r^T\bY\bV_r\boldsymbol\Sigma_r^{-1}\bU_r^T\bU_r\\
&=\bU_r^T\bY\bV_r\boldsymbol\Sigma_r^{-1}.
\end{align}
\] The last equality uses the orthonormal columns of \(\bU_r\). This proves the reduced formula as well as the least-squares assertion.









NoteDefinition: Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (EDMD)



Extended DMD (Williams et al. 2015) generalizes DMD by lifting state data through a dictionary of nonlinear observables \(\boldsymbol{\psi}(\bx) = (\psi_1(\bx), ..., \psi_K(\bx))^T \in \fR^K\).
Form data matrices \[
\begin{align}
\boldsymbol{\Psi}_X = [\boldsymbol{\psi}(\bx_1), ..., \boldsymbol{\psi}(\bx_M)] \in \fR^{K \times M}, \qquad
    \boldsymbol{\Psi}_Y = [\boldsymbol{\psi}(\by_1), ..., \boldsymbol{\psi}(\by_M)] \in \fR^{K \times M}.
\end{align}
\] The finite-dimensional representation \(\widehat{\bK}_h \in \fR^{K \times K}\) of the Koopman operator minimizes \(\|\boldsymbol{\Psi}_Y - \bK \boldsymbol{\Psi}_X\|_F^2\): \[
\begin{align}
\widehat{\bK}_h = \boldsymbol{\Psi}_Y \boldsymbol{\Psi}_X^\dagger = (\boldsymbol{\Psi}_Y \boldsymbol{\Psi}_X^T)(\boldsymbol{\Psi}_X \boldsymbol{\Psi}_X^T)^\dagger.
\end{align}
\] Left eigenvectors of \(\widehat{\bK}_h\) yield approximations to Koopman eigenfunctions.








WarningExercise



Let a row vector \(\bw^T\) satisfy \(\bw^T\widehat{\bK}_h=\mu\bw^T\) and define \(g(\bx)=\bw^T\boldsymbol\psi(\bx)\). If the fitted relation \(\boldsymbol\psi(F(\bx))=\widehat{\bK}_h\boldsymbol\psi(\bx)\) were exact, prove \(g(F(\bx))=\mu g(\bx)\). With a nonzero fit residual, express the error in this identity. Why does a small training residual not guarantee the identity at unobserved states?








TipRemark



(EDMD as a Galerkin method) When the dictionary consists of the coordinate functions, \(\boldsymbol{\psi}(\bx)=\bx\), the data matrices reduce to \(\bX\) and \(\bY\), and EDMD reduces to the least-squares map of the referenced result. For a richer dictionary, the matrices \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}_Y\boldsymbol{\Psi}_X^T/M\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}_X\boldsymbol{\Psi}_X^T/M\) are sample averages of inner products between dictionary functions. As the number of samples drawn from a measure \(\mu\) grows, they converge to the corresponding inner-product matrices in \(L^2(\mu)\), and \(\widehat{\bK}_h\) converges to the Galerkin projection of the Koopman operator onto the span of the dictionary (Williams et al. 2015). Enlarging the dictionary therefore raises a separate approximation question, namely how well that span represents the Koopman eigenfunctions of interest.

section: 34.3 CME Koopman Generator and Polynomial Closure
text:
34.3 CME Koopman Generator and Polynomial Closure






TipRemark



(Koopman generator for continuous Markov jump processes) For a continuous-time Markov process with master equation \(\dot{\bp}(t) = \bA(\bc) \bp(t)\), the expectation of an observable \(g(\bx)\) evolves according to \(\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}[g(\bx(t))] = \frac{d}{dt} \sum_{\bx} g(\bx) p(\bx, t) = \sum_{\bx} g(\bx) [\bA(\bc)\bp(t)]_{\bx} = \sum_{\bx} [\bA(\bc)^T g](\bx) p(\bx, t)\). The Koopman infinitesimal generator \(\mathcal{A}\) is the formal adjoint of the master operator: \(\mathcal{A} = \bA(\bc)^T\).








NoteDefinition: CME Koopman Generator



For a chemical reaction network with stoichiometry \(\bnu_k\) and propensities \(\alpha_k(\bx; \bc) = c_k h_k(\bx)\), the Koopman generator acts on observable \(g\) by \[
\begin{align}
(\mathcal{A}g)(\bx) = \sum_{k=1}^R \alpha_k(\bx; \bc) \Big( g(\bx + \bnu_k) - g(\bx) \Big).
\end{align}
\]


The generator contains a difference \(g(\bx+\bnu)-g(\bx)\), so it can reduce polynomial degree before multiplication by the propensity raises it. For instance, if \(g(x)=x^2\), then \((x+1)^2-x^2=2x+1\). Multiplying by a constant or linear propensity leaves degree at most two. A quadratic propensity can produce degree three. This degree count determines whether finitely many moments form a closed system.






NoteTheorem: Polynomial Closure in Chemical Kinetics



Under mass-action kinetics, propensity functions are falling factorial polynomials: \[
\begin{align}
h_k(\bx) = \prod_{s=1}^S x_s^{(\nu_{ks}^-)}, \qquad x_s^{(m)} = x_s(x_s - 1)\cdots(x_s - m + 1).
\end{align}
\] Let \(\mathcal{P}_d\) denote the space of polynomials in \(\bx\) of degree at most \(d\).

Unimolecular networks: If all reactions have reactant order at most 1 (including immigration, conversion, and first-order degradation), then \(\mathcal{A}\mathcal{P}_d \subseteq \mathcal{P}_d\) for all \(d \geq 0\). The subspace \(\mathcal{P}_d\) is invariant under \(\mathcal{A}\), yielding exact finite-dimensional closure.
Bimolecular networks: For reactions of reactant order at most 2, \(\mathcal{A}\mathcal{P}_d \subseteq \mathcal{P}_{d+1}\). A quadratic propensity can produce degree-\((d+1)\) terms, so the moment equations generally fail to close at degree \(d\) unless additional cancellations, conservation laws, or invariant subspaces are present.









TipProof





If \(d=0\), every observable in the space is constant, so every difference \(g(\bx+\bnu_k)-g(\bx)\) is zero. Its image is the zero polynomial and both closure assertions hold. We may therefore assume \(d\geq1\) in the degree calculation below.
Let \(g \in \mathcal{P}_d\) be a polynomial of degree \(d\). For each stoichiometric change vector \(\bnu_k\), the discrete difference operator expands via Taylor’s formula on polynomials: \[
\begin{align}
g(\bx + \bnu_k) - g(\bx) = \sum_{j=1}^d \frac{1}{j!} (\bnu_k \cdot \nabla)^j g(\bx).
\end{align}
\] Because differentiation reduces polynomial degree by at least one, each term in the sum has degree at most \(d - 1\), so \(g(\bx + \bnu_k) - g(\bx) \in \mathcal{P}_{d-1}\). Applying the Koopman generator (the referenced result): \[
\begin{align}
(\mathcal{A}g)(\bx) = \sum_{k=1}^R \alpha_k(\bx; \bc) \big( g(\bx + \bnu_k) - g(\bx) \big).
\end{align}
\] For unimolecular reactions, each propensity \(\alpha_k(\bx; \bc)\) has reactant order at most 1, so \(\alpha_k \in \mathcal{P}_1\). The product of a degree-1 polynomial and a degree-\((d-1)\) polynomial has degree at most \(1 + (d - 1) = d\), proving \(\mathcal{A}\mathcal{P}_d \subseteq \mathcal{P}_d\). For bimolecular reactions, reactant order is at most 2, so \(\alpha_k \in \mathcal{P}_2\). The product has degree at most \(2 + (d - 1) = d + 1\), giving \(\mathcal{A}\mathcal{P}_d \subseteq \mathcal{P}_{d+1}\).
The notation \(\mathcal A\mathcal P_d\subseteq\mathcal P_d\) means that applying the generator to any member of this finite-dimensional polynomial space produces another member of the same space. Choosing a basis then gives a matrix for its action, so the corresponding expectations form a closed linear system. For the quadratic-propensity case, the inclusion in \(\mathcal P_{d+1}\) only bounds the possible degree. It does not assert that a degree-\(d+1\) term occurs for every polynomial or every network.









WarningExercise



(Bimolecular moment hierarchy) Consider the dimerization reaction \(2A \xrightarrow{c} B\). The stoichiometry is \(\bnu = (-2, 1)^T\) and the propensity is \(\alpha(x) = c x(x-1)/2\).

Compute \((\mathcal{A}g)(x)\) for \(g(x) = x\). Show that the result is quadratic in \(x\).
Explain why computing the time derivative of the mean \(\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}[x]\) requires knowledge of the second moment \(\mathbb{E}[x^2]\).

34.5 Further Exercises






WarningExercise



(DMD residual) Compute \(\bA_*=\bY\bX^\dagger\) for a rank-one snapshot matrix and verify directly that the residual \(\bY-\bA_*\bX\) is orthogonal to the row space of \(\bX\), as predicted by the referenced result.








WarningExercise



(Polynomial closure in unimolecular reaction networks) Consider the reversible isomerization network \(A \underset{c_2}{\overset{c_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} B\). Let \(x_1, x_2\) denote the copy numbers of species \(A\) and \(B\).

Write down the propensities \(\alpha_1(\bx) = c_1 x_1\) and \(\alpha_2(\bx) = c_2 x_2\), and the stoichiometry vectors \(\bnu_1 = (-1, 1)^T\) and \(\bnu_2 = (1, -1)^T\).
Apply the Koopman generator \(\mathcal{A}\) to the linear observable \(g(\bx) = x_1\). Show that \((\mathcal{A}g)(\bx) = -c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2\), which is strictly linear.
Apply \(\mathcal{A}\) to the second-order observable \(g(\bx) = x_1^2\). Show that \((\mathcal{A}g)(\bx)\) contains only polynomials of degree at most 2.
Explain why the subspace of polynomials of degree at most \(d\) is invariant under \(\mathcal{A}\) for any unimolecular network.









WarningExercise



(Sensitivity of recovered decay rates) Suppose a continuous dynamical system has decay rates \(\lambda_1 = -1\) and \(\lambda_2 = -50\). Data snapshots are collected at sampling interval \(h = 0.1\).

Compute the true discrete eigenvalues \(\mu_1 = \exp(h\lambda_1)\) and \(\mu_2 = \exp(h\lambda_2)\).
Suppose statistical noise perturbs the discrete estimates by \(\Delta \mu = 10^{-3}\). Compute the resulting perturbation \(\Delta \lambda_1 \approx \frac{\Delta \mu}{h \mu_1}\).
Compute the resulting perturbation \(\Delta \lambda_2 \approx \frac{\Delta \mu}{h \mu_2}\).
Explain why recovering continuous generators from discrete snapshots may benefit from regularized regression. Explain why regularization cannot recover a fast mode that the sampling interval has suppressed below the noise level.









NoteFurther reading



Koopman’s original paper gives the operator viewpoint for Hamiltonian systems (Koopman 1931). Schmid introduces dynamic mode decomposition in its fluid-mechanics form, and Williams, Kevrekidis, and Rowley connect a dictionary-based extension to the Koopman operator (Schmid 2010; Williams et al. 2015).






Koopman, Bernard O. 1931. “Hamiltonian Systems and Transformation in Hilbert Space.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 17 (5): 315–18. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.17.5.315.


Schmid, Peter J. 2010. “Dynamic Mode Decomposition of Numerical and Experimental Data.” Journal of Fluid Mechanics 656: 5–28. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112010001217.


Williams, Matthew O., Ioannis G. Kevrekidis, and Clarence W. Rowley. 2015. “A Data-Driven Approximation of the Koopman Operator: Extending Dynamic Mode Decomposition.” Journal of Nonlinear Science 25 (6): 1307–46. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00332-015-9258-5.

35.1 Logic and Set Notation
This section establishes the logical, set-theoretic, and matrix notation used throughout these notes, together with the standard proof structures.
crumbs: 35  Mathematical Notation and Proof Techniques

title: 35  Mathematical Notation and Proof Techniques
text:
NoteDefinition: Logical Quantifiers




Universal (\(\forall\)): ``For all.’’
Existential (\(\exists\)): ``There exists.’’
Example: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\;\exists \delta > 0$'' reads asfor every positive \(\varepsilon\) there is a positive \(\delta\).’’









WarningExercise



Compare for every real $x$ there exists a real $y$ with $y>x$'' withthere exists a real \(y\) such that \(y>x\) for every real \(x\).’’ Which statement is true? Explain why reversing the quantifiers changes the assertion. In an error estimate, what changes if its constant is allowed to depend on the problem size?








NoteDefinition: Implication and Equivalence




Implication (\(P \Rightarrow Q\)): \(P\) implies \(Q\).
Equivalence (\(P \Leftrightarrow Q\)): \(P\) if and only if \(Q\) (iff).
Contrapositive: \(\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P\). Logically equivalent to \(P \Rightarrow Q\).









WarningExercise



For a square matrix, compare the statements if $\bA$ is invertible, then $\bA\bx=\bb$ has a solution'' andif \(\bA\bx=\bb\) has a solution, then \(\bA\) is invertible.’’ Give a counterexample to the second statement for one right-hand side. How must the solvability statement be strengthened to become equivalent to invertibility?








NoteDefinition: Set Notation




\(x \in S\): \(x\) is an element of \(S\).
\(S \subseteq T\): \(S\) is a subset of \(T\).
\(S \cup T\) (union), \(S \cap T\) (intersection), and \(S \setminus T\) (set difference).
\(\{x \in S : P(x)\}\): Set builder notation.
Number Sets: \(\fZ\) (integers), \(\fR\) (reals), \(\fC\) (complex), \(\fR^n\) (vectors), \(\fR^{m \times n}\) (matrices).









WarningExercise




Write ``every invertible matrix has a nonzero determinant’’ using quantifiers and implication.
State the contrapositive of: ``if \(\bA\) is invertible, then \(\bA\bx = \bzero \Rightarrow \bx = \bzero\).’’
Let \(S = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) and \(T = \{3, 4, 5, 6\}\). Compute \(S \cup T, S \cap T, S \setminus T\).

title: 35  Mathematical Notation and Proof Techniques
text:
35.2 Proof Techniques






NoteDefinition: Direct Proof



Assume \(P\) is true and derive \(Q\) through a chain of valid logical steps.








NoteDefinition: Proof by Contradiction



Assume \(\neg P\) and derive a logical contradiction (\(R \wedge \neg R\)). Proves \(P\) must hold.








NoteDefinition: Proof by Induction



To prove \(P(n)\) holds for all integers \(n \geq n_0\):

Base case: Verify \(P(n_0)\) directly.
Inductive step: Assume \(P(k)\) and prove \(P(k+1)\).









TipRemark



(Proof and numerical evidence) A proof establishes a claim for every input satisfying its hypotheses. A finite experiment can test an implementation or expose a counterexample, but agreement on a sample does not prove a universal claim. In an error bound, state the norm, the limiting parameter, and which quantities the constant may depend on.








WarningExercise




Prove: if \(\bA\) and \(\bB\) are symmetric, then \(\bA + \bB\) is symmetric.
Prove by contradiction: if \(\bA\bx = \bzero \Rightarrow \bx = \bzero\), then \(\bA\) has no zero eigenvalue.
By induction, prove \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\).

title: 35  Mathematical Notation and Proof Techniques
text:
35.3 Notation Conventions






TipRemark



(Scalars, Vectors, and Matrices)

Scalars: Lowercase italic (\(a, b, x\)).
Vectors: Lowercase bold (\(\bx, \by, \ba\)). Default is column vector.
Matrices: Uppercase bold (\(\bA, \bB, \bQ\)).
Indexing: Usually begins at one, unlike Python. The Fourier sections explicitly begin at zero. Here \(x_i\) denotes a vector entry and \(a_{ij}\) a matrix entry.









TipRemark



(Transpose and Inverse)

\(\bA^T\): Transpose. The notation \(\bA^*\) denotes the conjugate transpose, which agrees with \(\bA^T\) for real entries.
\(\bA^{-1}\): Matrix inverse (square, nonsingular matrices).
\(\bA^{-T}\): Transpose of the inverse \((\bA^{-1})^T\).
\(\bA^k\): \(k\)-th power. \(\bA^0 = \bI\).









TipRemark



(Sums and Products) \[
\begin{align}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i = a_1 + ... + a_n, \qquad
  \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_i = a_1 ... a_n.
\end{align}
\]








TipRemark



(Functions)

\(f : \fR^n \to \fR^m\): Maps \(n\)-vectors to \(m\)-vectors.
\(f \circ g\): Function composition \((f \circ g)(\bx) = f(g(\bx))\).









TipRemark



(Asymptotic Notation) Scaling of algorithms is described using Big-O notation (\(O(n^2), O(n^3)\)). Details in the Computational Complexity section.

title: 36  Python and NumPy Primer
text:
36.1 Arrays and Basic Operations
This section summarizes the NumPy array conventions, linear-algebra operations, and indexing idioms used throughout the computational examples in these notes.

title: 36  Python and NumPy Primer
text:
NoteDefinition: NumPy Arrays



The ndarray is the fundamental structure.

Creation: np.array([1, 2]), np.zeros((m, n)), np.random.randn(m, n).
Indexing: 0-indexed. A[i, j] for entries, A[i, :] for rows, and A[:, j] for columns.









TipRemark



(Shapes and one-dimensional arrays) A.shape returns (m, n). A 1D array has shape (n,), which is not equivalent to a column vector (n, 1). These one-dimensional arrays can behave differently from column arrays under broadcasting. Use x[:, None] or x.reshape(-1, 1) to convert to 2D.








WarningExercise




Create \(4 \times 4\) identity matrix. Verify shape and dtype.
Extract row 2 and column 3 from a random \(3 \times 3\) \(\bA\).
Compare A @ x for x.shape == (3,) and x.shape == (3,1). Record the output shape in each case, then explain why the two representations behave differently under broadcasting.

title: 36  Python and NumPy Primer
text:
36.2 Linear Algebra Operations
The core routines in numpy.linalg provide access to standard BLAS and LAPACK implementations:






TipRemark



(Vectorization and performance) Explicit for loops in Python are slow. Push heavy lifting into NumPy/BLAS routines by vectorizing operations. For example, use A @ B instead of triple-nested loops.








TipRemark



(Linear solve versus inversion) np.linalg.solve(A, b) is faster and more stable than np.linalg.inv(A) @ b. Explicit inversion is almost never desirable in scientific computation.








TipRemark



(Computed equality) For computed floating-point quantities, compare the error with a tolerance appropriate to their scale. Functions such as np.allclose and np.isclose perform tolerance tests. Their default tolerances do not establish mathematical equality or certify accuracy for every problem. Exact equality is appropriate for integers, booleans, and deliberately exact structural checks.








TipRemark



(Sparse matrices) Large discretized PDE and graph problems should usually use scipy.sparse, not dense NumPy arrays. Use scipy.sparse.linalg for sparse solves, eigenvalue computations, CG, and GMRES.








WarningExercise




Solve a \(2 \times 2\) system and verify the residual \(\|\bA\bx - \bb\|\).
Profile solve vs inv @ b for \(n=1000\).
Compare np.linalg.eig and np.linalg.eigh (optimized for symmetric matrices).









WarningExercise



For a \(3\times3\) matrix, form an approximation x with shape (3,1) and a right-hand side b with shape (3,). Predict the shape of b - A @ x before evaluating it. Explain why that array is not the residual vector you intended. Make the shapes consistent and recompute the residual.

title: 36  Python and NumPy Primer
text:
36.3 Key Idioms

Element-wise: * and ** are entry-wise. Matrix powers use np.linalg.matrix\_power.
Broadcasting: Automatic dimension expansion. For A.shape == (m,n) and v.shape == (n,), A * v scales columns by the entries of v. To scale rows by a vector of length m, use A * v[:,None].
Aliases, Views, Copies: B = A makes a second name for the same array. Slices are usually views. Use B = A.copy() for independent data.
Sparse construction: The scipy.sparse module provides diags for banded matrices and csr\_matrix for compressed sparse row storage.







WarningExercise




Let \(\bA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\). Compare A * A and A @ A.
Demonstrate the ``view pitfall’’ by modifying a slice of a matrix.
Use broadcasting to perform diagonal scaling \(\bA\bD\) without constructing \(\bD = \text{diag}(d)\).









NoteFurther reading



Heath gives a broad introduction to scientific computing at roughly the level of these notes (Heath 2018). For the effects of floating-point arithmetic, Higham is the standard detailed reference (Higham 2002). Meyer provides an accessible bridge from undergraduate linear algebra to matrix computation (Meyer 2000).

Higham, Nicholas J. 2002. Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms. 2nd ed. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718027.


Meyer, Carl D. 2000. Matrix Analysis and Applied Linear Algebra. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898719512.
